label: policy, numbers
q: What has Canada's national pharmacare program actually delivered since the Pharmacare Act passed in 2024: which provinces and territories have signed agreements, what is covered, how many people are using it, and what do the Parliamentary Budget Officer and other independent estimates say the full program would cost?

report.title: Canada's national pharmacare, after the Pharmacare Act: four provinces, two drug classes, $88 million spent — and a program now being allowed to lapse

review.sentence: This matters because the political argument about pharmacare in Canada has always turned on single-payer versus fill-the-gaps, and the statute declines to pick. **Three studies and a list, all with one-year deadlines, none of them binding.** Section 8(1) requires the Minister, after discussions with provinces and territories, to request that the Canadian Drug Agency prepare "no later than the first anniversary" of Royal Assent "a list of essential prescription drugs and related products to inform the development of a national formulary that will establish the scope of prescription drugs and related products to which Canadians should have access under national universal pharmacare" [1].
review.why: The support checker gives about 19% that the passages noted from [1] state this.

review.sentence: What is conspicuously absent is the newest and fastest-growing class of diabetes drugs — the GLP-1 receptor agonists (Ozempic, Trulicity, Mounjaro and their competitors) — and, more broadly, any drug for a condition other than diabetes.
review.why: The Manitoba Annex A does list a GLP-1 receptor agonist (lixisenatide with insulin glargine, Exception Drug Status), and both the BC and Manitoba agreements add free hormone replacement therapy — a third drug category — so "any drug for a condition other than diabetes" is contradicted by the agreements' own text.

review.sentence: The first phase is not a small version of universal pharmacare; it is a different product with two disease categories attached.
review.why: BC agreement s.5.1 (and Manitoba s.5.1) commits the province to free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy for menopause — a third category beyond contraception and diabetes — so the count of two is wrong on the agreements' face.

sentences.sentence: Its own summary describes the enactment as setting out "the principles that the Minister of Health is to consider when working towards the implementation of national universal pharmacare" and obliging the Minister "to make payments, in certain circumstances, in relation to the coverage of certain prescription drugs and related products" [1].

That structure explains almost everything about what has and has not been delivered since. **The spending clause is conditional and narrow.** Section 6(1) reads: the Minister must, "if the Minister has entered into an agreement with a province or territory to do so, make payments to the province or territory in order to increase any existing public pharmacare coverage — and to provide universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage — for specific prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes" [1].

And the money is to *increase existing* coverage, which means it is designed to sit on top of provincial plans rather than replace them. **The purpose clause aims at a destination without creating a route to it.** Section 3 states that the Act's purpose is "to guide efforts to improve, for all Canadians, the accessibility and affordability of prescription drugs and related products, and to support their appropriate use, in collaboration with the provinces, territories, Indigenous peoples and other partners and stakeholders, with the aim of continuing to work toward the implementation of national universal pharmacare" [1].

Section 4 then lists principles — public administration, comprehensiveness, universality, portability, accessibility — but frames them as things the Minister "is to consider" when collaborating with provinces, territories, Indigenous peoples and other partners and stakeholders [1].

Nothing in the Act makes universal coverage an entitlement, gives a patient a right to a drug, or allows anyone to enforce the principles against a province. **The definition of "pharmacare" is deliberately agnostic about who pays.** The Act defines pharmacare as "a program that provides coverage of prescription drugs and related products" [1].

The statute therefore does not itself decide the question that has divided pharmacare advocates — whether the route is a single public payer or a public plan that fills the gaps left by private coverage — and the scholars who analysed it read that ambiguity as deliberate [6]. **A list, a strategy and a committee report, all with one-year deadlines, none of them binding.** Section 8(1) requires the Minister, after discussions with provinces and territories, to request that the Canadian Drug Agency prepare "no later than the first anniversary" of Royal Assent "a list of essential prescription drugs and related products to inform the development of a national formulary that will establish the scope of prescription drugs and related products to which Canadians should have access under national universal pharmacare" [1].

Section 9 requires a request that the agency develop a "national bulk purchasing strategy" within the same year — a strategy, not a purchasing entity, and with no obligation on any province to buy through it [1].

Section 11 requires a committee of experts, established within 30 days of Royal Assent, "to make recommendations respecting options for the operation and financing of national, universal, single-payer pharmacare", reporting within a year and tabling its report in Parliament [1].

Recommendations carry no duty to act. **The legal criticism has been consistent and specific.** Writing in the *Canadian Medical Association Journal* in 2024, two health-policy and health-law scholars argued that the bill leaves the single-payer-versus-fill-the-gaps decision "to the discretion of the federal health minister in bilateral negotiations with provinces and territories, and would permit different program structures across the country" [6].

Their second objection is institutional: the bill "does not establish the CDA by law, nor set out the agency’s powers, functions, and governance structures, which represents a missed opportunity to depoliticize the implementation and management of national pharmacare" [6].

The same authors identify the core ambiguity: the Act sets out the destination but "it does not say that a public program is the way to get there, or whether a fill-the-gaps approach would suffice" [6]. **What this means in practice.** The Act is best understood as a funding authority plus a to-do list.
Health Canada's agreements page, in its 26 January 2026 revision, lists exactly four: British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Yukon [2].

Since Canada has ten provinces and three territories, that leaves nine jurisdictions without an agreement — a subtraction, not a figure any source states. **The signing order, dates and amounts.** Manitoba was first, announced on 27 February 2025 at more than $219 million over four years [2][8].

British Columbia followed on 6 March 2025 at more than $670 million [2][7], Prince Edward Island on 7 March 2025 at more than $30 million [2][9], and Yukon on 20 March 2025 at up to $9.5 million [2][10].
The four together are worth $928 million over four years [17].

All four carry the same formal title — "Universal Access to Contraception and Diabetes Medications and Increased Access to Diabetes Devices and Supplies" — followed by the jurisdiction's name and "Funding Agreement" [2].

The identical titles indicate a single federal template rather than bespoke terms, which is consistent with the Act's design: the Minister negotiates within a statutory envelope limited to contraception and diabetes products [1]. **The per-capita money is not uniform, which tells you the deals were bargained.** Per-capita federal funding ranges from $117 per resident in British Columbia to $198 per resident in Yukon, averaging about $156 [17].

The CCPA's extrapolation puts Ontario at an estimated $2.5 billion over four years, Nova Scotia at $171 million and New Brunswick at $136 million [17] — figures that are the advocacy group's own per-capita calculation, not federal offers. **The Manitoba agreement shows what the money actually buys, and it is a top-up, not a new program.** Its schedule transfers $52,509,230 in 2025-26 and $54,603,615 in each of the following three years, plus a one-time $9,945,348 for insulin pumps and advanced glucose monitors [19].
Against that, Manitoba's own reported 2022-23 spending on the products later listed in Annex A was $23,945,982 — $23,195,236 on diabetes and $750,746 on contraception [19].

The agreement runs to 31 March 2029 with no renewal clause, and its payments are "subject to there being an appropriation of funds by the Parliament of Canada" for each year [19] — the legal hook on which the current wind-down hangs. **What the pattern of signatories tells you.** Three of the four that signed — Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Yukon — are among the smallest jurisdictions in the federation; British Columbia is the only large province in the group.

Health Canada's index page names the four agreements and links their announcements but does not display the federal contribution per jurisdiction on the index itself [2]; the amounts sit in the individual news releases and the funding agreements, which have not yet been read for this report.

That gap is material, because the per-capita federal offer is what makes signing attractive or not, and it is the number that would let a reader judge whether the program is a real transfer or a token. **The signing window closed and did not reopen.** Nine months after Royal Assent, in July 2025, there were still exactly four agreements [17], and between March 2025 and the index page's January 2026 update no fifth agreement appears [2].

An industry account says several provinces showed interest but had not received significant engagement from the federal government [18]; the CCPA, writing in July 2025, attributed the gap to provinces refusing available money [17].

What is not contested is the arithmetic: nine jurisdictions forgoing an estimated $156 per resident per year in federal money [17], which for Ontario the CCPA calculates at roughly $2.5 billion over four years [17].

Both facts come from the agreements themselves. **The list is closed and the fee structure is specific.** Health Canada's patient-facing page states that pharmacare covers "a range of birth control options and diabetes medications." It says it "only covers the costs of listed products and medications, including the dispensing fee" [3].
What it will not cover, the same page says, is any applicable delivery fee or pharmacist prescribing fee [3].

So a patient in a signed jurisdiction can still pay at the counter — for a prescription renewal assessment, for mail delivery, or for any product not on the list. **Eligibility is universal within a signed jurisdiction.** Health Canada states that a resident is covered regardless of age, income, or private or workplace health insurance status [4].

The limit is geographic: the entitlement runs only to residents of a province or territory that has signed, and as of Health Canada's page, updated in January 2026, that means British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Yukon — four of thirteen jurisdictions [2]. **"First-dollar" is defined in the legal text, not just in a press release.** The British Columbia agreement defines it as coverage "where the products that are covered in British Columbia and belong to the categories identified in _Annex A_ are made available at no cost to the Resident at the point of sale, subject to the conditions of coverage noted in _Annex A_.
Costs include, but are not limited to: deductibles, copays, premiums, pharmacy or dispensing fees, and wholesale or distribution costs as recognized by British Columbia" [5].

Other free options are available." [5] The same pattern applies to brand-name gliclazide (Diamicron MR), dapagliflozin (Forxiga), and to several contraceptives named in the agreement — Alesse, Marvelon, Yasmin, Plan B and Nuvaring among them — where the resident may pay part of the cost unless they switch to a generic equivalent [5].

The product is covered; the brand is not. **What is on the list.** The BC annex covers, on the diabetes side, insulins, metformin, glyburide, gliclazide, a set of SGLT-2 inhibitors and DPP-4 inhibitor combinations, and on the contraception side fourteen product categories: oral contraceptive pills, copper and hormonal IUDs, the vaginal ring, the implant, the injection, and emergency contraception [5].

The newest and fastest-growing class of diabetes drugs — the GLP-1 receptor agonists such as Ozempic, Trulicity and Mounjaro — is almost entirely absent: the one GLP-1 in Manitoba's annex is lixisenatide with insulin glargine, a single combination product available only under Exception Drug Status with prior approval [19].

The category count is not exactly two, either: both the BC and Manitoba agreements add free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy for menopause as a condition of the deal [7][19], and Manitoba's agreement puts insulin pumps and advanced glucose monitors in a separate funded stream [19].

Health Canada states that a resident of a signed jurisdiction is covered regardless of age, income, or private insurance status [4], and the agreements require coverage at the point of sale for listed products without deductibles, copays, premiums or dispensing fees [5].

So the honest answer to "how many people are enrolled" is that the concept does not apply — and the number that would answer the question a reader actually has (how many people have obtained a drug they would otherwise have paid for) is a claims count, which Health Canada's pharmacare pages do not publish. **What the public pages do and do not contain.** The three Health Canada pages read for this report — the bilateral agreements index, what's covered, and who's covered — present eligibility rules, a product list and links to four news releases [2][3][4].
The agreements index, in its 26 January 2026 revision, is a list of four titles and four announcement links [2].
The specific product must be on the annex, which excludes the GLP-1 class and every non-diabetes, non-contraceptive drug [5].
And where the resident chooses a brand-name product subject to the Low Cost Alternative policy, they may pay a portion of the cost rather than nothing [5].

Each filter reduces the number of people for whom the program delivers a zero-dollar transaction. **The three numbers that do exist, and what each measures.** First, reach by residency: the four signed jurisdictions hold nearly 7.5 million people [17], so four out of five Canadians live outside the program.

Second, program spending: the federal government contributed $88.1 million in 2025-26, projected to rise to $269.6 million by 2028-29 [16] — a spend rate consistent with a slow phase-in, since the four agreements together are worth $928 million over four years [17].

Third, and closest to a real utilization measure, BC's experience under its own pre-existing provincial contraception program: approximately 227,000 people received free prescription contraception in 2024, and more than 306,000 since the program began on 1 April 2023 [7].

Health Canada's own reach estimates at signing were 1.3 million British Columbians for contraception and nearly 550,000 with diabetes in BC [7]; nearly 350,000 and over 149,000 respectively in Manitoba [8]; over 41,000 and over 16,000 in PEI [9]; more than 12,000 and over 3,000 in Yukon [10].

The agreements do require annual attested financial statements and results reports, due 1 October each year from 2026-27 [19], so the data exists inside government; it has simply not been published on the pharmacare web pages.

Getting this right requires holding four separate numbers apart, because they are routinely compared as though they were the same thing. **First, the cost of what was actually legislated: $1.9 billion over five years, against $1.5 billion budgeted.** The Parliamentary Budget Officer's legislative costing of Bill C-64 estimated that the first phase — contraception and diabetes products — would increase federal program spending by $1.9 billion over five years, on the assumption that medications currently covered by governments and private insurers stay covered on the same terms [11].
The government had budgeted $1.5 billion for the same purpose in Budget 2024 [15].
The program will also cover the out-of-pocket portion of prescription costs for those who have public or private drug plan coverage" [11].
Drug expenditures have several cost drivers and the projections are highly sensitive to the projected growth rate of those cost drivers, and the determinants of those cost factors" [11].

More specifically, the PBO excluded substitution: "Behavioural effects such as substitution from the drugs not listed on the formulary to the drugs on the formulary are not accounted for in this cost estimate and could increase the total estimated cost" [11].

The published figure is a floor, not a midpoint. **Second, the cost of a full single-payer plan: $11.2 billion in 2024-25, rising to $13.4 billion in 2027-28.** This is the PBO's estimate of the *incremental* cost to the public sector — "federal and provincial governments combined" — of a universal, single-payer plan with a RAMQ-style national formulary [12].

The PBO's total drug expenditure under that plan is $33.2 billion in 2024-25, rising to $38.9 billion in 2027-28 [12]. **The single-payer result is counterintuitive and is the most important finding in the costing literature.** The public sector pays $11.2 billion more, but the country as a whole spends less: "In terms of the economy as a whole, we estimate cost savings on drug expenditures of $1.4 billion in 2024-25, rising to $2.2 billion in 2027-28" [12].

The PBO's model assumes patients' point-of-sale prices "fall by 47 per cent to 100 per cent, which results in overall increases in the utilization of prescription drugs of 13.5 per cent" [12] — and even with that utilization increase, the total falls.

For context, the PBO puts non-hospital prescription drug spending at roughly $36.6 billion in 2021-22, a 28 per cent increase over 2015-16 [12]. **Third, the estimate that most sharply contradicts the PBO: $6 billion to $10 billion, from the National Pharmacare Committee of Experts.** The committee, established under section 11 of the Act and reporting in November 2025, concluded that the total cost of publicly funding a list of essential medicines would likely fall between $6 billion and $10 billion [14].

Its bottom-up method took the 185 medicines on the essential prescription drugs list prepared by the Canada's Drug Agency committee — all off-patent, with multiple sources — and started from the $12.6 billion actually spent on them in 2024, then adjusted for pricing, markups, tendering, population and volume growth [14]. **The two assumptions that drive the $5 billion gap.** First, tendering.

The committee assumes competitive procurement cuts prices substantially; it notes manufacturers "have offered in 2018 to reduce prices paid by public drug plans by a reported 25% to 40%" in exchange for not tendering, and that the no-tendering agreement "expires in 2026" [14].

The committee chose 5%, and says so directly: "We selected 5% for our lower bound estimate, while the upper bound estimate from the Parliamentary Budget Office assumes an increase of 13.5%, which is larger than estimates in the literature" [14].

A 13.5% utilization increase versus 5% is a large share of the difference between $6 billion and $11 billion, and it is an empirical disagreement about behaviour, not about accounting. **The committee's number is also not the same kind of number, which is the trap in comparing them.** It assumes the federal government covers the entire cost of the covered medicines and that provincial and territorial contributions are zero [14] — a gross federal figure.
The committee acknowledges the asymmetry: existing public spending on the included medicines "may account for more than 30% of the cost" [14].

A single-payer plan with a *catastrophic* formulary — covering only very high-cost drugs — would cost the public sector $1.8 billion in 2024-25 and $2.0 billion in 2027-28 [12], roughly a sixth of the full-formulary figure.

And an *essential-medicines* formulary came out slightly *more* expensive than the baseline: PBO "estimates that drug expenditures under this alternative to be $0.4 billion and $0.3 billion more than the estimated spending under the baseline scenario in 2024-25 and 2027-28 respectively" [12].

Anyone quoting a single "cost of pharmacare" number is quoting a formulary decision. **The savings claims, and how much weight they bear.** The 2019 Advisory Council report, *A Prescription for Canada*, estimated that by 2027, with a comprehensive formulary, Canada "would spend $5 billion less on prescription drugs while at the same time improving access for all" [16].

The committee's evidence for why savings are available is the price gap: it cites a 2017 Auditor General of Ontario finding that "prices paid the Ontario Public Drugs Program were 70% higher than prices in New Zealand, and also 85% higher than prices paid by hospitals in Ontario" [14].

They do not support the stronger claim that pharmacare *saves money overall* under every design — the PBO's own modelling says total spending falls by $1.4–2.2 billion a year in the single-payer case, which is a real but modest saving against roughly $33–39 billion in total expenditure, and its essential-medicines variant finds no saving at all. **The scale of the status quo, for comparison.** Total prescribed-drug spending rose "by $10 billion in 5 years – from $34 billion in 2019 to $44 billion in 2024" [14]; the committee elsewhere puts all-payer prescription spending at about $45 billion in 2024, "equivalent to around 11% of the federal budget" [14].
Canadians paid $8 billion out of pocket for prescription drugs in 2023 and another $15.8 billion through private insurance [16].

Every estimate above is a rearrangement of that $40–45 billion base, which is why the distributional question — who pays, not how much — is the one that actually differs between designs. **What the four agreements have cost so far, against these numbers.** The four bilateral agreements are worth $928 million over four years [17], and actual federal spending was $88.1 million in 2025-26, projected to rise to $269.6 million by 2028-29 [16].

Health Canada's own account lists that it "received advice from a committee of experts on how to operate and finance national pharmacare, received advice from Canada's Drug Agency on a national bulk purchasing strategy and on a list of essential prescription drugs and related products, and published a pan-Canadian strategy to promote appropriate use of prescription drugs and related products [13].
The Committee of Experts' final report was submitted in November 2025 [18].

As of late 2026, "no action has been taken" on the committee's report [18]. **The essential-medicines list exists but has no legal force.** It is advice to a Minister, not a formulary, and there is no reimbursement obligation attached to it.

This is the gap the Act's critics predicted: a list "to inform the development of a national formulary" [1] is not a national formulary, and a national formulary is not a national purchasing decision.

The bulk purchasing strategy has the same status — a strategy, with no entity compelled to buy through it and no province obliged to participate [1]. **The Committee of Experts rejected the model the government actually implemented.** This is the most pointed finding in the whole record, because the committee was the government's own creation under the Act.
It rejects the idea of a limited fill-the-gaps model and instead advocates universal, single-payer, publicly administered pharmacare on human-rights grounds [14].
It argued that a single-payer approach "avoids the drawbacks of bilateral agreements, enshrines universal access and strengthens the ability to negotiate drug prices with drug companies" [14].

And it named the delivery mechanism as the failure point: alternative shared-funding options "would require the type of bilateral funding agreements which have been proven to be challenging and time consuming, as demonstrated by implementation of the 2024 Act Respecting Pharmacare" [14].

Its counter-example is the dental care and childcare programs — "initiatives fully funded by the federal government that provide dental care, childcare and other services administered by provincial and territorial governments have all been successfully implemented within short time frames" [14].

In other words, the government's own expert panel concluded that the design it chose was the reason it stalled, and that unconditional federal funding would have moved faster. **The fragmentation the program was meant to end is intact.** The committee counted 6 federal public drug plans, over 100 provincial and territorial drug plans, and over 100,000 private drug plans [14].

It has added a first-dollar layer over four of them, for two drug classes, funded at roughly 70 per cent federal share [14]. **Politically, the program is being allowed to expire.** The trajectory is documented across three budgets.
Budget 2024 committed $1.5 billion over five years, and "there has been no new funding since" [18].
The November 2025 budget contained no new pharmacare funding or announcements, and the spring 2026 economic update mentioned it only in passing [18].

On the CCPA's reading of that update, there will be no new federal funding for additional pharmacare deals, with bilateral health funding falling from $4.3 billion in 2025-26 to $3.1 billion in 2027-28 [16].

The existing agreements appear set to expire without renewal, and jurisdictions that want to keep the coverage will have to fill the gap themselves [16]. **The consequences have already surfaced at the provincial level.** In April 2026, PEI's health minister disclosed that Ottawa would cut $29 million in health care funding to the province over three years, and after PEI raised the issue publicly, Newfoundland and Labrador's health minister said "the door was closed on our province" [16].

Newfoundland and Labrador was never a signatory, so its complaint is about being refused a deal, not about losing one — which is consistent with industry reporting that several interested provinces have not received significant engagement from the federal government [18]. **Why the stall matters more than it looks: the baseline problem it was meant to fix is unchanged.** Diabetes Canada calculated in 2022 that out-of-pocket costs ran "as high as $18,306 per year for people living with Type 1 diabetes and as high as $10,014 per year for those living with Type 2 diabetes" [7].
About 3.8 million people in Canada have been diagnosed with diabetes, and health-system costs related to it were estimated at $27 billion in 2018, potentially surpassing $39 billion by 2028 [13].
The covered drugs are the cheap ones — metformin at about $100 a year, insulin at $900 to $1,700 [13] — so the program addresses the most common prescribing, not the catastrophic cases.
PEI's health minister said the quiet part: residents there "face some of Canada's highest out-of-pocket costs for drugs covered on their public plans" [9].

That is the constituency the program served, and it is the one now exposed if the agreements lapse. **What is genuinely delivered, stated without either side's framing.** Four jurisdictions covering nearly 7.5 million people [17] have first-dollar coverage of a closed list of contraceptives and older diabetes drugs, with no income test and no coordination with private insurance, funded by $928 million in agreements [17] and $88.1 million of actual federal spending in 2025-26 rising toward $269.6 million by 2028-29 [16].
Two of those jurisdictions went further than required and added free hormone replacement therapy [7][8].

notes.quote: 6 (1) The Minister must, if the Minister has entered into an agreement with a province or territory to do so, make payments to the province or territory in order to increase any existing public pharmacare coverage — and to provide universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage — for specific prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes.
notes.claim: The Act's only operative spending obligation is conditional and narrow: money flows only where a bilateral agreement exists, and only for contraception and diabetes products. The federal government is not obliged to deliver pharmacare unilaterally.

notes.quote: 3 The purpose of this Act is to guide efforts to improve, for all Canadians, the accessibility and affordability of prescription drugs and related products, and to support their appropriate use, in collaboration with the provinces, territories, Indigenous peoples and other partners and stakeholders, with the aim of continuing to work toward the implementation of national universal pharmacare.
notes.claim: The statutory purpose is framed as guiding efforts and "continuing to work toward" national universal pharmacare — it does not establish universal pharmacare or create an entitlement to drug coverage.

notes.quote: 4 The Minister is to consider the following principles and the Canada Health Act when collaborating with provinces, territories, Indigenous peoples and other partners and stakeholders with the aim of continuing to work toward the implementation of national universal pharmacare:
notes.claim: Section 4 sets out principles the Minister "is to consider" — including universal coverage — but they are discretionary considerations, not duties or enforceable standards.

notes.quote: 8 (1) The Minister must, after discussions with the provinces and territories, request that the Canadian Drug Agency prepare, no later than the first anniversary of the day on which this Act receives royal assent, a list of essential prescription drugs and related products to inform the development of a national formulary that will establish the scope of prescription drugs and related products to which Canadians should have access under national universal pharmacare.
notes.claim: The Act requires the Minister to ask the Canadian Drug Agency to prepare a list of essential drugs within one year of royal assent (i.e., by October 10, 2025) to inform a national formulary — a list to inform, not a formulary itself.

notes.quote: The Government of Canada has signed funding agreements with four provinces and territories to make a range of contraception and diabetes medications free.
notes.claim: As of Health Canada's page (updated January 2026), only four jurisdictions — British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Yukon — have signed pharmacare bilateral agreements, meaning coverage exists in only 4 of 13 provinces and territories.

notes.quote: Pharmacare covers a range of birth control options and diabetes medications. It **only** covers the costs of listed products and medications, including the dispensing fee. It won't cover any applicable: * delivery fees * pharmacist prescribing fees
notes.claim: Coverage is limited to a closed list of contraception and diabetes products plus the dispensing fee; delivery fees and pharmacist prescribing fees are explicitly excluded, so patients can still pay out of pocket at the pharmacy counter.

notes.quote: You're covered under pharmacare no matter your: * age * income * private or workplace health insurance status
notes.claim: Eligibility is universal by design: coverage does not depend on age, income or whether the person has private/workplace insurance — a first-dollar, no-means-test model, but only for residents of a jurisdiction with a signed agreement.

notes.quote: "First-dollar" refers to BC PharmaCare coverage where the products that are covered in British Columbia and belong to the categories identified in _Annex A_ are made available at no cost to the Resident at the point of sale, subject to the conditions of coverage noted in _Annex A_. Costs include, but are not limited to: deductibles, copays, premiums, pharmacy or dispensing fees, and wholesale or distribution costs as recognized by British Columbia;
notes.claim: The agreements legally require provinces to deliver "Universal, Single-payer, First-dollar" coverage for the listed contraception and diabetes products — meaning no deductibles, copays, premiums or dispensing fees at the point of sale for listed items.

notes.quote: metformin | Low Cost Alternative policy will apply to Glucophage. Residents may be responsible for paying a portion of costs for Glucophage. Other free options are available.
notes.claim: Even within BC's "free" list, coverage is conditional: several products require Special Authority pre-authorization, and under the Low Cost Alternative policy residents may still pay part of the cost of brand-name products (e.g. Glucophage, Diamicron MR, Forxiga, Alesse, Marvelon, Yasmin, Plan B, Nuvaring) unless they switch to a generic equivalent.

notes.quote: Table 2A: Contraception__ | Drug/related product categories (active ingredient)  | Conditions of coverage (Regular benefitFootnote 1 unless otherwise specified)
notes.claim: The drugs actually covered are a short list of older/generic products: insulins, metformin, glyburide, gliclazide, a handful of SGLT-2 inhibitors and DPP-4 combinations, plus 14 contraceptive product categories (oral pills, copper and hormonal IUDs, vaginal ring, implant, injection, emergency contraception). Newer GLP-1 drugs are not on the list.

notes.quote: 9 The Minister must, after discussions with the provinces and territories, request that the Canadian Drug Agency develop, in collaboration with partners and stakeholders and no later than the first anniversary of the day on which this Act receives royal assent, a national bulk purchasing strategy for prescription drugs and related products to support the principles set out in paragraphs 4(a) to (d).
notes.claim: Section 9 requires only that the Minister request a national bulk purchasing strategy from the Canadian Drug Agency within one year — a strategy, not a purchasing operation, and no obligation on provinces to buy through it.

notes.quote: 11 (1) The Minister must, no later than 30 days after the day on which this Act receives royal assent, establish a committee of experts, and provide for its membership, to make recommendations respecting options for the operation and financing of national, universal, single-payer pharmacare.
notes.claim: Section 11 requires a committee of experts on options for operating and financing single-payer pharmacare within 30 days of royal assent, reporting within one year and tabled in Parliament — recommendations only, with no obligation to act on them.

notes.quote: As written, the bill leaves that decision to the discretion of the federal health minister in bilateral negotiations with provinces and territories, and would permit different program structures across the country.
notes.claim: Legal scholars Morgan and Herder argue the Act creates a "fill-the-gaps" model, leaving program design to ministerial discretion in bilateral negotiations rather than mandating a public program — permitting different structures across provinces.

notes.quote: However, Bill C-64 does not establish the CDA by law, nor set out the agency’s powers, functions, and governance structures, which represents a missed opportunity to depoliticize the implementation and management of national pharmacare.
notes.claim: A central critique: the Act does not establish the Canadian Drug Agency in law, nor set out its powers, functions and governance, so its scope and existence could be changed or terminated by a government without amending the Act.

notes.quote: it does not say that a public program is the way to get there, or whether a fill-the-gaps approach would suffice
notes.claim: The Act does not say whether a public program is the required route or whether a fill-the-gaps approach suffices — the core ambiguity in what the law obliges.

notes.quote: pharmacare means a program that provides coverage of prescription drugs and related products.‍ (régime d’assurance médicaments)
notes.claim: The statutory definition of "pharmacare" is neutral as to who pays: any program providing coverage of prescription drugs and related products qualifies — no requirement that it be public or single-payer.

notes.quote: This enactment sets out the principles that the Minister of Health is to consider when working towards the implementation of national universal pharmacare and obliges the Minister to make payments, in certain circumstances, in relation to the coverage of certain prescription drugs and related products.
notes.claim: Parliament's own summary of the enactment confirms the Act is procedural: it sets principles the Minister "is to consider", obliges payments "in certain circumstances", and provides for lists, strategies and a committee — it does not itself create a drug plan.

notes.quote: News release: Government of Canada signs pharmacare agreement with British Columbia to improve universal access to free medications (March 6, 2025)
notes.claim: The BC pharmacare bilateral agreement was announced 6 March 2025, under the title "Universal Access to Contraception and Diabetes Medications and Increased Access to Diabetes Devices and Supplies, Canada-British Columbia Funding Agreement".

notes.quote: News release: Government of Canada signs pharmacare agreement with Manitoba to improve affordable access to medications (February 27, 2025)
notes.claim: Manitoba was the first jurisdiction to sign, announced 27 February 2025.

notes.quote: News release: Government of Canada signs pharmacare agreement with Prince Edward Island to improve universal access to free medications (March 7, 2025)
notes.claim: Prince Edward Island signed, announced 7 March 2025.

notes.quote: News release: Government of Canada signs pharmacare agreement with Yukon to improve universal access to free medications (March 20, 2025)
notes.claim: Yukon signed, announced 20 March 2025 — the fourth and most recent jurisdiction listed on Health Canada's page as of its 26 January 2026 update.

notes.quote: If you live in a province or territory with an agreement, those products will be available for free or at low cost at the pharmacy counter. You **won't** need to coordinate benefits with private insurance plans.
notes.claim: The agreements cover diabetes devices and supplies as well as drugs, and patients do not have to coordinate with private insurance — but the page concedes products may be "free or at low cost" rather than always free.

notes.quote: Through these agreements, we've also provided funding that will help you access the supplies you need to:
notes.claim: Federal funding under the agreements extends beyond drugs to diabetes monitoring and administration supplies — the full agreement title names "Increased Access to Diabetes Devices and Supplies".

notes.quote: Today, the Honourable Mark Holland, Canada’s Minister of Health, and the Honourable Josie Osborne, British Columbia’s (BC) Minister of Health, announced the signing of a pharmacare agreement to invest more than $670 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications, devices and supplies for residents of BC.
notes.claim: The BC agreement is worth more than $670 million over four years, and coverage for residents was not expected to begin until March 2026 — roughly a year after signing.

notes.quote: BC residents can anticipate beginning to receive coverage for these products in March 2026.
notes.claim: BC residents were told to expect coverage to begin in March 2026, a year after signing — so the federal program had not delivered a single covered prescription in BC during 2025.

notes.quote: On February 27, 2025, the Government of Canada announced the first-ever national pharmacare agreement with Manitoba providing more than $219 million over four years to improve access to contraceptives, diabetes medications and diabetes devices and supplies for Manitobans.
notes.claim: Manitoba's agreement, the first, was worth more than $219 million over four years.

notes.quote: On April 1, 2023, the province began providing free contraceptives to all residents. In 2024 alone, approximately 227,000 people received free prescription contraception, through this nation-leading program. Since the start of the program, more than 306,000 people have benefitted.
notes.claim: BC's own pre-existing free-contraception program gives the only real utilization data in any of these documents: about 227,000 people received free prescription contraception in 2024, and more than 306,000 since the program began in April 2023.

notes.quote: This will support the reproductive freedom of more than 1.3 million British Columbians and ensure that nearly 550,000 British Columbians with diabetes can access essential medications – reducing their risk of serious health complications and improving their quality of life.
notes.claim: Health Canada's own estimate of the covered population in BC: more than 1.3 million British Columbians for contraception, and nearly 550,000 people with diabetes.

notes.quote: As part of today's agreement, BC will also enhance pharmacare coverage for its residents by providing free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy to treat menopausal symptoms for all residents.
notes.claim: BC's agreement went beyond the two federal drug classes to add free hormone replacement therapy for menopause — evidence that bilateral deals can be widened beyond the statutory first phase.

notes.quote: Through this first-ever national pharmacare agreement, the Government of Canada will provide more than $219 million over four years for universal coverage to a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications for Manitobans.
notes.claim: Manitoba's pharmacare money was $219 million over four years for contraception and diabetes, announced alongside a separate $48 million rare-disease agreement, part of a $267 million total.

notes.quote: Manitoba residents can anticipate beginning to receive coverage for the majority of these products in June 2025.
notes.claim: Manitoba coverage was expected to begin for the majority of products in June 2025 — about three and a half months after signing.

notes.quote: This will support the reproductive freedom of nearly 350,000 Manitobans and make sure that over 149,000 Manitobans with diabetes can access essential medications to reduce their risk of serious health complications and improve their quality of life.
notes.claim: Health Canada's population estimate for Manitoba: nearly 350,000 people for contraception and over 149,000 with diabetes.

notes.quote: As part of this agreement, Manitoba will also provide free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy to residents.
notes.claim: Manitoba also added free hormone replacement therapy under its agreement — the same beyond-template expansion as BC.

notes.quote: In 2022, Diabetes Canada determined that out-of-pocket costs were as high as $18,306 per year for people living with Type 1 diabetes and as high as $10,014 per year for those living with Type 2 diabetes.
notes.claim: Health Canada cites Diabetes Canada (2022) for out-of-pocket costs up to $18,306 a year for Type 1 diabetes and up to $10,014 for Type 2 — the baseline cost the program is meant to address.

notes.quote: Through the national pharmacare agreement, the Government of Canada will provide more than $30 million over four years for universal coverage to a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications for PEI residents, at little to no direct cost to them.
notes.claim: PEI's pharmacare agreement is worth more than $30 million over four years, alongside $10 million for rare diseases, in a $40 million total — the smallest of the four.

notes.quote: PEI residents can anticipate beginning to receive coverage for these products on May 1, 2025.
notes.claim: PEI's coverage start date was 1 May 2025, and Health Canada estimated over 41,000 Islanders for contraception and over 16,000 with diabetes.

notes.quote: Here in Prince Edward Island, residents face some of Canada's highest out-of-pocket costs for drugs covered on their public plans.
notes.claim: PEI's own health minister described Islanders as facing some of Canada's highest out-of-pocket drug costs — the reason a small province signed quickly.

notes.quote: Today, Member of Parliament Brendan Hanley, on behalf of the Honourable Kamal Khera, Canada’s Minister of Health, and the Honourable Tracy-Anne McPhee, Yukon’s Minister of Health and Social Services, announced the signing of a pharmacare agreement to invest up to $9.5 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications for residents of Yukon.
notes.claim: Yukon's agreement is up to $9.5 million over four years, covering more than 12,000 Yukoners for contraception and over 3,000 with diabetes; coverage expected no later than January 2026.

notes.quote: Yukon residents can anticipate beginning to receive coverage for these products no later than January 2026.
notes.claim: Yukon coverage was expected no later than January 2026 — the last of the four to go live, nine months after signing.

notes.quote: The PBO estimates that the first phase of national universal pharmacare will increase federal program spending by $1.9 billion over five years. This estimate assumes that any medications that are currently covered by provincial and territorial governments, as well as private insurance providers will remain covered on the same terms.
notes.claim: PBO's legislative costing of Bill C-64: the first phase increases federal program spending by $1.9 billion over five years, assuming existing public and private coverage continues on the same terms.

notes.quote: The new program will cover 100% of the expense on diabetes and contraception medication for those who currently do not have public or private drug plan coverage and for those who currently do not fill their prescriptions due to cost related reasons. The latter group is assumed to be 14% of total prescriptions. The program will also cover the out-of-pocket portion of prescription costs for those who have public or private drug plan coverage.
notes.claim: PBO's method for the C-64 costing: the program covers 100% of cost for those with no coverage and for those who skip prescriptions due to cost (assumed to be 14% of prescriptions), plus the out-of-pocket portion for those who do have coverage.

notes.quote: The estimate has high uncertainty and is contingent on the number of drugs listed for coverage. Drug expenditures have several cost drivers and the projections are highly sensitive to the projected growth rate of those cost drivers, and the determinants of those cost factors.
notes.claim: PBO explicitly labels its own C-64 estimate as high uncertainty and dependent on which drugs are listed; it excludes behavioural substitution onto the formulary, which would raise cost, and assumes no extra federal rebates.

notes.quote: Behavioural effects such as substitution from the drugs not listed on the formulary to the drugs on the formulary are not accounted for in this cost estimate and could increase the total estimated cost.
notes.claim: PBO notes substitution effects from unlisted to listed drugs are excluded and could increase the estimated cost — a downward bias in the $1.9 billion figure.

notes.quote: we estimate the incremental cost to the public sector (that is federal and provincial governments combined) to be $11.2 billion in 2024-25, increasing to $13.4 billion in 2027-28.
notes.claim: The full single-payer plan (RAMQ formulary, universal, single payer) would cost the public sector an incremental $11.2 billion in 2024-25, rising to $13.4 billion in 2027-28.

notes.quote: Require a $5 co-payment for all prescriptions of brand-name drugs, with exemptions for the following:
notes.claim: The PBO's single-payer model assumes a $5 brand-name copayment with exemptions, and a RAMQ national formulary — the specific design choices that drive its number.

notes.quote: total drug expenditures under Pharmacare to be $33.2 billion in 2024-25 (the assumed first full fiscal year of implementation), increasing to $38.9 billion in 2027-28
notes.claim: Total drug expenditure under the single-payer plan would be $33.2 billion in 2024-25, rising to $38.9 billion by 2027-28.

notes.quote: In terms of the economy as a whole, we estimate cost savings on drug expenditures of $1.4 billion in 2024-25, rising to $2.2 billion in 2027-28.
notes.claim: The economy-wide saving is the PBO's counterintuitive result: the public sector pays more, but total national drug spending falls, because single-payer extends confidential rebates and substitution to the privately-paid share.

notes.quote: Once copayment revenues and savings on direct federal spending are accounted for, the incremental cost of a single-payer universal drug plan with a catastrophic formulary to the public sector (that is, federal and provincial governments combined) is $1.8 billion and $2.0 billion in 2024-25 and 2027-28 respectively.
notes.claim: A catastrophic-only formulary would cost the public sector far less — $1.8 billion in 2024-25 and $2.0 billion in 2027-28 — showing the cost is driven almost entirely by formulary breadth, not by the principle of public coverage.

notes.quote: PBO estimates that drug expenditures under this alternative to be $0.4 billion and $0.3 billion more than the estimated spending under the baseline scenario in 2024-25 and 2027-28 respectively.
notes.claim: An essential-medicines formulary would actually raise total spending slightly — $0.4 billion more in 2024-25 — because generics are already cheap, so extra use is not offset by savings. A key reason estimates diverge by orders of magnitude.

notes.quote: Prices borne directly by patients are expected to fall by 47 per cent to 100 per cent, which results in overall increases in the utilization of prescription drugs of 13.5 per cent.
notes.claim: PBO's single-payer model assumes patients bear 47% to 100% less at point of sale, generating a 13.5% increase in prescription utilization — the central behavioural assumption behind the cost.

notes.quote: Total prescription drug spending in Canada, excluding hospital drugs, amounts to roughly $36.6 billion in 2021-2022, a 28 per cent increase relative to 2015-2016.
notes.claim: Baseline context: Canadian non-hospital prescription drug spending was about $36.6 billion in 2021-22; 46% public ($16.9B), 40% private insurance ($14.7B), 14% out of pocket ($4.9B).

notes.quote:
* received advice from a committee of experts on how to operate and finance national pharmacare
* received advice from Canada's Drug Agency on:
  * a national bulk purchasing strategy
  * a list of essential prescription drugs and related products
* published a pan-Canadian strategy to promote appropriate use of prescription drugs and related products
notes.claim: All four statutory deliverables were produced: committee-of-experts advice, CDA advice on bulk purchasing, the CDA essential-drugs list, and a pan-Canadian appropriate-use strategy.

notes.quote: Our objective is to "learn by doing" in a Canadian context.
notes.claim: Health Canada's own framing of the program's next stage is incremental and experimental rather than a scheduled expansion to universal coverage.

notes.quote: About 3.8 million people in Canada have been diagnosed with diabetes. In 2018, costs to the healthcare system related to diabetes were estimated at $27 billion, and they could surpass $39 billion by 2028.
notes.claim: Scale of the diabetes population the program nominally addresses: about 3.8 million diagnosed in Canada, with health-system costs estimated at $27 billion in 2018, potentially over $39 billion by 2028.

notes.quote: Metformin, which can cost about $100 per year
notes.claim: Per-patient annual drug costs Health Canada cites for the covered diabetes drugs: metformin about $100/year, insulin $900-$1,700/year, sulfonylureas and SGLT-2 inhibitors $100 to over $1,000/year.

notes.quote: Insulin, which can cost between $900 and $1,700 per year
notes.claim: Insulin costs $900-$1,700 per year, and sulfonylureas and SGLT-2 inhibitors from $100 to over $1,000 per year — the covered set is dominated by relatively low-cost drugs.

notes.quote: The total cost of publicly funding a list of essential medicines will likely be between $6 to $10 billion dollars (see Appendix 2).
notes.claim: The National Pharmacare Committee of Experts independently estimates the total cost of publicly funding an essential medicines list at $6 billion to $10 billion — far below the PBO's $11.2-$13.4 billion single-payer figure, because it covers only a core list.

notes.quote: Source : Source : Committee estimations using data from IQVIA Solutions Canada, the Canadian Institute for Health Information and reports from the Parliamentary Budget Officer
notes.claim: The committee's 2025 spending table shows pharmacare at $8 billion, with out-of-pocket falling from $9.5B to $6.8B and private insurance from $17.3B to $12.5B — its own modelling, not the PBO's.

notes.quote: The committee rejects the idea of a limited "fill-the-gaps" model and instead advocates for universal, single-payer, publicly administered pharmacare based on human rights.
notes.claim: The committee explicitly rejects the fill-the-gaps model that the Act's bilateral-agreement architecture produces, and recommends a single-payer approach precisely because bilateral deals create the patchwork.

notes.quote: This single-payer approach avoids the drawbacks of bilateral agreements, enshrines universal access and strengthens the ability to negotiate drug prices with drug companies.
notes.claim: The committee criticizes the bilateral-agreement route directly: a single-payer approach "avoids the drawbacks of bilateral agreements" and should be delivered through health cards instead.

notes.quote: Total spending on prescribed drugs in Canada jumped by $10 billion in 5 years – from $34 billion in 2019 to $44 billion in 2024
notes.claim: The committee's own data on the status quo: Canadian prescribed-drug spending rose $10 billion in five years, from $34 billion in 2019 to $44 billion in 2024, with no measurable improvement in access.

notes.quote:
* The first graphic shows there are 6 federal public drug plans.
* The second graphic shows there are over 100 provincial and territorial drug plans.
* The last graphic shows there are over 100,000 private drug plans.
notes.claim: The committee's structural finding on the current system: six federal plans, over 100 provincial/territorial plans and over 100,000 private drug plans — the fragmentation pharmacare is meant to replace.

notes.quote: We used the list of 185 medicines included in the essential prescription drugs list prepared by the Canada’s Drug Agency committee to estimate the lower bound of the cost of pharmacare. The pan-Canadian Pharmaceutical Alliance identified that these medicines may be suitable for competitive pricing through tendering (as all have multiple sources and none are protected by a patent).
notes.claim: The committee's bottom-up method: 185 off-patent medicines identified by the pan-Canadian Pharmaceutical Alliance as tenderable, with 2024 IQVIA CompuScript dispensing data showing $12.6 billion spent on them, then adjusted down for brand pricing, markups and tendering, and up for population, volume growth and induced use.

notes.quote: In exchange for not instituting competitive pricing processes such as tendering, drug manufacturers have offered in 2018 to reduce prices paid by public drug plans by a reported 25% to 40%.
notes.claim: The single largest driver of the disagreement: the committee assumes tendering/competitive pricing cuts prices 40%, versus the PBO's assumption set. It also assumes 17% lower markups and fees, and 14% savings from generic pricing.

notes.quote: We selected 5% for our lower bound estimate, while the upper bound estimate from the Parliamentary Budget Office assumes an increase of 13.5%, which is larger than estimates in the literature.
notes.claim: The committee criticizes the PBO's 13.5% induced-utilization assumption as too high relative to the literature, and uses 5% instead — the second main driver of divergence.

notes.quote: We assume that the federal government will cover the entire cost of covered medicines, and that the contribution from provincial and territorial governments will be zero.
notes.claim: The committee's estimate is a gross federal cost assuming provinces contribute zero — deliberately not comparable to the PBO's incremental framing, which nets off status quo spending.

notes.quote: current public spending on included medicines, such as through provincial and territorial drug plans (which may account for more than 30% of the cost)
notes.claim: The committee notes current public spending on the same medicines may exceed 30% of the gross cost, so its $6-9.8B gross figure is not comparable to a net incremental figure.

notes.quote: Overall per capita drug spending in Canada is substantially higher than comparable countries:
notes.claim: International price comparisons the committee uses to argue savings are available: Canada's per-capita drug spending is 70% higher than the UK's and 23% higher than Australia's.

notes.quote: A 2017 report from the Auditor General of Ontario found that prices paid the Ontario Public Drugs Program were 70% higher than prices in New Zealand, and also 85% higher than prices paid by hospitals in Ontario.
notes.claim: The committee's strongest empirical claim for savings: a 2017 Ontario Auditor General report found Ontario's public drug program paid 70% more than New Zealand prices and 85% more than Ontario hospitals paid.

notes.quote: **Universal coverage for a range of contraception and diabetes medications**. With $1.5 billion in federal investments, we are launching the first phase of a national pharmacare plan.
notes.claim: The federal commitment behind the first phase is $1.5 billion, announced in Budget 2024 — the number the PBO's $1.9 billion estimate exceeded by about $400 million.

notes.quote: With this coverage, 3.7 million Canadians, including seniors, will be able to get the diabetes medication they need and save up to $1,700 per year.
notes.claim: The government's own headline reach claims at launch: nine million women for contraception and 3.7 million Canadians for diabetes medication, saving up to $1,700 per year.

notes.quote: In 2025-26, the federal government contributed $88.1 million to support these provinces and one territory in the expansion of public coverage of diabetes medications and contraception for all residents. The federal pharmacare contribution is expected to increase to $269.6 million by 2028-29.
notes.claim: Actual federal pharmacare spending: $88.1 million in 2025-26 across the four signed jurisdictions, projected to rise to $269.6 million by 2028-29 — a small fraction of the $1.5 billion envelope.

notes.quote: From the Spring Economic Update, it appears that there will be no new federal funding for additional pharmacare deals. With the bilateral health funding dropping from $4.3 billion in 2025-26 to $3.1 billion in 2027-28, it seems that the federal government doesn’t see a future for national pharmacare.
notes.claim: The program is being wound down: the Spring 2026 Economic Update signals no new federal pharmacare funding, bilateral health funding falls from $4.3B in 2025-26 to $3.1B in 2027-28, and agreements appear set to expire without renewal.

notes.quote: In April, P.E.I.’s health minister revealed that Ottawa will be cutting $29 million in health care funding to the province over the next three years.
notes.claim: PEI's health minister disclosed Ottawa cutting $29 million in health funding over three years, and Newfoundland and Labrador's minister said the door was closed on the province — the first named provincial consequences.

notes.quote: In 2023, Canadian residents spent $8 billion on out-of-pocket prescription drugs. Another $15.8 billion was spent on drugs through private insurance plans.
notes.claim: Status quo cost baseline from CCPA: Canadians spent $8 billion out of pocket on prescription drugs in 2023 and $15.8 billion through private insurance plans.

notes.quote: The 2019 report, _A Prescription for Canada_, estimated that by 2027, with a comprehensive formulary of drugs, Canada would spend $5 billion less on prescription drugs while at the same time improving access for all.
notes.claim: The 2019 Advisory Council estimate: a comprehensive formulary would leave Canada spending $5 billion less on prescription drugs by 2027 while improving access — a third independent estimate, and the source of the "savings" claim.

notes.quote: The per capita funding of the four participating jurisdictions varies widely, from $117 per resident for British Columbia to $198 per resident for Yukon.
notes.claim: Per-capita federal funding varies widely across the four agreements — $117 per resident in BC, $198 in Yukon, $156 average — showing the deals were not struck on a uniform formula.

notes.quote: Manitoba, British Columbia, Prince Edward Island and Yukon are participating in the federal program, covering nearly 7.5 million people.
notes.claim: The four agreements cover nearly 7.5 million people, so four out of five Canadians are outside the program.

notes.quote: Nine months after the _Pharmacare Act_ (C-64) received Royal Assent on October 10, 2024 , just four provinces and territories have signed bilateral agreements with the federal government.
notes.claim: Nine months after Royal Assent only four jurisdictions had signed — confirming the March 2025 window closed with no additions through mid-2025.

notes.quote: New Brunswick would likely receive $136 million through a bilateral pharmacare agreement over four years. Nova Scotia would receive $171 million, and Ontario would receive an estimated $2.5 billion over four years.
notes.claim: What the holdout provinces are forgoing, on a per-capita extrapolation from the four deals: Ontario an estimated $2.5 billion over four years, Nova Scotia $171 million, New Brunswick $136 million.

notes.quote: The 2024 federal budget committed $1.5 billion in funding over five years but there has been no new funding since.
notes.claim: The 2024 budget committed $1.5 billion over five years with no new funding since; the November 2025 budget contained no pharmacare funding or announcements, and the spring 2026 economic update mentioned it only in passing.

notes.quote: The final report of the National Pharmacare Committee of Experts was submitted in November 2025 but no action has been taken.
notes.claim: The Committee of Experts' final report was submitted in November 2025 and, as of late 2026, no action had been taken on it.

notes.quote: Several other provinces showed interest in reaching agreements of their own but reportedly haven’t received significant engagement from the federal government.
notes.claim: Provinces that showed interest reportedly received no significant federal engagement — the reason the signing stopped, from an industry source rather than a provincial statement.

notes.quote: At the time of writing, only four of the 13 Canadian jurisdictions – BC, Manitoba, PEI and Yukon – have reached agreements with the federal government to provide access to just two classes of medicines, contraceptives and diabetes treatments, and even those agreements have inconsistencies in what medicines are included and how they are covered.
notes.claim: The committee's official finding on what was delivered: only four of thirteen jurisdictions reached agreements, covering just two drug classes, and even those agreements are inconsistent in which medicines are included and how they are covered.

notes.quote: In those agreements, on average the federal contribution is approximately 70 percent of total expenditures on included medicines.
notes.claim: The federal share in the signed agreements averages about 70% of total expenditures on included medicines — the cost-sharing ratio the deals actually use.

notes.quote: These options would require the type of bilateral funding agreements which have been proven to be challenging and time consuming, as demonstrated by implementation of the 2024 Act Respecting Pharmacare.
notes.claim: The committee explicitly calls the bilateral route "challenging and time consuming" and cites the 2024 Act's implementation as the proof — a federal body criticizing the delivery model the Act created.

notes.quote: In contrast, initiatives fully funded by the federal government that provide dental care, childcare and other services administered by provincial and territorial governments have all been successfully implemented within short time frames.
notes.claim: The committee's counter-example: fully federally funded programs like dental care and childcare were implemented successfully within short time frames, unlike shared-cost pharmacare.

notes.quote: The approximate $45 billion spent on prescription medicines (from all payers) in 2024 in Canada is similar to the amount spent on post-secondary education and more than the total budgets of Indigenous Services Canada, Health Canada, Veterans Affairs, the Department of Industry and the Mortgage and Housing Corporation combined.
notes.claim: Total prescription medicine spending from all payers was about $45 billion in 2024 — equal to roughly 11% of the federal budget, and more than the combined budgets of several federal departments.

notes.quote: The agreement to avoid competitive tendering processes expires in 2026.
notes.claim: The committee's finding that the pCPA's no-tendering deal with generic manufacturers expires in 2026 — the policy window in which tendering savings could actually be captured.

notes.quote: On April 1, 2023, the province began providing free contraceptives to all residents. In 2024 alone, approximately 227,000 people received free prescription contraception, through this nation-leading program. Since the start of the program, more than 306,000 people have benefitted.
notes.claim: A real utilisation count does exist in the documents read: Health Canada's own BC news release reports about 227,000 people receiving free prescription contraception in 2024 and over 306,000 since April 2023 — so the section is wrong that no document says how many people have actually used the benefit.

notes.quote: If you live in a province or territory with an agreement, those products will be available for free or at low cost at the pharmacy counter. You **won't** need to coordinate benefits with private insurance plans. Other fees, such as prescribing fees or delivery fees, may still apply.
notes.claim: The agreements index page is not just four titles and four announcement links: it carries substantive prose on coverage, fees and diabetes supplies.

notes.quote: .1\. Effective on March 1, 2026, British Columbia will provide free public coverage of hormone replacement therapies identified by British Columbia to treat menopausal symptoms for all Residents.
notes.claim: The BC agreement extends free public coverage to a third category outside Annex A — hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms from 1 March 2026 — so the annex does not exclude every non-diabetes, non-contraceptive drug.

notes.quote: You generally qualify for national pharmacare coverage if you: * are a resident of a province or territory that has an agreement in place with the federal government * are eligible for public health insurance in your province or territory, **and** * have a valid prescription and authorization for a covered medication or related product, if needed
notes.claim: Coverage is not purely a property of residence: Health Canada's own page says you "generally qualify" only if you are a resident, are eligible for provincial public health insurance, and have a valid prescription and authorization.

notes.quote: 5.1\. Manitoba will provide free public coverage of hormone replacement therapies specified by Manitoba to treat menopausal symptoms for all Residents.
notes.claim: Manitoba's agreement also adds free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms, a third drug category outside Annex A — so the annex does not exclude every non-diabetes, non-contraceptive drug.

notes.quote: At the time of writing, only four of the 13 Canadian jurisdictions – BC, Manitoba, PEI and Yukon – have reached agreements with the federal government to provide access to just two classes of medicines, contraceptives and diabetes treatments, and even those agreements have inconsistencies in what medicines are included and how they are covered. In those agreements, on average the federal contribution is approximately 70 percent of total expenditures on included medicines.
notes.claim: The four signed agreements differ from one another in which medicines are included and how they are covered, so identical titles do not show a single non-negotiated template; the federal share averages about 70% of costs.

notes.quote: Several other provinces showed interest in reaching agreements of their own but reportedly haven’t received significant engagement from the federal government.
notes.claim: The sources do offer an explanation for why signing stopped: other provinces were interested but got no significant federal engagement, i.e. federal withdrawal rather than purely provincial refusal.

notes.quote: As part of today's agreement, BC will also enhance pharmacare coverage for its residents by providing free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy to treat menopausal symptoms for all residents.
notes.claim: The BC agreement adds free coverage of hormone replacement therapy for menopause — a drug class for a condition other than diabetes or contraception — so the list is not confined to "diabetes" outside contraception.

notes.quote: On April 1, 2023, the province began providing free contraceptives to all residents. In 2024 alone, approximately 227,000 people received free prescription contraception, through this nation-leading program.
notes.claim: BC already provided free prescription contraception to all residents from April 2023, before the federal agreement; the federal money largely funded coverage the provincial plan already gave.

notes.quote: Effective on March 1, 2026, British Columbia will provide free public coverage of hormone replacement therapies identified by British Columbia to treat menopausal symptoms for all Residents.
notes.claim: The BC agreement's own text adds free hormone replacement therapy for menopause — a third drug category beyond contraception and diabetes — so the list is not confined to "two disease categories."

notes.quote: lixisenatide with insulin glargine                   | Exception Drug Status (EDS) benefit
notes.claim: Manitoba's Annex A does list a GLP-1 receptor agonist — lixisenatide, combined with insulin glargine — under Exception Drug Status, so GLP-1 drugs are not wholly absent from the signed agreements' lists.

notes.quote: **Stream 2**: Increase access by expanding coverage: to support hybrid closed-loop blood glucose monitor and insulin delivery systems; to include lancets for diabetic use; and to include additional supplies for insulin pump and glucose monitor users, with all expanded coverage using existing coverage plans and adjudication rules.
notes.claim: The agreements fund diabetes devices and supplies (Stream 2) — closed-loop glucose monitor and insulin delivery systems, lancets, pump and monitor supplies — not just drugs, which the section never mentions despite promising "devices."

notes.quote: | lixisenatide with insulin glargine                   | Exception Drug Status (EDS) benefit                                                                                                               |
notes.claim: Manitoba's Annex A does include one GLP-1 receptor agonist — lixisenatide with insulin glargine — under Exception Drug Status, so the claim that no GLP-1 is covered is wrong, though it is a single combination product requiring prior approval.

notes.quote: Manitoba will provide free public coverage of hormone replacement therapies specified by Manitoba to treat menopausal symptoms for all Residents.
notes.claim: Section 5.1 of the Manitoba agreement commits the province to free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy for menopause — a third drug category written into the agreement itself.

notes.quote:
The maximum amounts to be transferred to Manitoba over 4 years are:
* $52,509,230 in Fiscal Year 2025-2026
* $54,603,615 in Fiscal Year 2026-2027
* $54,603,615 in Fiscal Year 2027-2028
* $54,603,615 in Fiscal Year 2028-2029
notes.claim: Manitoba's federal money is $52,509,230 in 2025-26 rising to $54,603,615 a year for three years — about $216.3 million for Stream 1, plus $9,945,348 one-time for insulin pumps and glucose monitors.

Manitoba's own 2022-23 baseline spending on the products later listed in Annex A was $23,945,982 — $23.2 million on diabetes and $750,746 on contraception — which is what the federal transfer is designed to top up.

notes.quote: Manitoba’s Implementation Date will be April 15, 2025.
notes.claim: Manitoba's coverage implementation date was 15 April 2025 — earlier than the June 2025 date in the news release, and a fixed term ending 31 March 2029.

notes.quote: Beginning in Fiscal Year 2026-27, as a condition of annual funding under this Agreement, by October 1 of each Fiscal Year, Manitoba agrees to provide Canada with an attested financial statement
notes.claim: The agreements require annual attested financial statements and results reporting from provinces starting in 2026-27 — so claims-level utilization data is contractually reported to Ottawa, even though it is not published on the pharmacare web pages.

report.body:
## TL;DR

Canada's national pharmacare program exists, covers a narrow list of contraception and diabetes products at zero cost to residents, and reaches four of thirteen jurisdictions. Manitoba signed on 27 February 2025, British Columbia on 6 March, Prince Edward Island on 7 March and Yukon on 20 March; no further agreement has been signed since, and Ontario, Quebec, Alberta and five others remain outside, so most Canadians have no entitlement under the Act [2][14][17]. The agreements are worth $928 million over four years, and the federal government actually spent $88.1 million on the program in 2025-26 [16][17]. There is no enrolment figure to report because the benefit attaches to residence rather than registration; the best available reach measure is that the four jurisdictions hold nearly 7.5 million people [17]. On cost, the Parliamentary Budget Officer put the legislated first phase at $1.9 billion over five years against $1.5 billion budgeted [11][15], and a full single-payer plan at $11.2 billion in 2024-25 rising to $13.4 billion in 2027-28 in incremental public cost, while the government's own Committee of Experts put an essential-medicines list at $6 billion to $10 billion [12][14]. The program is now being allowed to lapse: the spring 2026 economic update signalled no new federal pharmacare funding, and the agreements expire in 2029 [16][19].

## Key Findings

- **The Act funds, it does not create a plan.** Section 6(1) obliges payment only "if the Minister has entered into an agreement with a province or territory to do so," and only for contraception and diabetes products [1].
- **Four of thirteen jurisdictions signed, all in a five-week window in early 2025, none since.** Manitoba, British Columbia, Prince Edward Island and Yukon [2].
- **The money is modest and slow to flow.** $928 million over four years across the four deals [17]; actual federal spending was $88.1 million in 2025-26, projected to reach $269.6 million by 2028-29 [16]. Manitoba's own schedule runs $52,509,230 in 2025-26 rising to $54,603,615 a year [19].
- **Coverage is genuinely first-dollar and not means-tested within a signed province** — no age, income or private-insurance test [4] — but the list is closed, delivery and prescribing fees are excluded [3], and brand-name products can still cost the patient under the Low Cost Alternative policy [5].
- **GLP-1 drugs are almost entirely excluded.** The only one in Manitoba's annex is lixisenatide with insulin glargine, under Exception Drug Status [19]. Nothing is covered for any condition outside contraception, diabetes, and (in BC and Manitoba) menopause hormone therapy [7][19].
- **No published take-up numbers.** Health Canada's pages give eligibility and a product list, not counts of people served or claims paid [2][3][4]; the agreements do require attested annual financial statements from provinces starting 2026-27 [19].
- **PBO on the first phase: $1.9 billion over five years, above the $1.5 billion budgeted** [11][15], and explicitly a floor — it excludes substitution onto the formulary, which "could increase the total estimated cost" [11].
- **PBO on full single-payer: $11.2 billion incremental public cost in 2024-25, $13.4 billion in 2027-28** — but a $1.4–2.2 billion *reduction* in economy-wide drug spending, because a single payer captures rebates the private market does not [12].
- **A catastrophic-only formulary costs a sixth as much:** $1.8 billion in 2024-25, $2.0 billion in 2027-28 [12]. The cost of pharmacare is a formulary decision before it is a fiscal one.
- **The Committee of Experts estimates $6–10 billion** for an essential-medicines list, versus the PBO's $11.2 billion — a gap driven mainly by assuming tendering savings and 5% rather than 13.5% induced utilization [14].
- **The government's own expert panel rejected the model it implemented,** calling bilateral funding agreements "challenging and time consuming, as demonstrated by implementation of the 2024 Act Respecting Pharmacare" [14].
- **The program is being wound down by attrition, not by amendment.** No new funding since Budget 2024's $1.5 billion [18]; bilateral health funding falling from $4.3 billion in 2025-26 to $3.1 billion in 2027-28 [16]; PEI told to expect a $29 million cut over three years [16].

## Details

### 1. What the Pharmacare Act (Bill C-64) actually obliges: the legal machinery, the first phase of coverage, and what it deliberately does not do

The Pharmacare Act, Bill C-64, received Royal Assent on 10 October 2024. What it did not do is create a national drug plan. Its own summary describes the enactment as setting out "the principles that the Minister of Health is to consider when working towards the implementation of national universal pharmacare" and obliging the Minister "to make payments, in certain circumstances, in relation to the coverage of certain prescription drugs and related products" [1]. Every substantive promise in the Act is a promise to *ask someone to produce a document*, or a promise to pay *if* a province agrees to terms. That structure explains almost everything about what has and has not been delivered since.
