**The spending clause is conditional and narrow.** Section 6(1) reads: the Minister must, "if the Minister has entered into an agreement with a province or territory to do so, make payments to the province or territory in order to increase any existing public pharmacare coverage — and to provide universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage — for specific prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes" [1]. Three limits sit inside that sentence. The obligation to pay is triggered only by a signed bilateral agreement, so a province that never signs costs the federal government nothing and loses nothing statutory. The coverage to be purchased is limited to contraception and diabetes products — the "first phase" — not prescription drugs generally. And the money is to *increase existing* coverage, which means it is designed to sit on top of provincial plans rather than replace them.

**The purpose clause aims at a destination without creating a route to it.** Section 3 states that the Act's purpose is "to guide efforts to improve, for all Canadians, the accessibility and affordability of prescription drugs and related products, and to support their appropriate use, in collaboration with the provinces, territories, Indigenous peoples and other partners and stakeholders, with the aim of continuing to work toward the implementation of national universal pharmacare" [1]. Section 4 then lists principles — public administration, comprehensiveness, universality, portability, accessibility — but frames them as things the Minister "is to consider" when collaborating with provinces, territories, Indigenous peoples and other partners and stakeholders [1]. Consideration is not compliance. Nothing in the Act makes universal coverage an entitlement, gives a patient a right to a drug, or allows anyone to enforce the principles against a province.

**The definition of "pharmacare" is deliberately agnostic about who pays.** The Act defines pharmacare as "a program that provides coverage of prescription drugs and related products" [1]. It does not require that program to be public, single-payer, or administered by government. A private insurer topping up a workplace plan would satisfy the words as readily as a Crown corporation. The statute therefore does not itself decide the question that has divided pharmacare advocates — whether the route is a single public payer or a public plan that fills the gaps left by private coverage — and the scholars who analysed it read that ambiguity as deliberate [6].

**A list, a strategy and a committee report, all with one-year deadlines, none of them binding.** Section 8(1) requires the Minister, after discussions with provinces and territories, to request that the Canadian Drug Agency prepare "no later than the first anniversary" of Royal Assent "a list of essential prescription drugs and related products to inform the development of a national formulary that will establish the scope of prescription drugs and related products to which Canadians should have access under national universal pharmacare" [1]. The object is a *list to inform* a formulary, not a formulary; and a national formulary is not a national reimbursement decision. Section 9 requires a request that the agency develop a "national bulk purchasing strategy" within the same year — a strategy, not a purchasing entity, and with no obligation on any province to buy through it [1]. Section 11 requires a committee of experts, established within 30 days of Royal Assent, "to make recommendations respecting options for the operation and financing of national, universal, single-payer pharmacare", reporting within a year and tabling its report in Parliament [1]. Recommendations carry no duty to act.

**The legal criticism has been consistent and specific.** Writing in the *Canadian Medical Association Journal* in 2024, two health-policy and health-law scholars argued that the bill leaves the single-payer-versus-fill-the-gaps decision "to the discretion of the federal health minister in bilateral negotiations with provinces and territories, and would permit different program structures across the country" [6]. Their second objection is institutional: the bill "does not establish the CDA by law, nor set out the agency’s powers, functions, and governance structures, which represents a missed opportunity to depoliticize the implementation and management of national pharmacare" [6]. The Canadian Drug Agency exists as an operational entity, not as a statutory body with entrenched functions — so its scope can be narrowed, redirected or wound down by a government without amending the Act. The same authors identify the core ambiguity: the Act sets out the destination but "it does not say that a public program is the way to get there, or whether a fill-the-gaps approach would suffice" [6].

**What this means in practice.** The Act is best understood as a funding authority plus a to-do list. It creates a legal channel for federal money to flow to provinces that sign, on terms the federal Minister negotiates, for two drug classes only. Everything else — a formulary with force, a single payer, a national purchasing monopoly, coverage of the drugs most Canadians actually spend money on — requires either subsequent legislation or provincial cooperation that the Act cannot compel. Judged against its own text, the Act does not fail when coverage is patchy across provinces; patchiness is what its architecture produces. Judged against the 2019 Advisory Council report that recommended universal single-payer coverage, it is a first instalment with no statutory schedule for the second — a comparison this report has not yet verified against that report's text.

### 2. Which provinces and territories have signed bilateral agreements, when, for how much, and who has not signed and why

Four jurisdictions have signed, all within a five-week window in early 2025, and no further agreement has been announced since. Health Canada's agreements page, in its 26 January 2026 revision, lists exactly four: British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Yukon [2]. Since Canada has ten provinces and three territories, that leaves nine jurisdictions without an agreement — a subtraction, not a figure any source states.

**The signing order, dates and amounts.** Manitoba was first, announced on 27 February 2025 at more than $219 million over four years [2][8]. British Columbia followed on 6 March 2025 at more than $670 million [2][7], Prince Edward Island on 7 March 2025 at more than $30 million [2][9], and Yukon on 20 March 2025 at up to $9.5 million [2][10]. The four together are worth $928 million over four years [17]. All four carry the same formal title — "Universal Access to Contraception and Diabetes Medications and Increased Access to Diabetes Devices and Supplies" — followed by the jurisdiction's name and "Funding Agreement" [2]. The identical titles indicate a single federal template rather than bespoke terms, which is consistent with the Act's design: the Minister negotiates within a statutory envelope limited to contraception and diabetes products [1].

**The per-capita money is not uniform, which tells you the deals were bargained.** Per-capita federal funding ranges from $117 per resident in British Columbia to $198 per resident in Yukon, averaging about $156 [17]. Yukon's small population and high delivery costs plausibly explain its premium; BC's size plausibly explains its discount. The practical consequence is that a holdout province cannot infer its offer from the published deals with confidence. The CCPA's extrapolation puts Ontario at an estimated $2.5 billion over four years, Nova Scotia at $171 million and New Brunswick at $136 million [17] — figures that are the advocacy group's own per-capita calculation, not federal offers.

**The Manitoba agreement shows what the money actually buys, and it is a top-up, not a new program.** Its schedule transfers $52,509,230 in 2025-26 and $54,603,615 in each of the following three years, plus a one-time $9,945,348 for insulin pumps and advanced glucose monitors [19]. Against that, Manitoba's own reported 2022-23 spending on the products later listed in Annex A was $23,945,982 — $23,195,236 on diabetes and $750,746 on contraception [19]. The federal transfer is therefore, by my own comparison of the two figures, more than twice what the province was already spending on those drugs — which is what makes first-dollar coverage possible without a provincial tax increase, and explains why the money was attractive to a small province. The agreement runs to 31 March 2029 with no renewal clause, and its payments are "subject to there being an appropriation of funds by the Parliament of Canada" for each year [19] — the legal hook on which the current wind-down hangs.

**What the pattern of signatories tells you.** Three of the four that signed — Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Yukon — are among the smallest jurisdictions in the federation; British Columbia is the only large province in the group. Ontario, Quebec, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, the Northwest Territories and Nunavut have all not signed. That is the single most important fact about the program's reach: the jurisdictions holding the large majority of Canada's population, and the large majority of its diabetes patients, are outside the program entirely. A resident of Toronto, Montreal, Calgary or Halifax has no pharmacare entitlement under this Act, regardless of income or need.

**Why the large provinces have not signed is not documented in the sources read here.** The obvious candidates — Alberta's stated preference for a private-insurance approach, Quebec's insistence on opting out with full compensation and its own drug plan, Ontario's existing OHIP+ coverage for under-25s and its preference for enhanced federal transfers over program-specific funding — are widely reported positions, but this report has not yet verified them against the news releases or provincial statements, and they are not asserted as findings here. The same applies to the dollar value of each agreement. Health Canada's index page names the four agreements and links their announcements but does not display the federal contribution per jurisdiction on the index itself [2]; the amounts sit in the individual news releases and the funding agreements, which have not yet been read for this report. That gap is material, because the per-capita federal offer is what makes signing attractive or not, and it is the number that would let a reader judge whether the program is a real transfer or a token.

**The signing window closed and did not reopen.** Nine months after Royal Assent, in July 2025, there were still exactly four agreements [17], and between March 2025 and the index page's January 2026 update no fifth agreement appears [2]. The reasons are contested. An industry account says several provinces showed interest but had not received significant engagement from the federal government [18]; the CCPA, writing in July 2025, attributed the gap to provinces refusing available money [17]. Those two accounts point in opposite directions — federal disengagement versus provincial refusal — and this report cannot adjudicate between them, because neither is a provincial statement of position. What is not contested is the arithmetic: nine jurisdictions forgoing an estimated $156 per resident per year in federal money [17], which for Ontario the CCPA calculates at roughly $2.5 billion over four years [17]. What can be said is that the program's geographic footprint at the start of 2026 is the same as it was at the end of March 2025.

### 3. What is actually covered under the signed agreements: drugs, devices, eligibility rules, and what patients still pay

Coverage under the signed agreements is narrower than the phrase free birth control and diabetes medication implies, and it is also more generous than most provincial plans it sits on top of. Both facts come from the agreements themselves.

**The list is closed and the fee structure is specific.** Health Canada's patient-facing page states that pharmacare covers "a range of birth control options and diabetes medications." It says it "only covers the costs of listed products and medications, including the dispensing fee" [3]. What it will not cover, the same page says, is any applicable delivery fee or pharmacist prescribing fee [3]. The dispensing fee is inside the benefit; delivery and prescribing fees are outside it. So a patient in a signed jurisdiction can still pay at the counter — for a prescription renewal assessment, for mail delivery, or for any product not on the list.

**Eligibility is universal within a signed jurisdiction.** Health Canada states that a resident is covered regardless of age, income, or private or workplace health insurance status [4]. That is a genuinely unusual design in Canadian drug policy, where most public programs are last-resort payers for people who cannot afford premiums or who fall into a high-cost category. The pharmacare benefit is first-dollar and not income-tested, and a person with a workplace plan does not have to exhaust it first. The limit is geographic: the entitlement runs only to residents of a province or territory that has signed, and as of Health Canada's page, updated in January 2026, that means British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Yukon — four of thirteen jurisdictions [2].

**"First-dollar" is defined in the legal text, not just in a press release.** The British Columbia agreement defines it as coverage "where the products that are covered in British Columbia and belong to the categories identified in _Annex A_ are made available at no cost to the Resident at the point of sale, subject to the conditions of coverage noted in _Annex A_. Costs include, but are not limited to: deductibles, copays, premiums, pharmacy or dispensing fees, and wholesale or distribution costs as recognized by British Columbia" [5]. That is the strongest form of the commitment in the Canadian system: not a subsidy, not a deductible-then-coverage formula, but zero at the point of sale for listed items, with the federal transfer compensating the province.

**But the conditions inside Annex A reintroduce cost-sharing for some products.** In the BC agreement, several products carry Special Authority requirements — a prescriber must apply for pre-authorization before the drug is covered — and the Low Cost Alternative policy applies to brand-name versions. The metformin line reads: "metformin | Low Cost Alternative policy will apply to Glucophage. Residents may be responsible for paying a portion of costs for Glucophage. Other free options are available." [5] The same pattern applies to brand-name gliclazide (Diamicron MR), dapagliflozin (Forxiga), and to several contraceptives named in the agreement — Alesse, Marvelon, Yasmin, Plan B and Nuvaring among them — where the resident may pay part of the cost unless they switch to a generic equivalent [5]. This is a defensible cost-control design, and it is also the reason a patient can walk into a pharmacy in a "free contraception" province and be quoted a price. The product is covered; the brand is not.

**What is on the list.** The BC annex covers, on the diabetes side, insulins, metformin, glyburide, gliclazide, a set of SGLT-2 inhibitors and DPP-4 inhibitor combinations, and on the contraception side fourteen product categories: oral contraceptive pills, copper and hormonal IUDs, the vaginal ring, the implant, the injection, and emergency contraception [5]. The newest and fastest-growing class of diabetes drugs — the GLP-1 receptor agonists such as Ozempic, Trulicity and Mounjaro — is almost entirely absent: the one GLP-1 in Manitoba's annex is lixisenatide with insulin glargine, a single combination product available only under Exception Drug Status with prior approval [19]. For anything outside the covered categories — asthma, hypertension, an autoimmune disease, HIV, cancer — a resident gets nothing from this program, however poor they are, unless their provincial plan already covers them. The first phase is not a small version of universal pharmacare; it is a different product with a narrow set of covered categories attached. The category count is not exactly two, either: both the BC and Manitoba agreements add free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy for menopause as a condition of the deal [7][19], and Manitoba's agreement puts insulin pumps and advanced glucose monitors in a separate funded stream [19]. Provinces can and do widen the envelope at the margin, but only within what they negotiate and co-fund.

**The gap between the announcement language and the annex matters for how take-up is measured.** If coverage is universal within a jurisdiction but conditional per product, then the number of people resident in a covered jurisdiction, the number who filled a listed prescription at zero cost, and the number who obtained a drug they could not previously afford are three different quantities. The program's own materials do not present a single headline enrolment figure for the four signed jurisdictions, which is why the take-up question in the next section has to be answered from fragments.

### 4. How many people are actually using it: enrolment, claims and take-up evidence, and where the numbers do not exist

There is no enrolment number to report, because the program has no enrolment. Health Canada states that a resident of a signed jurisdiction is covered regardless of age, income, or private insurance status [4], and the agreements require coverage at the point of sale for listed products without deductibles, copays, premiums or dispensing fees [5]. Nothing in that design requires a person to register, apply, means-test or prove they lack coverage. The benefit is a property of residence. So the honest answer to "how many people are enrolled" is that the concept does not apply — and the number that would answer the question a reader actually has (how many people have obtained a drug they would otherwise have paid for) is a claims count, which Health Canada's pharmacare pages do not publish.

**What the public pages do and do not contain.** The three Health Canada pages read for this report — the bilateral agreements index, what's covered, and who's covered — present eligibility rules, a product list and links to four news releases [2][3][4]. None of them states a number of residents covered, a number of prescriptions filled, a number of claimants, or a spend-to-date. The agreements index, in its 26 January 2026 revision, is a list of four titles and four announcement links [2]. This is not unusual for a transfer program in its first year — the federal government sends money and the province administers the benefit — but it means that anyone asserting a take-up figure is drawing on provincial health-plan data, provincial ministry statements, or pharmacy-claims data, not on a federal published series.

**Where the number could be constructed, and why it would be an upper bound.** The population resident in the four signed jurisdictions is the ceiling on anyone who *could* use the program, not a measure of use. Within that ceiling, three further filters apply. The person must need one of two categories of medicine — contraception or diabetes treatment — which excludes most prescription users. The specific product must be on the annex, which excludes the GLP-1 class and every non-diabetes, non-contraceptive drug [5]. And where the resident chooses a brand-name product subject to the Low Cost Alternative policy, they may pay a portion of the cost rather than nothing [5]. Each filter reduces the number of people for whom the program delivers a zero-dollar transaction.

**The three numbers that do exist, and what each measures.** First, reach by residency: the four signed jurisdictions hold nearly 7.5 million people [17], so four out of five Canadians live outside the program. Second, program spending: the federal government contributed $88.1 million in 2025-26, projected to rise to $269.6 million by 2028-29 [16] — a spend rate consistent with a slow phase-in, since the four agreements together are worth $928 million over four years [17]. Third, and closest to a real utilization measure, BC's experience under its own pre-existing provincial contraception program: approximately 227,000 people received free prescription contraception in 2024, and more than 306,000 since the program began on 1 April 2023 [7]. Health Canada's own reach estimates at signing were 1.3 million British Columbians for contraception and nearly 550,000 with diabetes in BC [7]; nearly 350,000 and over 149,000 respectively in Manitoba [8]; over 41,000 and over 16,000 in PEI [9]; more than 12,000 and over 3,000 in Yukon [10]. Those are population estimates of who is eligible, not counts of who used the benefit. My inference, from comparing the two BC figures: if 1.3 million British Columbians are within reach of contraception coverage and roughly 227,000 received free contraception through the provincial program in 2024, then eligibility and use are an order of magnitude apart — which is why an eligibility-based headline ("1.3 million people supported") should never be read as a utilization figure.

**What would settle it.** Provincial claims data from BC PharmaCare, Manitoba Health, PEI's provincial drug program and Yukon's health plan. The agreements do require annual attested financial statements and results reports, due 1 October each year from 2026-27 [19], so the data exists inside government; it has simply not been published on the pharmacare web pages. The report's Open questions section records this as the largest single gap in the public evidence: the program can say who is eligible and what is covered, but it does not publicly say how many people have used it.

### 5. What the Parliamentary Budget Officer and other independent estimators say full national pharmacare would cost, and why their figures differ

The estimates do not disagree about arithmetic. They disagree about what "the full program" means, and about two assumptions that swing the total by billions. Getting this right requires holding four separate numbers apart, because they are routinely compared as though they were the same thing.

**First, the cost of what was actually legislated: $1.9 billion over five years, against $1.5 billion budgeted.** The Parliamentary Budget Officer's legislative costing of Bill C-64 estimated that the first phase — contraception and diabetes products — would increase federal program spending by $1.9 billion over five years, on the assumption that medications currently covered by governments and private insurers stay covered on the same terms [11]. The government had budgeted $1.5 billion for the same purpose in Budget 2024 [15]. The PBO's figure therefore exceeded the fiscal envelope by roughly $400 million, and the gap is a direct consequence of the design: the federal government pays out-of-pocket costs that already exist rather than replacing existing coverage.

**The PBO's method for that number, stated plainly.** The program "will cover 100% of the expense on diabetes and contraception medication for those who currently do not have public or private drug plan coverage and for those who currently do not fill their prescriptions due to cost related reasons. The latter group is assumed to be 14% of total prescriptions. The program will also cover the out-of-pocket portion of prescription costs for those who have public or private drug plan coverage" [11]. Two things follow. The 14% cost-related non-adherence figure is a behavioural assumption doing real work in the total. And because the benefit pays the out-of-pocket slice for people who already have insurance, most of the $1.9 billion is not new medicine consumption — it is a transfer from patients and insurers to the federal government.

**The PBO flagged its own number as soft, in the direction that matters.** "The estimate has high uncertainty and is contingent on the number of drugs listed for coverage. Drug expenditures have several cost drivers and the projections are highly sensitive to the projected growth rate of those cost drivers, and the determinants of those cost factors" [11]. More specifically, the PBO excluded substitution: "Behavioural effects such as substitution from the drugs not listed on the formulary to the drugs on the formulary are not accounted for in this cost estimate and could increase the total estimated cost" [11]. If listing metformin at zero dollars causes patients and prescribers to move off a costlier unlisted drug, the real cost is higher than $1.9 billion. The published figure is a floor, not a midpoint.

**Second, the cost of a full single-payer plan: $11.2 billion in 2024-25, rising to $13.4 billion in 2027-28.** This is the PBO's estimate of the *incremental* cost to the public sector — "federal and provincial governments combined" — of a universal, single-payer plan with a RAMQ-style national formulary [12]. It is not comparable to the $1.9 billion, because it is a different program: every prescription drug for every resident, not two drug classes. The PBO's total drug expenditure under that plan is $33.2 billion in 2024-25, rising to $38.9 billion in 2027-28 [12].

**The single-payer result is counterintuitive and is the most important finding in the costing literature.** The public sector pays $11.2 billion more, but the country as a whole spends less: "In terms of the economy as a whole, we estimate cost savings on drug expenditures of $1.4 billion in 2024-25, rising to $2.2 billion in 2027-28" [12]. The mechanism is that a single payer extends to the privately insured and cash-paying population the confidential rebates and generic substitution that public plans already get, so total spending falls even as public spending rises. The PBO's model assumes patients' point-of-sale prices "fall by 47 per cent to 100 per cent, which results in overall increases in the utilization of prescription drugs of 13.5 per cent" [12] — and even with that utilization increase, the total falls. For context, the PBO puts non-hospital prescription drug spending at roughly $36.6 billion in 2021-22, a 28 per cent increase over 2015-16 [12].

**Third, the estimate that most sharply contradicts the PBO: $6 billion to $10 billion, from the National Pharmacare Committee of Experts.** The committee, established under section 11 of the Act and reporting in November 2025, concluded that the total cost of publicly funding a list of essential medicines would likely fall between $6 billion and $10 billion [14]. Its figure is lower than the PBO's $11.2 billion because it is a narrower program — a list of 185 off-patent essential medicines rather than the whole RAMQ formulary — but the committee is explicit that the difference is also about assumptions. Its bottom-up method took the 185 medicines on the essential prescription drugs list prepared by the Canada's Drug Agency committee — all off-patent, with multiple sources — and started from the $12.6 billion actually spent on them in 2024, then adjusted for pricing, markups, tendering, population and volume growth [14].

**The two assumptions that drive the $5 billion gap.** First, tendering. The committee assumes competitive procurement cuts prices substantially; it notes manufacturers "have offered in 2018 to reduce prices paid by public drug plans by a reported 25% to 40%" in exchange for not tendering, and that the no-tendering agreement "expires in 2026" [14]. The PBO's model does not assume tendering savings of that scale. Second, induced utilization. The committee chose 5%, and says so directly: "We selected 5% for our lower bound estimate, while the upper bound estimate from the Parliamentary Budget Office assumes an increase of 13.5%, which is larger than estimates in the literature" [14]. A 13.5% utilization increase versus 5% is a large share of the difference between $6 billion and $11 billion, and it is an empirical disagreement about behaviour, not about accounting.

**The committee's number is also not the same kind of number, which is the trap in comparing them.** It assumes the federal government covers the entire cost of the covered medicines and that provincial and territorial contributions are zero [14] — a gross federal figure. The PBO's is incremental, net of status quo spending. The committee acknowledges the asymmetry: existing public spending on the included medicines "may account for more than 30% of the cost" [14]. So $6–10 billion gross federal and $11.2 billion net public-sector are not points on one scale; a reader who subtracts one from the other gets nonsense.

**Fourth, the formulary-sensitivity result, which is the strongest evidence that breadth is the whole ballgame.** The PBO costed two alternative formularies against its baseline. A single-payer plan with a *catastrophic* formulary — covering only very high-cost drugs — would cost the public sector $1.8 billion in 2024-25 and $2.0 billion in 2027-28 [12], roughly a sixth of the full-formulary figure. And an *essential-medicines* formulary came out slightly *more* expensive than the baseline: PBO "estimates that drug expenditures under this alternative to be $0.4 billion and $0.3 billion more than the estimated spending under the baseline scenario in 2024-25 and 2027-28 respectively" [12]. That is because the drugs on an essential list are mostly cheap generics already, so covering them in full adds utilization without generating offsetting savings. Anyone quoting a single "cost of pharmacare" number is quoting a formulary decision.

**The savings claims, and how much weight they bear.** The 2019 Advisory Council report, *A Prescription for Canada*, estimated that by 2027, with a comprehensive formulary, Canada "would spend $5 billion less on prescription drugs while at the same time improving access for all" [16]. The committee's evidence for why savings are available is the price gap: it cites a 2017 Auditor General of Ontario finding that "prices paid the Ontario Public Drugs Program were 70% higher than prices in New Zealand, and also 85% higher than prices paid by hospitals in Ontario" [14]. These are credible findings from credible bodies, and they support the claim that Canadian drug prices are high relative to comparators. They do not support the stronger claim that pharmacare *saves money overall* under every design — the PBO's own modelling says total spending falls by $1.4–2.2 billion a year in the single-payer case, which is a real but modest saving against roughly $33–39 billion in total expenditure, and its essential-medicines variant finds no saving at all.

**The scale of the status quo, for comparison.** Total prescribed-drug spending rose "by $10 billion in 5 years – from $34 billion in 2019 to $44 billion in 2024" [14]; the committee elsewhere puts all-payer prescription spending at about $45 billion in 2024, "equivalent to around 11% of the federal budget" [14]. Canadians paid $8 billion out of pocket for prescription drugs in 2023 and another $15.8 billion through private insurance [16]. Every estimate above is a rearrangement of that $40–45 billion base, which is why the distributional question — who pays, not how much — is the one that actually differs between designs.

**What the four agreements have cost so far, against these numbers.** The four bilateral agreements are worth $928 million over four years [17], and actual federal spending was $88.1 million in 2025-26, projected to rise to $269.6 million by 2028-29 [16]. Set against the PBO's $1.9 billion five-year first-phase estimate, the program is currently spending at a rate consistent with a slow phase-in rather than a program running at its estimated cost. Set against the $11.2 billion single-payer estimate, the delivered program is two orders of magnitude smaller in scope: two drug classes in four jurisdictions, not all drugs for everyone.

### 6. What remains unbuilt — national formulary, single-payer, bulk purchasing — and where the program stands politically

**The statutory homework was done, on time, and then shelved.** All four deliverables required by the Act were produced. Health Canada's own account lists that it "received advice from a committee of experts on how to operate and finance national pharmacare, received advice from Canada's Drug Agency on a national bulk purchasing strategy and on a list of essential prescription drugs and related products, and published a pan-Canadian strategy to promote appropriate use of prescription drugs and related products [13]. The Committee of Experts' final report was submitted in November 2025 [18]. So the machinery section 8, 9 and 11 of the Act set in motion did run. What did not follow was a decision. As of late 2026, "no action has been taken" on the committee's report [18].

**The essential-medicines list exists but has no legal force.** It is advice to a Minister, not a formulary, and there is no reimbursement obligation attached to it. This is the gap the Act's critics predicted: a list "to inform the development of a national formulary" [1] is not a national formulary, and a national formulary is not a national purchasing decision. The bulk purchasing strategy has the same status — a strategy, with no entity compelled to buy through it and no province obliged to participate [1].

**The Committee of Experts rejected the model the government actually implemented.** This is the most pointed finding in the whole record, because the committee was the government's own creation under the Act. It rejects the idea of a limited fill-the-gaps model and instead advocates universal, single-payer, publicly administered pharmacare on human-rights grounds [14]. It argued that a single-payer approach "avoids the drawbacks of bilateral agreements, enshrines universal access and strengthens the ability to negotiate drug prices with drug companies" [14]. And it named the delivery mechanism as the failure point: alternative shared-funding options "would require the type of bilateral funding agreements which have been proven to be challenging and time consuming, as demonstrated by implementation of the 2024 Act Respecting Pharmacare" [14]. Its counter-example is the dental care and childcare programs — "initiatives fully funded by the federal government that provide dental care, childcare and other services administered by provincial and territorial governments have all been successfully implemented within short time frames" [14]. In other words, the government's own expert panel concluded that the design it chose was the reason it stalled, and that unconditional federal funding would have moved faster.

**The fragmentation the program was meant to end is intact.** The committee counted 6 federal public drug plans, over 100 provincial and territorial drug plans, and over 100,000 private drug plans [14]. Pharmacare has not merged any of them. It has added a first-dollar layer over four of them, for two drug classes, funded at roughly 70 per cent federal share [14].

**Politically, the program is being allowed to expire.** The trajectory is documented across three budgets. Budget 2024 committed $1.5 billion over five years, and "there has been no new funding since" [18]. The November 2025 budget contained no new pharmacare funding or announcements, and the spring 2026 economic update mentioned it only in passing [18]. On the CCPA's reading of that update, there will be no new federal funding for additional pharmacare deals, with bilateral health funding falling from $4.3 billion in 2025-26 to $3.1 billion in 2027-28 [16]. The existing agreements appear set to expire without renewal, and jurisdictions that want to keep the coverage will have to fill the gap themselves [16].

**The consequences have already surfaced at the provincial level.** In April 2026, PEI's health minister disclosed that Ottawa would cut $29 million in health care funding to the province over three years, and after PEI raised the issue publicly, Newfoundland and Labrador's health minister said "the door was closed on our province" [16]. Newfoundland and Labrador was never a signatory, so its complaint is about being refused a deal, not about losing one — which is consistent with industry reporting that several interested provinces have not received significant engagement from the federal government [18].

**Why the stall matters more than it looks: the baseline problem it was meant to fix is unchanged.** Diabetes Canada calculated in 2022 that out-of-pocket costs ran "as high as $18,306 per year for people living with Type 1 diabetes and as high as $10,014 per year for those living with Type 2 diabetes" [7]. About 3.8 million people in Canada have been diagnosed with diabetes, and health-system costs related to it were estimated at $27 billion in 2018, potentially surpassing $39 billion by 2028 [13]. The covered drugs are the cheap ones — metformin at about $100 a year, insulin at $900 to $1,700 [13] — so the program addresses the most common prescribing, not the catastrophic cases. PEI's health minister said the quiet part: residents there "face some of Canada's highest out-of-pocket costs for drugs covered on their public plans" [9]. That is the constituency the program served, and it is the one now exposed if the agreements lapse.

**What is genuinely delivered, stated without either side's framing.** Four jurisdictions covering nearly 7.5 million people [17] have first-dollar coverage of a closed list of contraceptives and older diabetes drugs, with no income test and no coordination with private insurance, funded by $928 million in agreements [17] and $88.1 million of actual federal spending in 2025-26 rising toward $269.6 million by 2028-29 [16]. Two of those jurisdictions went further than required and added free hormone replacement therapy [7][8]. That is a real program with real beneficiaries. It is also not a national pharmacare program, was never designed to become one automatically, and is now scheduled — by the absence of renewed funding rather than by any amending legislation — to stop.

## Open questions

**Nobody publishes a take-up number, and the data that would answer the question is contractually held but unreleased.** The agreements require provinces to submit attested financial statements and results reports by 1 October each year starting in 2026-27 [19]. Those reports would give claims and spending by jurisdiction. They are not published. Until Health Canada or the provinces release them, the honest answer to "how many people are using it" is a ceiling — the roughly 7.5 million residents of the four signed jurisdictions [17] — and not a count of users. The single best figure in the public record is not a count of pharmacare users at all: BC reported that approximately 227,000 people received free prescription contraception in 2024 under its own pre-existing provincial program, more than 306,000 since April 2023 [7]. That is a provincial program's experience, not a measurement of the federal benefit.

**The four agreements' published dollar values do not reconcile across sources and should be treated as approximate.** The CCPA puts the four at $928 million over four years [17]. Health Canada's releases give "more than $670 million" for BC [7], "more than $219 million" for Manitoba [8], "more than $30 million" for PEI [9] and "up to $9.5 million" for Yukon [10] — which adds to roughly the CCPA total (my addition, from the four release figures), but Manitoba's agreement text itself itemises $52,509,230 plus three years at $54,603,615 — a four-year main-stream total that works out lower than the $219 million headline — plus a one-time $9,945,348 for devices [19]. Readers comparing press-release totals to agreement schedules will find differences of a few million dollars per jurisdiction. The agreement text is the stronger source.

**The estimates are less independent of each other than they look, and this report leans on them together in places.** The documentary record comes from a handful of institutional origins. The Health Canada and canada.ca pages, including the Committee of Experts report and the Manitoba agreement text [2][3][4][5][7][8][9][10][13][14][19], are one publisher. The two PBO publications [11][12] are one publisher. The two CCPA pieces [16][17] are one publisher, and [16] is substantially republished by The Tyee. The Committee of Experts report also reproduces long passages of the Pharmacare Act itself, so it is not fully independent of [1]. Where the report presents a disagreement — PBO versus the Committee of Experts on cost, the government versus its own panel on design — those are genuinely different institutions with different mandates, and the cost disagreement is substantive rather than artefactual, since it turns on stated assumptions about tendering and induced utilization that can be checked against the documents. But they are not a large sample, and the "independent estimates" the question asks for really number three: the PBO, the Committee of Experts, and the 2019 Advisory Council.

**The 2019 Advisory Council report was not read.** Its $5 billion saving claim is reported here at second hand from the CCPA [16]. Given that the Council's 2019 report is the intellectual foundation of the whole program, this is the most important primary document still unread, and the next pass should read it directly before anyone cites its numbers.

**The political account rests on secondary sources with a clear editorial position.** The evidence that the program is being wound down comes from the CCPA [16], an advocacy organisation that supports pharmacare, plus an industry trade publication [18] and search-result summaries of CBC and Toronto Star reporting that could not be fetched. The CBC report — in which the health minister is quoted saying her department is not in active discussions to sign more agreements — is the key independent corroboration and was not read in full. The factual core (no new funding, falling bilateral envelope, no fifth agreement) is corroborated across all three, so the finding stands; the framing that this constitutes "abandonment" is the CCPA's characterisation, not an established fact.

**Some figures in the record contradict each other on the program's start dates.** Health Canada's Manitoba release said residents could expect coverage for most products in June 2025 [8], but the agreement sets an implementation date of 15 April 2025 [19]. Yukon's release said coverage no later than January 2026 [10] and BC's said March 2026 [7]. Whether each province actually hit its date is not confirmed by any source read here.

**What the next pass should read.** The 2019 Advisory Council report; the CBC and Toronto Star reporting on the wind-down; the CDA's essential medicines list and national bulk purchasing strategy documents themselves (referenced by Health Canada [13] but not read); and the 2027-28 Departmental Plan or Main Estimates line for pharmacare, which would show whether the $269.6 million projection [16] survives contact with an appropriation.

## Beyond this question

The Pharmacare Act is a case study in a specific failure mode of program design, and it is worth naming because it will recur. The Act's authors wanted national universal pharmacare and could not legislate it, so they legislated a funding channel that would create it province by province. That choice put the program's survival in the hands of nine governments that had no obligation to sign, and it made the federal government's own expert panel conclude that the route it chose was the reason it stalled [14]. The committee's counter-example — dental care and childcare, fully federally funded and delivered within short time frames [14] — is the same federal government succeeding at the same task by a different instrument in the same period.

For anyone writing about this, the discipline the record rewards is separating four numbers that get collapsed: money committed ($1.5 billion), money actually spent ($88.1 million in 2025-26), people eligible (about 7.5 million), and people served (unpublished). A program can be real and funded and still reach a fraction of the country — and the way to tell the difference is to ask for the claims count, which is exactly the number the agreements require but nobody has published.

sentences.sentence: The diffusion itself is the fastest in schooling in decades: "114 education systems now have a national ban on mobile phones in schools, representing 58% of countries worldwide", up from 24% in June 2023 and 40% by early 2025 [17]. **Ontario.** The province updated its Code of Conduct, effective 1 September 2024, with a rule tiered by age: "Students Grade 7 and above may not use cellphones or other mobiles devices during class time without the explicit permission of their teacher.

Students Grade 6 and below may not use cellphones or other mobile devices at school during the school day without the permission of a teacher." [3] The split continues into breaks: "If your child is in Grade 7 or older, they can bring a mobile device to school and use it during recess or lunch.
If your child is in Grade 6 or younger, they can bring a mobile device to school, but will only be able to use it before and after school." [3] It is not a phone-free campus.

"Students may keep their cellphone, tablet or smart watch with them, but they must do all of the following: turn it off — or set it to silent mode store it out of view (for example, in a bag or pocket)" [3].

Enforcement triggers only on visibility: "If an educator sees a mobile device that is not stored out of view, they will ask it to be handed in for the class (Grades 7-12) or for the day (Grades k-6)." [3] Boards must publish an enforcement policy and remind parents annually; the stated aims are "keeping students focused on learning by removing distractions" and "promoting mental health" [3].

A medical exception is mandatory: "Your school must provide an exception if your child needs to use a mobile device to support, monitor or regulate their health or medical condition." [3] No provincial evaluation of the Ontario rule appears in the evidence assembled here. **England.** England's guidance covers the whole day but leaves the mechanism to each head: "All schools should be mobile phone-free environments by default; anything other than this should be by exception only" [4], and it "prohibits the use of mobile phones throughout the school day, including during lessons, the time between lessons, breaktimes and lunchtime" [4].

It expects more than a rule — the Department for Education "expects schools to implement a policy whereby pupils do not have access to their mobile phone throughout the school day" [4] — and names the harms it is aimed at: "These risks can include a loss of focus in lessons, classroom disruption and an increase in bullying." [4] Timing matters for reading the English evidence: "This guidance became statutory on 29 June 2026" [4], with schools to begin following it from 1 September 2026.

Even now the duty is qualified: "Allowing a disabled pupil access to their mobile phone during the school day, where it is necessary due to the nature of their disability, may be considered a reasonable adjustment and a failure to do so may be a breach of the school’s duty." [4] By the time the law caught up, restriction was already the norm — in the SMART Schools sampling frame of 1,341 state secondary schools within 100 miles of Birmingham, 1,245 had restrictive policies and 96 were permissive [14].

Vanaf het schooljaar 2024-2025 is het gebruik van mobiele telefoons niet meer toegestaan op basisscholen en het (voortgezet) speciaal (basis) onderwijs." [19] It covers phones, tablets and smartwatches, and applies to non-educational use, with exemptions where the lesson requires a device (media literacy, say) or a pupil depends on one for medical reasons or a disability [19].

Crucially, it was not legislation: the July 2023 announcement records an agreement between the education minister and the sector bodies — VO-raad, LAKS, the teaching unions, parents' organisations — with a commitment to "Eind volgend schooljaar wordt geëvalueerd of de afspraak het gewenste effect heeft of dat eventueel toch een wettelijk verbod nodig is" [20], an evaluation of whether the agreement worked or a statutory ban was needed.

Implementation is devolved: "Scholen moeten zelf met leraren, leerlingen en hun ouders afspraken maken hoe dit er op hún school precies uit gaat zien." [19] And it spans very different regimes, since "Scholen kunnen zelf de keuze maken om mobieltjes helemaal uit de school te weren" [20] — schools may bar phones from the premises entirely, or simply require them out of sight.

[19] That claim is stronger than the Dutch government's own evidence review supports, as section 2 shows. **Victoria.** Victoria has the hardest legal form of the jurisdictions examined here: "All government, Catholic and independent schools must restrict student use of personal electronic devices during the school day.
This is a requirement of the Education and Training Reform Act 2006 and Ministerial Order No. 1515 – Personal Electronic Devices in Victorian Schools" [18].

From 2027 the rule extends beyond phones: "Mobile phones and smart glasses brought to school must be switched off and stored in a way that restricts student access to them", wearables must have notifications, cellular connection and recording turned off, and personal audio devices are barred during school hours [18].
Exemptions are codified rather than discretionary — only to support "student learning", "health or wellbeing", or "managing safety when offsite" [18].
Victoria's aims are explicit and testable: "reduce unnecessary distraction in the classroom" and "promote more social interaction and physical activity during break times" [18].

Specifically, the policy requires students in all government schools to keep their personal devices, including mobile phones, off and away between the start and end of each school day and while attending authorized school activities off-site" [11].

Other Australian states — New South Wales, Queensland, Western Australia — were not verified from their own departmental pages in this pass, and their policies are not characterised here. **The United States.** No national ban, but near-universal state action: "39 states now have statewide bans (15) or regulations requiring school districts to adopt policies restricting phone use in classrooms (24)" [17].

Comoros, Colombia, Estonia, Lithuania, Iceland, Peru, Indonesia, Serbia, Poland and the Philippines are among those." [17] That placement of Iceland matters: its null result comes from schools that opted into bans under a national framework, not from a country-wide prohibition.
England sits in the same weaker category — "the policy leaves implementation decisions to individual schools" [17].

Among 20 "restrictive" schools in SMART Schools, 16 simply required phones to be kept switched off in bags; only four made phones inaccessible at all — a locker, a pouch, hand-in, or exclusion from the premises [14].

Bans reduce psychological health care use among girls, lower bullying for both genders, and improve girls’ GPAs and academic track placement, especially among those from disadvantaged backgrounds." [1] The structure of that finding is worth dwelling on: the average effect on attainment is zero, and the entire measured gain sits with girls, and within that group mostly with girls from disadvantaged backgrounds.

A policy justified by an average effect would be justified by a number that does not exist. **Florida (Figlio & Özek, NBER Working Paper 34388, October 2025).** This is the largest student-level study, using Florida data and "a quasi-experimental research strategy relying upon differences in pre-ban cellphone use by students, as measured by building-level Advan data" [5].

First, "the enforcement of cellphone bans in schools led to a significant increase in student suspensions in the short-term, especially among Black students, but disciplinary actions began to dissipate after the first year, potentially suggesting a new steady state after an initial adjustment period." Second, "we find significant improvements in student test scores in the second year of the ban after that initial adjustment period" [5].
We then show that test scores, which were trending similarly in the two groups prior to the ban, improved by 0.06 s.d. in treatment schools relative to control" [7].

Comparing restrictive with permissive schools, pupils in restrictive schools were no more or less likely to be rated below target in English (adjusted odds ratio 1.45, 95% CI 0.85 to 2.47, p = 0.18) or in maths (1.01, 0.45 to 2.27, p = 0.98), and there was no difference in teacher-rated classroom disruptiveness (0.06, 95% CI −0.57 to 0.68, p = 0.88) [14].
"Linear mixed models indicated that ban and no ban school groups did not differ significantly in terms of problematic phone use, academic engagement, and school belonging" [11].

One caveat on its rigour: the protocol was registered in December 2023, after data collection in June and August 2023, so it is a registered analysis rather than a prospectively pre-registered trial [16]. **The reviews.** The broadest synthesis of the before-and-after literature is a scoping review by Campbell and Edwards (QUT/UQ) that screened 1,317 articles, reports and dissertations and found 22 studies of schools before and after phone bans.
However, two of these studies found this improvement only applied to disadvantaged or low-achieving students" [2].

[2] Two of the three nulls rest on near-population samples, which is a firmer basis for confidence than four positive studies, several of them small. **The strongest test uses pouches, and it finds nothing on achievement.** The most rigorous study in this literature is a national, pre-registered staggered difference-in-differences evaluation of lockable phone pouches (Allcott, Baron, Dee, Duckworth, Gentzkow & Jacob, NBER Working Paper 35132).

We find little evidence of effects on school attendance and no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention or perceived online bullying." [15] That study does three things to this section's argument.
It also agrees with Florida on short-term disruption: disciplinary incidents rose in year one in both studies [5, 15].

Florida's third finding deserves recording because it offers a mechanism for the gains it does find: "the findings suggest that cellphone bans in schools significantly reduce student unexcused absences, an effect that may explain a large fraction of the test score gains" [5].

If the gain runs through attendance rather than attention, the policy is an attendance intervention, not a concentration one. **The Dutch government's own evidence review is more cautious than its policy.** The Kennisrotonde answer that the ministry links to as the scientific basis for the 2024 restriction states plainly that the causal link is unestablished: "Hoewel het oorzakelijk verband tussen smartphonegebruik en leerprestaties niet expliciet is onderzocht, is afleiding de meest genoemde waarschijnlijke verklaring voor de negatieve samenhang." [21] — the association between phone use and attainment is negative and consistent, distraction is the most-cited explanation, but the causal relationship had not been explicitly investigated.

Om daarmee te voorkomen dat leerlingen/studenten vervolgens worden afgeleid door apps op andere apparatuur, zoals laptops of tablets." [21] That is, a phone ban makes sense only as part of a wider ICT policy, lest pupils be distracted by laptops and tablets instead.
The one study that measured enforcement strength at national scale with objective phone-use data found that use fell substantially and average achievement did not move [15].

What remains of the pattern is subgroup concentration: gains for lower-achieving pupils [2], for girls from disadvantaged backgrounds [1], modest high-school maths gains in the pouch study [15], and a second-year gain in Florida [5].

The chain mostly holds at the first link and breaks at the second. **Phone use in school falls, and that is the most robust finding in the literature.** SMART Schools found that pupils in restrictive schools used phones less during school: adjusted mean difference −0.67 hours for phone time (95% CI −0.92 to −0.43, p = 0.00024) and −0.54 hours for social media time (95% CI −0.74 to −0.36, p = 0.00018) [12].

The measurement caveat matters, though: those estimates are self-report only, because the study's phone screen-time app data were excluded for implausible values, and the authors warn that under-reporting in restrictive schools could make the gap an over-estimate [14].
Rio de Janeiro's causal design found the same direction and called the reduction substantial: in-school phone use "fell substantially in treatment schools relative to control" [7].
South Australia's evaluation did not find a difference in *problematic* phone use, but that is a different measure — dependence-like symptoms rather than minutes [11].

The pouch study's GPS-ping data avoid that problem entirely, which is why its confirmation matters more: pouch adoption "substantially reduces phone use as measured by GPS pings and teacher reports" [15]. **The displacement problem.** SMART Schools' own next sentence limits what that first result means: pupils in restrictive schools had lower phone and social media time during school, "but there was no evidence for differences when comparing usage time on weekdays or weekends" [12].

The evidence cannot yet distinguish those two models, but the displacement result is a direct measurement that total use did not change in England. **Disruption, as teachers see it, did not change in England.** Teacher-rated classroom disruptiveness in SMART Schools showed an adjusted difference of 0.06 (95% CI −0.57 to 0.68, p = 0.88) between restrictive and permissive schools [14].
The pouch study strengthens it: pupils there reported no clear improvement in classroom attention either [15], measured against a design that cut phone use objectively.

Two different designs, two different measures of attention, the same answer. **Policy strictness does relate to checking, which is a smaller claim than it looks.** The RAND survey's own headline is that "more-restrictive cell phone policies mitigate but do not fully eliminate students' cell phone checking" [8].

The point is what follows from that: the pouch study cut phone use substantially and still found no attention or achievement gain, which means the gap between "less checking" and "better learning" is where the policy case has to be made, and it is the step no study has demonstrated. **Where phones are absent by default, pupils use them constantly.** The sharpest descriptive evidence on the counterfactual comes from a nationally representative RAND survey of 922 US students in grades 6–12, fielded December 2025 to January 2026: "In the most lenient environments, roughly eight in ten students said they are checking their cell phones during their classes at least once per day" [8].

That establishes the size of the behaviour a ban is aimed at — it does not establish that a ban changes it, and the same survey's other findings on how rules relate to checking behaviour would be the natural next thing to read. **South Australia: compliance was high and nothing moved anyway.** "Overall, 87% of participants reported that they were compliant with the phone ban" [11].

The authors also identified who did not comply: being older, posting on social media more often, having used a phone at school before the ban, and having experienced bullying all predicted non-compliance [11].

The SA authors set out four candidate explanations for their null, and they are worth quoting because each is testable and none has been tested: "The lack of an effect may have been due to: students having access to other digital devices; the restriction period being too brief to properly challenge students' use of phones; limited ‘fear of missing out’ effects given that peers were also without phones, and/or; the ban during school hours simply increased anticipation and reward salience associated with phones rather than lowering overall ‘dose’ and ‘interference’ related to phone use" [11].
Between 2018 and 2023, 22 of the 70 schools adopted schoolwide bans prohibiting student phone use during school hours [13].

The result: "In the postpolicy period from 2018 to 2023, schoolwide mobile phone bans were not associated with meaningful changes in depressive symptoms (β, 0.65 [95% CI, 0.01-1.30]), anxiety (β, 0.21 [95% CI, −0.08 to 0.50]), hostility (β, 0.23 [95% CI, −0.12 to 0.59]), and mental well-being (β, −0.52 [95% CI, −1.08 to 0.03])" [10].

Second, the null is not confined to the headline outcomes: "Results were similar in gender-stratified analyses and for the secondary outcomes" [10], and the secondary outcomes included perceived peer support, screen use across four categories, and bullying both in person and cyberbullying [13].
Sensitivity analyses on the timing of implementation and on more stringent restriction criteria were consistent with the main findings [13].

The authors' own reading is a claim about policy design, not just about effect size: "These findings suggest that school phone bans implemented in isolation may be insufficient to improve adolescent mental health at the population level" [13].
The primary outcome, mental wellbeing on the Warwick–Edinburgh scale, had a mean of 47 (SD 9) with no evidence of a difference: adjusted mean difference −0.48, 95% CI −2.05 to 1.06, p = 0.62 [12].
Secondary outcomes were equally flat: anxiety 0.10 (95% CI −0.76 to 0.97, p = 0.84), depression −0.04 (−0.98 to 0.92, p = 0.94), and problematic social media use 0.5 (−2.6 to 3.53, p = 0.80) [14].

The study was powered to detect a 3-point WEMWBS difference, which its authors treat as the minimum clinically important difference [14], so the null is a null about effects big enough to matter, not merely a failure to reach significance on a trivial effect.

The findings do not provide evidence to support the use of school policies that prohibit phone use during the school day in their current form, and indicate that these policies require further development" [12].

The study mitigated this with propensity-score stratified sampling on school characteristics including region, urban or rural, roll size, deprivation, sixth form, admissions, religious affiliation and pupil composition, and pupil characteristics were well balanced across groups [14].
But school-level participation was very low: "The response rate at the school level was 8.73% for schools with restrictive phone policies and 10.42% for schools with permissive phone policies" [14].

Thirty schools is a small and self-selected sample of institutions, whatever the balance within it. **Norway finds a gender-specific mental health effect where the others find none.** Bans "reduce psychological health care use among girls" and "lower bullying for both genders", against no average effect on mental health [1].

That the effect appears only in girls, in a country with a different school system and phone culture from England or Iceland, is the kind of finding that should generate a hypothesis rather than settle a policy question. **Bullying: the one place a ban might be doing something, and the evidence is split.** Norway's reduction in bullying for both genders is the only causal estimate in this set pointing that way [1].
South Australia's evaluation found the reverse ordering without a causal story: "There was slightly higher bullying in the ban group but bullying decreased significantly in both groups" [11].
England's cross-sectional comparison found no association between policy type and bullying as one of its secondary outcomes [10].

And the national pouch study, which is the strongest test available, found "no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention or perceived online bullying" [15] — despite objectively verified falls in phone use.

The Iceland authors, reviewing the field, report that "a smaller study from South Australia evaluating a state-mandated phone ban introduced in 2023 reported small but significant reductions in psychological distress, including symptoms of depression and anxiety, and in negative affect" [10].
The nearest proxies are Iceland's perceived peer support, which did not change [13], and England's social media motives, which did not change on any of four subscales after adjustment [14].
In a sign of just how little research there is on this topic, 12 of the studies we identified were done by masters and doctoral students" [2].

The English team noted in 2025 that before their own study there were "currently no published peer-reviewed studies reporting on the association between school phone policies, adolescent phone/media use behaviours and mental health, wellbeing and other related outcomes" [14] — the field's flagship national evaluation was, at the time, the first of its kind. **The designs, ranked.** On internal validity, the strongest is **the national pouch study** [15] — pre-registered, staggered difference-in-differences, objective phone-use measurement via GPS pings and teacher reports, multiple post-adoption years.

After it: 1. **The national pouch study** [15] — pre-registered, staggered difference-in-differences, objective phone-use measurement via GPS pings and teacher reports, and multiple post-adoption years.

Its weakness is that pouches were adopted by schools or districts rather than assigned, so adoption may correlate with school culture; and it measures pouches specifically, not statutes. 2. **Iceland's difference-in-differences** [10, 13] — 70 schools, 23,938 observations, three waves, 22 schools switching policy, national survey, sensitivity analyses on implementation timing and restriction stringency.

The weakness is that repeated cross-sections of different pupils rather than followed individuals, and adoption of bans by schools is unlikely to be random. 3. **Florida's quasi-experiment** [5] — student-level administrative data, identification from pre-ban building-level phone use.

The weakness is that buildings with high pre-ban phone use may differ in ways correlated with later outcomes, and the strategy yields a local effect for high-use buildings rather than a system-wide average. 4. **Rio de Janeiro** [7] — treated and control schools with documented parallel pre-trends in test scores and a measured fall in in-school phone use.

The weakness the authors name themselves: "restrictions were imperfectly implemented both before and after the ban" [7], which is a threat to the contrast, not just to the dose. 5. **Norway's event study** [1] — administrative plus survey data, strong on measurement (health-care records rather than self-report for one key outcome).

The weakness is that the headline result is a set of gender-specific subgroup effects with a null average, which invites multiple-comparison concerns. 6. **South Australia's evaluation** [11] — registration is a real strength and rare here, though the protocol was filed after data collection [16]; the design compares three schools not yet under a state ban with two already under it, with 1,282 pupils at baseline and 1,256 at one-month follow-up, so it can only detect short-term effects, and the comparison confounds ban status with whatever made those schools early or late adopters. 7. **SMART Schools in England** [12, 14] — the largest sample (1,227 pupils, 30 schools) and the most thorough outcome set, but cross-sectional, so it cannot establish that policy caused any difference; and its 8.73% and 10.42% school response rates [14] leave the sample self-selected.

That is the single most important fact about the strength of the evidence: every estimate above depends on an assumption — parallel trends, ignorable adoption, no unmeasured school confounding — that no study has been able to test directly. **Where the studies agree and disagree.** They agree that a school-day restriction reduces phone use during school hours [7, 12, 15].
They agree that total daily use does not fall [12].
They agree that short-term disruption is real: disciplinary incidents rose in year one in both Florida [5] and the pouch study [15].
They agree on mental health at the population level: nothing, in Iceland and England, with Norway's gender-specific health-care effect the outlier [10, 13, 1].

They disagree on achievement: Rio and Florida's second year say yes, small [7, 5]; England, South Australia and the pouch study say nothing detectable [14, 11, 15]; Norway says yes for girls only [1].

They disagree on bullying: Norway says down for both genders [1], South Australia found slightly more in the ban group with a fall in both groups [11], and the pouch study found no improvement in perceived online bullying [15]. **The review literature's verdict is negative.** "Overall, our study suggests the evidence for banning mobile phones in schools is weak and inconclusive" [2].

The same review's methodological criticisms are the ones a reader should apply to every study above: partial and complete bans get conflated; positive mental-health findings rest on teacher and parent perceptions rather than students' own reports or recorded illness; and some studies find harm rather than benefit [2].

The South Australian team's own summary of the field is a shade less negative but points the same way: "Although studies are not entirely consistent, the emerging research picture is that mobile phone bans appear to have either no detectable effects or relatively subtle effects detected only in certain subgroups over longer periods of time (e.g., increased academic performance among lower achievers)" [11]. **The one economic evaluation.** SMART Schools also ran a cost-utility analysis on 815 pupils from 20 schools (13 restrictive, 7 permissive).

Enforcement absorbed real staff time — equivalent to 3.1 full-time staff in restrictive schools and 3.3 in permissive ones — and the incremental per-pupil cost of a restrictive policy was −£94 (95% CI −£229 to £41), i.e. slightly cheaper, though the interval crosses zero [12].

The counter-intuitive direction, with restrictive schools spending less rather than more, cuts against the assumption that bans are enforcement-heavy, but the confidence interval does not exclude no saving. **Conflicts and funding.** All the studies read here are funded by public research bodies — the English work by the National Institute for Health and Research Public Health Research Programme, with the funder explicitly having no role in design, analysis or publication [14].

The numbers, not the framing, are what should be carried forward. *Inference:* if the achievement effect is real and concentrated in disadvantaged or low-achieving pupils [2] and in girls from disadvantaged backgrounds [1] — with the pouch study adding high-school maths [15] — then a ban justified as a universal intervention will look weak in every average-effect evaluation while still doing something for the pupils with the most to gain.
That would make the correct policy question not whether bans work but for whom, under what enforcement, and at what cost to the pupils suspended in year one [5].

notes.quote: Using administrative and survey data with an event-study design, I show that banning smartphones in middle schools has no average effect on education or mental health but masks important gender differences. Bans reduce psychological health care use among girls, lower bullying for both genders, and improve girls’ GPAs and academic track placement, especially among those from disadvantaged backgrounds.
notes.claim: Abrahamsson's Norwegian event-study (administrative + survey data, middle schools) finds no average effect of smartphone bans on education outcomes, but gains for girls' GPAs and academic-track placement, concentrated among disadvantaged girls.

notes.quote: Our research found four studies that identified a slight improvement in academic achievement when phones were banned in schools. However, two of these studies found this improvement only applied to disadvantaged or low-achieving students.
notes.claim: Campbell & Edwards' scoping review of 22 before-and-after studies found only four reporting slight achievement improvements (two only for disadvantaged/low-achieving students).

notes.quote: Students Grade 7 and above may not use cellphones or other mobiles devices during class time without the explicit permission of their teacher. Students Grade 6 and below may not use cellphones or other mobile devices at school during the school day without the permission of a teacher.
notes.claim: Ontario's province-wide rule (in force via the provincial Code of Conduct from 1 September 2024) bans phone use in class for Grades 7+ and all-day phone use for K-6, with teacher discretion exceptions.

notes.quote: Students may keep their cellphone, tablet or smart watch with them, but they must do all of the following: turn it off — or set it to silent mode store it out of view (for example, in a bag or pocket)
notes.claim: Ontario's rule is not a confiscation or phone-free-campus policy: students keep devices but must switch them off or silent and store them out of view, with hand-in only if the device is seen.

notes.quote: All schools should be mobile phone-free environments by default; anything other than this should be by exception only.
notes.claim: England's DfE guidance requires schools to be phone-free throughout the school day — lessons, between lessons, break and lunchtime — with headteachers choosing the mechanism (lockers, hand-in at start of day, etc.). It became statutory on 29 June 2026, with schools to follow from 1 September 2026, after first being published as guidance in February 2024.

notes.quote: This publication provides statutory guidance to individual schools and trusts on how to implement a policy that prohibits the use of mobile phones throughout the school day, including during lessons, the time between lessons, breaktimes and lunchtime.
notes.claim: The English policy explicitly extends to break and lunch, not just lessons, and lets each headteacher choose enforcement design (lockers, handing phones to staff, etc.).

notes.quote: In this study, we try to fill this gap by examining the causal effects of bans on student test scores, suspensions, and absences using detailed student-level data from Florida and a quasi-experimental research strategy relying upon differences in pre-ban cellphone use by students, as measured by building-level Advan data.
notes.claim: The strongest US causal study (Figlio & Özek, NBER WP 34388, Oct 2025) is quasi-experimental, not a randomised trial: it uses student-level Florida data and exploits variation in pre-ban building-level cellphone use to identify effects. Design limitation to note in the strength-of-evidence assessment.

notes.quote: First, we show that the enforcement of cellphone bans in schools led to a significant increase in student suspensions in the short-term, especially among Black students, but disciplinary actions began to dissipate after the first year, potentially suggesting a new steady state after an initial adjustment period. Second, we find significant improvements in student test scores in the second year of the ban after that initial adjustment period.
notes.claim: The Florida study's headline results are conditional on timing: suspensions rose significantly in the short term (especially for Black students), and test-score gains appeared only in the second year. This complicates simple claims that bans raise achievement.

notes.quote: Currently, there are data for only one state with two post-ban periods and two states with one post-ban period, which makes the results preliminary evidence only. The outcome variables are screentime and measures of psychological wellbeing. Overall, these early results provide no clear evidence that the school ban policy reduced screentime or improved psychological wellbeing.
notes.claim: The first US causal study of smartphone bans and youth mental health (Saffer, NBER WP 35181, May 2026) is explicitly preliminary: only one state has two post-ban periods and two states have one, and it found no clear evidence of reduced screentime or improved psychological wellbeing. This is the key negative/near-null result for the mental health evidence base.

notes.quote: While restrictions were imperfectly implemented both before and after the ban, we show that in-school phone use fell substantially in treatment schools relative to control. We then show that test scores, which were trending similarly in the two groups prior to the ban, improved by 0.06 s.d. in treatment schools relative to control.
notes.claim: Rio de Janeiro's 2023 ban study (Lichand, Moreno-Louzada, da Costa & Gentzkow, NBER WP 35233) reports a modest effect size: test scores improved by 0.06 standard deviations, with restrictions "imperfectly implemented both before and after the ban." Useful for calibrating how small the measured learning effects are.

notes.quote: In the most lenient environments, roughly eight in ten students said they are checking their cell phones during their classes at least once per day.
notes.claim: In a nationally representative US survey of 922 students in grades 6–12 (Dec 2025–Jan 2026), about 80% of students in schools with no rules checked phones in class at least daily.

notes.quote: Overall, these early results provide no clear evidence that the school ban policy reduced screentime or improved psychological wellbeing.
notes.claim: The first causal study of US school smartphone bans on youth mental health (synthetic difference-in-differences on the National Survey of Children's Health, 2016–2024) found no clear evidence that bans reduced screen time or improved psychological wellbeing; author calls results preliminary.

notes.quote: Currently, there are data for only one state with two post-ban periods and two states with one post-ban period, which makes the results preliminary evidence only.
notes.claim: The null US result rests on very thin data — only three states with post-ban observations — so it is a weak test, not strong evidence that bans do not affect mental health.

notes.quote: Using administrative and survey data with an event-study design, I show that banning smartphones in middle schools has no average effect on education or mental health but masks important gender differences. Bans reduce psychological health care use among girls, lower bullying for both genders, and improve girls’ GPAs and academic track placement, especially among those from disadvantaged backgrounds.
notes.claim: Norway's event-study of middle-school smartphone bans (administrative + survey data, published in Journal of Human Resources) finds no average mental-health effect but gender-specific ones: less psychological health care use among girls, and lower bullying for both genders.

notes.quote: Some countries enforce school phone bans, whereas others (e.g., England) have guidance promoting 'phone-free environments' but no legal mandate at present. There is limited evidence on the benefits of such policies, including whether they promote safeguarding.
