**The suspension and wellbeing costs need replication and costing.** Florida's first-year rise in suspensions concentrated among Black students [5] and the pouch study's first-year dip in subjective wellbeing [15] both point the same way, and neither has been replicated or costed against the achievement gains.

**Australian states beyond South Australia and Victoria are unverified here.** New South Wales, Queensland and Western Australia all restrict phones, but their departmental pages could not be retrieved in this pass, so their rules are not characterised. The Netherlands' promised evaluation — the commitment to assess by the end of the following school year whether the agreement worked [20] — was not located either. These are gaps of coverage, not findings that nothing exists.

**Nobody has measured the displacement cost.** England found school-day phone time fell 0.67 hours with no change in weekday or weekend totals [12]. Where that time went, and whether it went somewhere worse, is unmeasured.

**The Norwegian gender effect stands alone.** A health-care-use reduction among girls with a null average is exactly the pattern multiple subgroup testing produces, and it is the only causal mental-health signal in the field.

q: What did Marshall McLuhan's laws of media (the tetrad) actually claim, how have scholars applied, extended or criticised it since Laws of Media appeared in 1988, and has anyone tried to test it empirically?

report.title: The Tetrad After Laws of Media: What the Four Laws Claim, What Scholars Did With Them, and the Test That Was Never Run

review.sentence: Bolton also adopts the widest definition of medium in the literature, treating anything from which change emerges as a medium — a television, a teething ring, a tautology [2]. **The applied literature.** Beyond these streams sits a large body of work that applies the tetrad to a new technology and stops there.

sentences.sentence: The tetrad is the late, systematising move in McLuhan's work, and its full statement is the posthumous *Laws of Media: The New Science*, written with his son Eric and published by the University of Toronto Press in 1988 — the subtitle is part of the claim, not decoration [4].
The applied literature reproduces this structure faithfully and treats the four as "complementary" rather than sequential, translatable into four questions about any artefact [3].

The four effects are described in the secondary and applied literature as "inevitable" and applying "universally" [3]. *Laws of Media* goes further: the publisher's description presents the four questions as a new scientific basis for media studies, testable and able to allow for prediction, and adds that anything which does not contain answers to these four questions is not the product of human creation.

In Michael Bolton's application for software testers, a medium is not merely a communication channel but anything from which change emerges — tools, descriptions, devices, thoughts, artefacts, technologies or concepts, anything humans invent, develop or use, from a television to a teething ring to a tautology [2].

Tyler records the sequence: McLuhan asserted that the laws constituted testable hypotheses and were a scientific method modelled on Popper's principle of falsifiability, citing the 1975 *Technology and Culture* article and the 1977 *ETC* piece [1].

The book's subtitle is *The New Science*, and the publisher's description presents the four questions as a new scientific basis for media studies, testable and able to allow for prediction, adding that anything which does not contain answers to these four questions is not the product of human creation [4].

This is the single most consequential step in the whole history of the tetrad, and it was taken by the authors, not by their critics. **How the McLuhans defended the laws when challenged.** The most revealing moment came in 1976, when William Henry Venable, an engineer and lawyer, took up the invitation to refute in an article titled "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" (*Technology and Culture*, April 1976, p. 256); McLuhan's reply, in the same issue, was titled "Misunderstanding the Media's Laws" (p. 263) [8].

Tyler's summary of the position is that treating the tetrad as scientific laws in any ordinary sense of the phrase is preposterous, and that what remains is a heuristic device in the form of a set of questions [1].

Bolton, a software tester, presents the tetrad to engineers as four probes — testing heuristics — for examining requirements, features, test approaches and organisational changes, and credits the framing to conversations with Federman [2].

His use is prospective rather than retrospective: faced with a requirement to evaluate, a feature to test or an organisational change, the laws of media might help you notice what might be extended, retrieved and obsolesced, and how you might anticipate and manage some of the reversal effects [2].

The smartphone essay in *Glocality* (2016) finds that the smartphone enhances internet accessibility and convenience, obsolesces feature phones and reduces use of personal computers and home printers, retrieves the camera and the e-book along with linear reading, and reverses into augmented-reality devices and into communication that restricts rather than facilitates interaction [3].

A 2020 Indonesian communication-studies article extracts enhancement, obsolescence, flip/reverse and retrieval from 23 international journals to analyse telemedicine, finding that telemedicine enhances accessibility and flexibility, obsolesces face-to-face doctor-patient interaction, retrieves the doctor's virtual presence at home, and reverses into an optimal impact available only to good communicators with digital access and money [6].
A 2022 article applies the tetrad to video conferencing [5].

A 2007 special issue of *Explorations in Media Ecology* devoted space to the tetrad, including an article titled "The Tetrad and Phenomenology" and a piece by Marshall and Eric McLuhan called "The Missing Media Laws" — the field's own journal treating the tetrad as a philosophical instrument two decades after the book [5][8].
A 2018 engineering volume applies it to laser cleaning machines as a case study in technological innovation analysis [7].

A 2025 Brazilian computing-systems paper, presented at SBSI, applies the tetrad to generative AI's disruption of intellectual property in Brazil, explicitly describing its approach as qualitative and its output as potential enhancements, obsolescence, retrievals and reversals [7][9].

A 2026 *Leonardo* paper builds "Media Farm," a framework for AI-based reinterpretation and generation of conceptual media art inspired by the tetrad, and reports on exploring its effectiveness in a practical educational setting [5].
Crossref also lists a collection titled *The Lost Tetrads of Marshall McLuhan*, which contains a chapter called "Tetrad development and examples of submissions" [7].

First, the applications are almost all qualitative, and the better ones say so: the telemedicine study describes its own method as qualitative descriptive [6], and a 2022 metatheoretical review in *Professional Communication and Translation Studies* concludes by arguing for tetrad media as a qualitative method of analysis in communication sciences [5] — a considered verdict from within the field that the tetrad's status is interpretive, not experimental.

The smartphone essay, for instance, concludes that multiple interpretations are always possible because interpretation rests on the analyst's own thoughts and perceptions — stated as a virtue, in a paper whose framework claims to be universal [3].

His abstract states the double verdict in one sentence: considered as a scientific theory, the four laws "risk violating communications research in a dangerously Procrustean manner", while conceived as an exploratory probe the tetrad "can provide illuminating insights into the social and psychological effects of individual technologies" [1].

Tyler warns that the method is itself in danger of operating according to Procrustean principles, meaning that bothersome empirical details which do not fit the theory get hammered or shorn so that they are made to fit [1].

Applying the tetrad to wine, the McLuhans find that it enhances "grape juice" through fermentation, obsolesces "commonplace flavours," retrieves "ritual observance," and reverses into "cooking wine vinegar." Then, on the same page, they do it again: wine enhances food and "the occasion," obsolesces "inhibition," retrieves "festive spontaneity of speech and gesture" and reverses into "hangover" and insult (1988, p. 206) [1].

Tyler draws the inference carefully rather than gloating: "If the authors themselves seem unsure as to the consistency of the results of the tetrad's application, it seems unlikely that the same conclusions will be drawn by anyone, anywhere, at any time" [1].

Tyler's reply is four words: "This is not, in fact, the case" [1]. **The double bind.** The core of the argument is that the tetrad fails in two opposite directions simultaneously, which is why neither loosening nor tightening it can save it.
On the second: the tetrad is, in Tyler's words, unrelentingly rigid, just like Procrustes' bed: it _requires_ us to fill the gaps [1].
Tyler's verdict on the status claim is blunt: the idea that these are scientific laws in anything like the ordinary sense of that phrase he calls preposterous [1].

In fact, it is best conceived, as McLuhan himself often did, as a heuristic device taking the form of a set of questions: _what_ does a technology enhance, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into (1977, p. 175)?" [1] The virtue he identifies is specific: the tetrad forces attention onto an artefact's operation and effects rather than onto the content of individual broadcasts, bottles or games.

He describes his result as "one amongst many possible surveys." The closing image ties the whole argument together: Theseus turned Procrustes' bed against its owner, and Tyler's last line is that the challenge is to make sure the probe works ultimately for us, as the bed did for Theseus, rather than to end up in thrall to our own technological invention, as Procrustes did [1]. **Where the critics divide.** Tyler and Graham Harman disagree about nearly everything except the conclusion that the tetrad is not ordinary empirical science.

What exists instead is one genuine attempt at refutation, one accidental replication failure, and a large applied literature that is qualitative by its own description. **The one genuine attempt to refute.** McLuhan invited refutation in "McLuhan's Laws of the Media" in *Technology and Culture* in 1975 (the article begins at p. 74) [8], and republished the laws in *ETC: A Review of General Semantics* in June 1977, pp. 173-179 [8].
In April 1976, William Henry Venable took him up on it in the same journal with an article titled "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" (p. 256) [8].
McLuhan's reply, in the same issue, was titled "Misunderstanding the Media's Laws" (p. 263) [8].

Two tetrads for the same artefact, produced by the same authors, on the same page of *Laws of Media* (1988, p. 206), give different answers in all four quadrants: grape juice versus food and the occasion; commonplace flavours versus inhibition; ritual observance versus festive spontaneity; cooking vinegar versus hangover and insult [1].
The telemedicine study describes its method as qualitative descriptive, reviewing 23 relevant international journals published between 2015 and 2020 [6].
A 2022 metatheoretical review in *Professional Communication and Translation Studies* concludes by arguing for the tetrad as a qualitative method of analysis in communication sciences [5].

The 2025 Brazilian study of generative AI and intellectual property states that it uses a qualitative approach and identifies potential enhancements, obsolescence, retrievals and reversals — "potential" being the operative word, since nothing is measured [9].

The smartphone essay assembles published findings per quadrant — the Google effect, nomophobia research, Oulasvirta's work on habitual use — and concludes that multiple interpretations are always possible because interpretation rests on the analyst's own thoughts and perceptions [3].
It also uses the tetrad prospectively, to speculate about future developments [3].

The smartphone essay's own admission — that interpretation depends on the interpreter [3] — directly contradicts the universal checkability claim, and is offered as a caveat rather than as a finding about the framework. **The search for a test, and what it returned.** A Crossref query combining "tetrad" and "McLuhan" with "quantitative", "experiment", "survey", "test" and "prediction" returns no study that tests the tetrad.

The only "tetrad test" results are the unrelated sensory-analysis Tetrad Test used in food science (ASTM E3009) — a name collision, and a useful reminder that the word "tetrad" is doing double duty across disciplines [9].
The field's own verdict, in the *Professional Communication and Translation Studies* review, is that the tetrad is a qualitative method [5].

Conceived as an _exploratory probe_, however, this "tetrad" can provide illuminating insights into the social and psychological effects of individual technologies.

report.body:
## TL;DR

Marshall and Eric McLuhan's tetrad (*Laws of Media: The New Science*, 1988) claims that every human artefact answers four simultaneous questions — what it enhances, what it obsolesces, what it retrieves from the past, and what it reverses into when pushed to its extreme — and that these answers can be checked by anyone, anywhere, at any time [1][3][4]. McLuhan offered the laws in 1975 as Popperian hypotheses readers were invited to disprove, and answered the one sustained attempt at refutation (Venable, 1976) by reclassifying them as analogical rather than falsifiable [8]. Since 1988 the tetrad has been extended richly — Levinson's tetrad wheels, Logan's spiral and Laws of Media Environments, Federman's management version, Bolton's testing heuristics, and dozens of applications from telemedicine to video conferencing to generative AI — and none of those extensions adds a test [2][5][6][7]. The most damaging evidence against the scientific claim is in the book itself: two incompatible tetrads for wine on a single page, which makes the "anyone, anywhere" claim fail on the authors' own desk [1]. No empirical test of the tetrad appears to exist; the applied literature is qualitative by its own description [5][6][9].

## Key Findings

- **The four laws are questions, not propositions.** What does it enhance, what does it obsolesce, what does it retrieve, what does it reverse into when pushed to its extreme. They are held to operate simultaneously rather than in sequence, with enhancement and retrieval as figure and obsolescence and reversal as ground [3].
- **The universality claim is what makes it a "law" claim, and it is very strong.** The four effects are described as inevitable and universal [3]; Eric McLuhan claimed the questions can be asked and the answers checked "by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" (1988, p. 7) [1]; the publisher presents the tetrad as testable and able to allow for prediction [4].
- **The book made the test impossible by stipulation.** Anything that does not answer all four questions is, by the publisher's own description, "not the product of human creation" — so no artefact can fail [1].
- **McLuhan invited refutation in Popperian terms in 1975 and then withdrew the claim when challenged.** Venable's "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" (*Technology and Culture*, April 1976, p. 256) drew McLuhan's reply, "Misunderstanding the Media's Laws" (p. 263), in which he argued the tetrads are analogical with no connections between the terms, only dynamic ratios [8].
- **The wine page is the decisive counter-example.** On *Laws of Media* p. 206 the McLuhans give two tetrads for wine that disagree in all four quadrants — grape juice versus food and the occasion; commonplace flavours versus inhibition; ritual observance versus festive spontaneity; cooking vinegar versus hangover and insult [1].
- **Tyler's 2008 critique states the double bind.** As science the tetrad is too vague to be falsifiable and, at the same time, unrelentingly rigid in requiring every gap to be filled; as an exploratory probe it is illuminating [1]. His verdict on the status claim: the idea that these are scientific laws in the ordinary sense is preposterous [1].
- **The extensions since 1988 add structure, not testability.** Levinson's tetrad wheel chains tetrads through time so each artefact's reversal becomes the next one's enhancement; Logan's spiral and Laws of Media Environments and Laws of Media Users extend it to environments and users; Federman's management material and Bolton's software-testing probes make it a practitioner heuristic [2][5].
- **The applied literature is qualitative by its own account.** The telemedicine study says its method is qualitative descriptive over 23 journals [6]; a 2022 metatheoretical review argues for the tetrad as a qualitative method in communication sciences [5]; the 2025 generative-AI and intellectual-property study states a qualitative approach and identifies "potential" quadrants [9].
- **Application has repeatedly been mistaken for evidence.** The smartphone essay assembles findings per quadrant and then concedes that interpretation depends on the analyst's own thoughts and perceptions — a direct contradiction of universal checkability, offered as a caveat [3].
- **No empirical test appears to exist.** A Crossref search pairing "tetrad" and "McLuhan" with quantitative, experiment, survey, test and prediction returns no such study; the only "tetrad test" hits are the unrelated food-science Tetrad Test (ASTM E3009) [9].
- **The nearest empirical evidence comes from adjacent claims, not the tetrad.** McLuhan's hot/cool binary has been examined against perceptual psychology, where the general principle of differing information density survives and the specific classifications do not — the best available guess at what a tetrad test would return, but not a result about the tetrad.

## Details

### 1. What the tetrad actually claims: the four laws as formulated in Laws of Media (1988), their origin in McLuhan's 1975 work, simultaneity, and what counts as an artefact

The tetrad is the late, systematising move in McLuhan's work, and its full statement is the posthumous *Laws of Media: The New Science*, written with his son Eric and published by the University of Toronto Press in 1988 — the subtitle is part of the claim, not decoration [4]. It did not arrive fully formed there. The four laws first appeared in print in McLuhan's 1975 article "McLuhan's Laws of the Media" in *Technology and Culture*, and again in *ETC: A Review of General Semantics* in June 1977, with a preface by Paul Levinson. Book-length treatment followed in the 1988 volume and in *The Global Village* (1989, with Bruce R. Powers).

**The four questions.** Stated as questions, the laws are short enough to memorise, which is part of why they spread:

1. What does the medium enhance, intensify, accelerate or enable?
2. What does it obsolesce — what earlier medium or practice does it push out of prominence?
3. What does it retrieve that had previously been obsolesced?
4. What does it reverse or flip into when pushed to its extreme?

The applied literature reproduces this structure faithfully and treats the four as "complementary" rather than sequential, translatable into four questions about any artefact [3]. Two features of the formulation matter more than the list. The first is **simultaneity**: the laws are held to operate at once, not in a chronology of adoption, maturation and decline. McLuhan's break with Harold Innis is precisely here — where Innis described media as biased toward time or space, McLuhan added the idea that a medium "overheats" and reverses into its opposite form when pushed to its limit, and that this reversal is happening at the same time as the enhancement. The second is the **figure/ground pairing**: enhancement and retrieval are treated as figure qualities, obsolescence and reversal as ground qualities, which is why the tetrad is drawn as four diamonds in an X with the medium at the centre rather than as a list of four bullets. Enhancement and retrieval are what the medium brings forward; obsolescence and reversal are what happens to the environment it moves into.

**The universality claim.** This is where the tetrad becomes a "law" claim rather than a checklist. The four effects are described in the secondary and applied literature as "inevitable" and applying "universally" [3]. *Laws of Media* goes further: the publisher's description presents the four questions as a new scientific basis for media studies, testable and able to allow for prediction, and adds that anything which does not contain answers to these four questions is not the product of human creation. Eric McLuhan's formulation, quoted by his critics because it is so exposed, is that the questions "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" (1988, p. 7). The claim is therefore doubly universal: every human artefact answers all four, and any competent questioner will get the same answers.

**What counts as an artefact.** McLuhan's sense of "medium" is much wider than a communications technology, and the tetrad inherits that width. In Michael Bolton's application for software testers, a medium is not merely a communication channel but anything from which change emerges — tools, descriptions, devices, thoughts, artefacts, technologies or concepts, anything humans invent, develop or use, from a television to a teething ring to a tautology [2]. The McLuhans applied the tetrad to money, to the cliché, and, notoriously, to wine. That breadth is the source of the tetrad's appeal and the source of its trouble: a claim that covers every artefact ever made is hard to state in a way that any artefact could refute.

**Where the laws came from.** Two genealogies are offered in the literature and they are not entirely compatible. The first is rhetorical and pedagogical: McLuhan had been arguing since *The Gutenberg Galaxy* (1962) that technologies retrieve obsolesced older forms, and the tetrad formalised a move he had been making intuitively for a decade. The second, pressed by Eric McLuhan and by Harman, is that the tetrad was a genuine discovery — Eric called it the single biggest intellectual discovery not only of his time but of at least the last couple of centuries, and according to Harman he reported that his father spent the rest of his life looking for a fifth law and for a single case where one of the four did not apply, and never found either. Read that way, the tetrad is offered as a completed inventory of media effects, not a hypothesis awaiting revision.

### 2. The scientific claim: Popper, falsifiability, 'testable and able to allow for prediction', and how the McLuhans defended the laws when challenged

The McLuhans did not present the tetrad as a metaphor. They presented it as science, and the specific model was Karl Popper's falsifiability. Tyler records the sequence: McLuhan asserted that the laws constituted testable hypotheses and were a scientific method modelled on Popper's principle of falsifiability, citing the 1975 *Technology and Culture* article and the 1977 *ETC* piece [1]. The 1975 article is explicit about the invitation. McLuhan introduced the laws in a Popperian spirit, telling readers they might enjoy and profit from attempting to disprove his laws, and defending the word "law" on the ground that the four questions represent an ordering of thought and experience which had not yet been disproved.

That is a coherent, falsificationist posture: propose four universal claims, publish them, invite refutation. *Laws of Media* then hardened it. The book's subtitle is *The New Science*, and the publisher's description presents the four questions as a new scientific basis for media studies, testable and able to allow for prediction, adding that anything which does not contain answers to these four questions is not the product of human creation [4]. Eric McLuhan's version, in the book itself, is that the questions "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" (1988, p. 7).

The trouble is visible in that sentence. "Anyone, anywhere, at any time" is a very strong empirical claim: it predicts inter-analyst reliability. It is the sort of claim that could be tested cheaply — give several analysts the same artefact, collect their four answers blind, and measure agreement. So far as I can establish, nobody did that, and the McLuhans did not either. What happened instead is that the book's definitional move made the test impossible. If anything that fails to answer all four questions is by definition not a human artefact, then no artefact can fail the test: the hypothesis has been converted into a stipulation. This is the single most consequential step in the whole history of the tetrad, and it was taken by the authors, not by their critics.

**How the McLuhans defended the laws when challenged.** The most revealing moment came in 1976, when William Henry Venable, an engineer and lawyer, took up the invitation to refute in an article titled "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" (*Technology and Culture*, April 1976, p. 256); McLuhan's reply, in the same issue, was titled "Misunderstanding the Media's Laws" (p. 263) [8]. The titles alone record the outcome. In an exchange in *Technology and Culture* — the same journal that had published the laws — Venable read the four terms through C. S. Peirce's logic of signs and objected that the four presuppose a single target that technologists have always aimed at, and he echoed Derek de Solla Price's warning against writing history as a single arrow pointing at the present. McLuhan's published reply moved the ground entirely. The whole point about his tetrads, he wrote, is that they are analogical: there are no connections between any of them, only dynamic ratios, and there was simply no point of contact whatever between them.

That reply is worth pausing on, because it concedes the critics' case while declining its terms. If the four terms have no point of contact with one another and are connected only by analogy, then the tetrad is not a set of hypotheses about causal relations that could be true or false. It is a device for generating analogies. When a critic took the falsifiability claim seriously, McLuhan stopped defending the falsifiability claim. Venable's letter is known in the secondary literature chiefly through summary; I could not obtain the full text, so the strength of his argument is less well established here than McLuhan's reply.

**Levinson's inside account.** Paul Levinson, who knew McLuhan and organised the 1978 Tetrad Conference, offers a gloss that reads the Popperian language as protective rather than programmatic. An article co-authored by Matthew Lindia and Levinson in *New Explorations* reports that McLuhan joked about adopting Popper, and Levinson's interpretation is that if the laws of media are capable of falsification they cannot do too much damage. On that reading the falsifiability framing was a hedge against overreach, not a research programme: a law that can be refuted is a law that cannot claim too much. The same article stresses the tetrad's non-comprehensive character as a heuristic tool. Levinson's own radio tetrad — radio retrieves the town crier and flips into television — is the example Tyler borrows when he wants to show the tetrad used well.

**The result.** The McLuhans claimed scientific status, then defended themselves with analogy, then hedged with a joke. The three moves cannot all be true at once. What survives is not the science claim but the ordering claim: the tetrad organises a field's findings and directs attention to effects rather than content. The evidence for that is the volume and persistence of its use, not a test. Tyler's summary of the position is that treating the tetrad as scientific laws in any ordinary sense of the phrase is preposterous, and that what remains is a heuristic device in the form of a set of questions [1].

### 3. Applications and extensions since 1988: Levinson's tetrad wheels, Logan, Federman, Strate and the media ecology tradition, design and game studies

The tetrad's post-1988 life divides into three streams that rarely cite each other: the media-ecology tradition that treats it as theory, the practitioner stream that treats it as a design and testing heuristic, and a large, scattered applied literature that treats it as a general-purpose interpretive grid for whatever technology happens to be new. The first stream is where the extensions live; the third is where most of the volume is.

**Levinson and the tetrad wheel.** Paul Levinson organised the 1978 Tetrad Conference, before the book appeared, and proposed the single most important formal extension: the "tetrad wheel." Where McLuhan's tetrad is a static snapshot of one artefact at one moment, the wheel chains tetrads through time so that each artefact's reversal quadrant becomes the enhancement quadrant of the next artefact. This converts the tetrad from a classification into a model of succession — which is what allows it to explain media history rather than merely describe media artefacts. Levinson's *Digital McLuhan* (1999) then made the tetrad operational for digital media, and his radio tetrad — radio retrieves the town crier and flips into television — has become the standard worked example, borrowed by later critics precisely because it is the strongest case.

**Logan and the spiral.** Robert K. Logan, who collaborated with McLuhan, extended the tetrad in two directions. The first is structural: he treats the tetrad as a spiral in which each artefact's reversal generates the enhancement quadrant of the next artefact, which is Levinson's wheel given a developmental reading. The second is taxonomic: Logan's work in the MDPI journal *Philosophies* proposes Laws of Media Environments and Laws of Media Users alongside the original four laws of media artefacts, on the reasoning that the 1988 tetrad was written for objects and does not cover the environments those objects create or the users they reshape. *Understanding New Media* (2010, second edition 2016) is the most direct academic application of figure/ground and the tetrad to digital media, and Logan's *McLuhan Misunderstood* (2011) is the tradition's main defence of McLuhan against the determinism charge.

**Strate, Federman and the media ecology institutions.** Lance Strate, Robert Logan and Corey Anton in the Media Ecology Association have argued that McLuhan's hot/cool distinction should be reinterpreted as a continuum rather than a binary — the laptop is hot when offline and cool when networked — which is a repair of a neighbouring concept rather than the tetrad itself. Strate's *Echoes and Reflections* (2006) and *Media Ecology* (2017) are the tradition's most systematic statements. Mark Federman, a McLuhan Program associate, wrote the practitioner-facing McLuhan for Managers material, which taught the tetrad to business audiences as a tool for anticipating the unintended consequences of a decision. That the same body of theory supports both a scholarly journal and a management seminar is itself evidence of the tetrad's defining property: it is portable because it constrains nothing.

**The practitioner stream.** The clearest example of the tetrad used as a working instrument rather than an interpretive one is Michael Bolton's 2007 column in *Better Software* magazine. Bolton, a software tester, presents the tetrad to engineers as four probes — testing heuristics — for examining requirements, features, test approaches and organisational changes, and credits the framing to conversations with Federman [2]. His use is prospective rather than retrospective: faced with a requirement to evaluate, a feature to test or an organisational change, the laws of media might help you notice what might be extended, retrieved and obsolesced, and how you might anticipate and manage some of the reversal effects [2]. Note what Bolton claims and does not: he offers the tetrad as a way of noticing, not a way of predicting, which is exactly the position Tyler argued for.

**The applied literature.** Beyond these streams sits a large body of work that applies the tetrad to a new technology and stops there. The pattern is remarkably consistent across disciplines and decades. The smartphone essay in *Glocality* (2016) finds that the smartphone enhances internet accessibility and convenience, obsolesces feature phones and reduces use of personal computers and home printers, retrieves the camera and the e-book along with linear reading, and reverses into augmented-reality devices and into communication that restricts rather than facilitates interaction [3]. A 2020 Indonesian communication-studies article extracts enhancement, obsolescence, flip/reverse and retrieval from 23 international journals to analyse telemedicine, finding that telemedicine enhances accessibility and flexibility, obsolesces face-to-face doctor-patient interaction, retrieves the doctor's virtual presence at home, and reverses into an optimal impact available only to good communicators with digital access and money [6]. A 2022 article applies the tetrad to video conferencing [5]. A 2007 special issue of *Explorations in Media Ecology* devoted space to the tetrad, including an article titled "The Tetrad and Phenomenology" and a piece by Marshall and Eric McLuhan called "The Missing Media Laws" — the field's own journal treating the tetrad as a philosophical instrument two decades after the book [5][8]. A 2018 engineering volume applies it to laser cleaning machines as a case study in technological innovation analysis [7]. A 2025 Brazilian computing-systems paper, presented at SBSI, applies the tetrad to generative AI's disruption of intellectual property in Brazil, explicitly describing its approach as qualitative and its output as potential enhancements, obsolescence, retrievals and reversals [7][9]. A 2026 *Leonardo* paper builds "Media Farm," a framework for AI-based reinterpretation and generation of conceptual media art inspired by the tetrad, and reports on exploring its effectiveness in a practical educational setting [5]. Crossref also lists a collection titled *The Lost Tetrads of Marshall McLuhan*, which contains a chapter called "Tetrad development and examples of submissions" [7].

Two features of this literature deserve to be stated plainly because they bear on the empirical question. First, the applications are almost all qualitative, and the better ones say so: the telemedicine study describes its own method as qualitative descriptive [6], and a 2022 metatheoretical review in *Professional Communication and Translation Studies* concludes by arguing for tetrad media as a qualitative method of analysis in communication sciences [5] — a considered verdict from within the field that the tetrad's status is interpretive, not experimental. Second, the applications converge on the same quadrants for the same technologies, which is either evidence of the tetrad's insight or evidence of its elasticity, and the literature almost never considers the second possibility. The smartphone essay, for instance, concludes that multiple interpretations are always possible because interpretation rests on the analyst's own thoughts and perceptions — stated as a virtue, in a paper whose framework claims to be universal [3]. Tyler's wine example predicts exactly this outcome; the applied literature reproduces it while calling it flexibility.

**What the extensions have in common.** Levinson's wheel, Logan's spiral and Laws of Media Environments, and Federman's management version all respond to the same weakness: a static four-box snapshot cannot handle change over time or the interaction between media. Each extension adds a dimension the 1988 book lacked — time (the wheel and spiral), environment and user (Logan), organisational consequence (Federman). None of them adds a test. That is the shape of the whole post-1988 literature: the tetrad has been made more elaborate, more portable and more useful, and it has not been made more falsifiable.

### 4. Criticism: Tyler's Procrustean double bind, the Venable exchange, Harman's metaphysical defence, and the charge that the tetrad is art rather than science

The most sustained published critique of the tetrad as a scientific instrument is Tom Tyler's "Play: A Procrustean Probe," which appeared in *Game Studies* in 2008 and remains the article anyone citing the tetrad's weaknesses has to deal with. Tyler was then a senior lecturer in philosophy and culture at Oxford Brookes, and his subject was digital games — the tetrad was a tool he wanted to use, not a target he wanted to destroy. That is what makes the critique hard to dismiss.

His abstract states the double verdict in one sentence: considered as a scientific theory, the four laws "risk violating communications research in a dangerously Procrustean manner", while conceived as an exploratory probe the tetrad "can provide illuminating insights into the social and psychological effects of individual technologies" [1]. The name comes from the myth of Procrustes, the bandit who stretched short guests and cut down tall ones to fit his bed. Tyler warns that the method is itself in danger of operating according to Procrustean principles, meaning that bothersome empirical details which do not fit the theory get hammered or shorn so that they are made to fit [1]. His stated aim is to use the tool "with sufficient caution" so that existing research "remain[s] intact."

**The wine problem.** Tyler's decisive exhibit is a single page of *Laws of Media*. Applying the tetrad to wine, the McLuhans find that it enhances "grape juice" through fermentation, obsolesces "commonplace flavours," retrieves "ritual observance," and reverses into "cooking wine vinegar." Then, on the same page, they do it again: wine enhances food and "the occasion," obsolesces "inhibition," retrieves "festive spontaneity of speech and gesture" and reverses into "hangover" and insult (1988, p. 206) [1]. Tyler draws the inference carefully rather than gloating: "If the authors themselves seem unsure as to the consistency of the results of the tetrad's application, it seems unlikely that the same conclusions will be drawn by anyone, anywhere, at any time" [1]. The target here is Eric McLuhan's claim, in the book itself, that the four questions "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" (1988, p. 7). Tyler's reply is four words: "This is not, in fact, the case" [1].

**The double bind.** The core of the argument is that the tetrad fails in two opposite directions simultaneously, which is why neither loosening nor tightening it can save it. On the first side, conceived as a universal scientific method the tetrad is "far too vague": "a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things which it might be considered to augment, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into", and the laws "do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since illustrative examples can readily be stretched to fit". On the second: the tetrad is, in Tyler's words, unrelentingly rigid, just like Procrustes' bed: it _requires_ us to fill the gaps [1]. Tyler presses the second point with a concrete question — do we really want to say that wine retrieves "ritual observance"? — and answers that we do violence to these complex notions when they are hewn to fit the tetrad's frame.

The same creative mind therefore plays two incompatible roles. It is the source of whatever value the probe has, because filling a quadrant well takes imagination; and it is the reason the probe cannot be science, because supply will always beat constraint. Tyler's verdict on the status claim is blunt: the idea that these are scientific laws in anything like the ordinary sense of that phrase he calls preposterous [1]. For a sustained earlier critique he points readers to the 1976 exchange between William Henry Venable and McLuhan in *Technology and Culture* — a pointer worth following, because McLuhan's own published reply to Venable is more revealing than any of his critics.

**What Tyler concedes.** The critique is not a demolition, and the concessions are what make the article usable. "And yet the tetrad has its uses. In fact, it is best conceived, as McLuhan himself often did, as a heuristic device taking the form of a set of questions: _what_ does a technology enhance, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into (1977, p. 175)?" [1] The virtue he identifies is specific: the tetrad forces attention onto an artefact's operation and effects rather than onto the content of individual broadcasts, bottles or games. It also delivers what McLuhan called an ordering of thought and experience, which can organise a field's findings and show where researchers have been "barking up the wrong trees." The key concession is that inconsistency across applications stops being a defect once the scientific pretension is dropped: diverse results are acceptable "so long as these provide illuminating insights into the matter at hand."

Tyler then demonstrates the disciplined use rather than prescribing it. Every quadrant of his game tetrad is anchored in cited research — Putnam's *Bowling Alone* and Arthur Asa Berger on the enhancement side, European and Kaiser Family Foundation media-use studies and Nick Yee's MMORPG data on obsolescence. Where the evidence does not support the expected answer, he says so: on whether games obsolesce television, he concludes that the existing studies are collectively uncertain, and rather than force the fit he redefines obsolescence as remediation, in the Bolter and Grusin sense, so that television is repurposed rather than replaced. He narrows his scope deliberately, confining enhancement to solo-play complexity, and he aims each quadrant at a named misconception — Berger's claim that solo gaming is alienating, naive claims that games displace television, the "immersive fallacy" identified by Salen and Zimmerman. He describes his result as "one amongst many possible surveys." The closing image ties the whole argument together: Theseus turned Procrustes' bed against its owner, and Tyler's last line is that the challenge is to make sure the probe works ultimately for us, as the bed did for Theseus, rather than to end up in thrall to our own technological invention, as Procrustes did [1].

**Where the critics divide.** Tyler and Graham Harman disagree about nearly everything except the conclusion that the tetrad is not ordinary empirical science. Harman, in "The McLuhans and Metaphysics" (in *New Waves in Philosophy of Technology*, 2009), takes Eric McLuhan's side against the sceptics: the tetrad should apply to all objects, not merely human artefacts, because on his reading of McLuhan "every object is a medium." That is a metaphysical claim rather than a methodological one, and it moves the argument to ground where falsifiability was never the point. Harman's contribution to practice is a test for any fourfold: a rigorous one comes from cross-breeding two dualisms, and he warns that even frivolous fourfolds can be generated — his joke example is daytime eating, daytime drinking, night-time eating, night-time drinking — so every fourfold has to ensure that its underlying dualisms are profound enough. He identifies the tetrad's underlying dualisms as figure/ground and metamorphosis. Read through Harman, the tetrad becomes a counterfactual engine rather than a predictive one: each enhancement is said to flip into an appearance of inevitability, so that an extension of man "silently murders other possible worlds."

The charge that the tetrad is art rather than science therefore has two very different outcomes depending on who is answering it. For Tyler it is a demotion that leaves a usable heuristic. For Harman it is a misdescription of something that was never trying to be a hypothesis in the first place.

### 5. Has anyone tried to test it empirically? What was attempted, what counts as a test, and what indirect evidence bears on the laws

The short answer is no. No study tests the tetrad as a hypothesis, and the absence is not for want of looking. What exists instead is one genuine attempt at refutation, one accidental replication failure, and a large applied literature that is qualitative by its own description.

**The one genuine attempt to refute.** McLuhan invited refutation in "McLuhan's Laws of the Media" in *Technology and Culture* in 1975 (the article begins at p. 74) [8], and republished the laws in *ETC: A Review of General Semantics* in June 1977, pp. 173-179 [8]. In April 1976, William Henry Venable took him up on it in the same journal with an article titled "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" (p. 256) [8]. McLuhan's reply, in the same issue, was titled "Misunderstanding the Media's Laws" (p. 263) [8]. The titles alone record the outcome: the one sustained attempt at refutation was answered on the ground that the critic had misunderstood, not that the laws needed revision.

The substance of the exchange, as reported in the secondary literature, is that Venable, an engineer and lawyer, read the four terms through C. S. Peirce's logic of signs and objected that they presuppose a single target technologists have always aimed at, adding Derek de Solla Price's warning against narrating history as a single arrow pointing at the present. McLuhan's published reply declined the terms entirely: the tetrads, he wrote, are analogical, there are no connections between any of them, only dynamic ratios, and there was simply no point of contact whatever between them. That is the decisive moment for the empirical question. A hypothesis that is withdrawn when tested has not been falsified; it has been reclassified as a device for generating analogies. I could not obtain the full text of either the Venable article or McLuhan's reply, so the strength of Venable's case is less well documented here than the fact and title of McLuhan's response.

**The closest thing to a replication test.** Tyler's wine example functions as an accidental replication study, and it fails. Two tetrads for the same artefact, produced by the same authors, on the same page of *Laws of Media* (1988, p. 206), give different answers in all four quadrants: grape juice versus food and the occasion; commonplace flavours versus inhibition; ritual observance versus festive spontaneity; cooking vinegar versus hangover and insult [1]. If the answers can be checked by anyone, anywhere, at any time, then the authors checking their own answers twice should converge. They do not. This is the strongest evidence against the tetrad's scientific claim that exists, and it is contained in the book itself.

**Application mistaken for evidence.** The applied literature is large, and it is qualitative by its own account. The telemedicine study describes its method as qualitative descriptive, reviewing 23 relevant international journals published between 2015 and 2020 [6]. A 2022 metatheoretical review in *Professional Communication and Translation Studies* concludes by arguing for the tetrad as a qualitative method of analysis in communication sciences [5]. The 2025 Brazilian study of generative AI and intellectual property states that it uses a qualitative approach and identifies potential enhancements, obsolescence, retrievals and reversals — "potential" being the operative word, since nothing is measured [9]. The smartphone essay assembles published findings per quadrant — the Google effect, nomophobia research, Oulasvirta's work on habitual use — and concludes that multiple interpretations are always possible because interpretation rests on the analyst's own thoughts and perceptions [3]. It also uses the tetrad prospectively, to speculate about future developments [3].

None of this is a test, and most of the authors do not claim it is. Citing a study inside a quadrant shows that something in that quadrant happened; it does not show that the medium caused it, that the other three quadrants were correctly identified, or that a different analyst would have found the same four things. The smartphone essay's own admission — that interpretation depends on the interpreter [3] — directly contradicts the universal checkability claim, and is offered as a caveat rather than as a finding about the framework.

**The search for a test, and what it returned.** A Crossref query combining "tetrad" and "McLuhan" with "quantitative", "experiment", "survey", "test" and "prediction" returns no study that tests the tetrad. The only "tetrad test" results are the unrelated sensory-analysis Tetrad Test used in food science (ASTM E3009) — a name collision, and a useful reminder that the word "tetrad" is doing double duty across disciplines [9]. The searches that do surface tetrad scholarship return applications, bibliographic records of McLuhan's own texts, and philosophical treatments. I take the absence to be real rather than an artefact of search: an empirical test would announce itself in a title or abstract, and none does.

**What a test would actually look like.** Three designs are available and cheap, which makes the absence of all three the more striking. I label this paragraph as my own inference rather than a finding.

The first is **inter-analyst reliability**. Give several analysts the same artefact, ask for four answers blind, and measure agreement. This tests the "anyone, anywhere" claim directly, and the wine page predicts it will fail. The second is **quadrant prediction**. Have an analyst fill enhancement, obsolescence and retrieval, seal the reversal quadrant, and check the sealed prediction against what happens. McLuhan's own instruction — never predict anything that hasn't already happened — complicates this, since reversal is supposed to be visible in the present, but a dated prediction with a resolve date would still be scoreable. The third is **comparative lens testing**. Run the tetrad against rival lenses — figure/ground alone, Bolter and Grusin's remediation, Innis's bias — on the same artefacts and see which produces claims that survive checking. No such comparison appears in the literature.

**Indirect evidence from adjacent McLuhan claims.** The tetrad is not the only McLuhan claim put in front of data. McLuhan's hot/cool distinction — the neighbouring binary, not the tetrad — has been examined against perceptual psychology and cognitive-load research, and the pattern is that the underlying principle (media differ in information density and in how much completion they demand) finds support while the specific classifications (radio hot, television cool) do not. If that pattern holds, it is the best available guess at what a tetrad test would return: the general intuition survives, the four specific boxes do not. But this is an inference from a neighbouring claim, not a result about the tetrad.

**Why nobody ran the test.** Two reasons are visible in the sources. The first is definitional: once the book stipulates that anything which does not answer all four questions is not a product of human creation, no artefact can fail, and a claim nothing could refute is not a research programme. The second is that the tradition chose interpretation. The extensions that followed — Levinson's wheel, Logan's spiral and Laws of Media Environments, Federman's management version — all add structure, and none adds a test. The field's own verdict, in the *Professional Communication and Translation Studies* review, is that the tetrad is a qualitative method [5]. That is a defensible settlement. It is not the one the McLuhans announced in 1975, and the gap between the announcement and the settlement has never been formally closed.


## Beyond this question

The tetrad's history is a clean case study in what happens to a framework that is offered as science and then defended as art. The practical lesson for anyone who wants to use it — Chris's own papers run tetrads on voice interfaces, drugs, and AI editors — is that the framework's value and its weakness come from the same property. Because it constrains nothing, it will always fill four boxes fluently; because it will always fill four boxes, a tetrad on its own carries no evidential weight.

Three habits follow from the evidence here, and they are worth stating as rules rather than suggestions.

**Publish rival tetrads, not a single one.** The wine page is the best thing in the book for a user of the tetrad, because it shows two competent analysts arriving at different four-box answers for the same artefact. That is not a scandal to be hidden; it is the honest output format. Two tetrads and the disagreement between them is more informative than one confident tetrad, and it makes the analyst's choices visible.

**Leave a quadrant empty when the evidence is not there.** Tyler's second objection — that the tetrad "requires" us to fill the gaps — is the one that does the most practical damage, because it turns a blank into a fabrication. An empty quadrant is data about the limits of the analysis.

**Convert reversal into a dated, checkable claim or drop it.** The reversal quadrant is where the tetrad makes its most interesting and most speculative moves, and where McLuhan's own rule — never predict anything that hasn't already happened — is most often broken. A reversal that cannot be dated and resolved is rhetoric.

The larger point is that the test nobody ran is cheap. An inter-analyst reliability study on twenty artefacts would settle the "anyone, anywhere" claim in a few weeks and would be publishable in *Explorations in Media Ecology* whether it succeeded or failed. The fact that it has not been run in thirty-eight years tells you what the field expects the answer to be.

## Open questions

**Whether any empirical test exists that this search could not reach.** I searched Crossref by bibliographic keyword and read what surfaced; I could not run the general web search or reach paywalled full texts after the search allowance was spent. A test published in a small communication-studies journal, a thesis, or a conference proceedings volume that Crossref does not index well would not have appeared. I think the absence is real — a test would name itself in a title — but it is not established with the confidence that a full-text search of the communication-studies literature would give.

**The contents of the Venable exchange.** I have the exact titles, journal, issue and page numbers for both "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" and "Misunderstanding the Media's Laws," and the substance of Venable's argument and McLuhan's reply only through secondary summary [8]. The single most important exchange in the tetrad's critical history has not been read in full here. Anyone taking this further should read both pieces; they are four pages apart in the same 1976 issue.

**What *Laws of Media* actually says, page by page.** The book is lending-restricted and I could not read it. Every claim in this report about the 1988 text comes through Tyler's quotations, the publisher's description, or the record's own synthesis — including the crucial page 7 claim and the wine page (p. 206). The wine example is quoted at length by Tyler and is reliable; other passages are secondhand and should be checked against the book before being relied on.

**Whether inter-analyst reliability has ever been measured informally.** Tetrad workshops and the 1978 Tetrad Conference presumably produced multiple tetrads for the same artefacts in the same room, which would be exactly the data needed. Whether anyone recorded and compared them is unknown to me, and the conference proceedings were not reachable.

**How the tradition would respond to a failed test.** The most interesting unanswered question is not empirical but sociological. Given that McLuhan himself answered Venable by reclassifying the tetrad as analogical, it is unclear what result would count as disconfirming for the media-ecology tradition — and a framework that cannot say in advance what would refute it is in the same position in 2026 that it was in 1976. Nobody in the literature reviewed here has stated the conditions under which the tetrad would be abandoned.

**Coverage note.** Sections 3 and 5 lean on Crossref index records and abstracts for several applications [5][6][7][9], and those records are one source in the sense that matters: the same database, retrieved by the same queries. The claims drawn from them are bibliographic (that a paper exists, what it says it does) rather than substantive, so the dependence is less serious than it would be for findings, but the applied-literature survey should not be read as independent confirmation of anything beyond the existence and stated method of those papers.

label: article from the record
q: Write an article from the record's research on algorithmic rent-setting software in Canada: what it does, what the record found about its use and its effects on rents, and what remains unproven. Argue from what the documents show, quoting them.

report.title: Algorithmic rent-setting in Canada: RealPage and Yardi in rental buildings, the retreat after 2024, and what both cases left undecided
report.body:
No Canadian decision has established whether rent-setting software raised rents. <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="Key Findings">The Competition Bureau discontinued its civil inquiry into RealPage Canada and Yardi Canada on November 10, 2025, finding adoption "not sufficiently widespread"</q>, and the tenant class action against RealPage and a list of landlord groups stopped short of certification. The question both left open is whether landlords who use the same algorithm have agreed with each other.

## The software pools private lease data and returns a daily rent

Landlords in Canada buy revenue-management software from RealPage — YieldStar, AI Revenue Management and Lease Rent Options — and from Yardi, whose Revenue IQ used to be called RENTmaximizer. The products do not set a rent on their own authority. They take figures a landlord would never publish and turn them into a recommendation: <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="1. The Vendors and How the Products Work">competing landlords feed nonpublic, granular lease-transaction data (effective rents, lease terms, occupancy, future availability) into a common algorithm, which returns daily price recommendations</q>.

Compliance is designed in rather than left to the landlord's judgement: <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="1. The Vendors and How the Products Work">an "auto-accept" function and human "pricing advisors" raise compliance</q>. RealPage described the aim internally as <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="1. The Vendors and How the Products Work">driving every possible opportunity to increase price</q>, and its own phrase for what the software does to a market was <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="1. The Vendors and How the Products Work">a rising tide raises all ships</q>. The newer product wraps the same engine in a machine-learning layer that, in the Bureau's account, <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="1. The Vendors and How the Products Work">purportedly generates faster and more accurate predictions</q>.

Yardi disputes the premise of the complaint. Its product, the company says, uses the client's own property data plus publicly available asking rents and <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="1. The Vendors and How the Products Work">never confidential competitor pricing data</q>. Courts have split on what that design claim is worth: <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="1. The Vendors and How the Products Work">a California state court (Oct 2025) accepted Yardi's design defence</q>, while a federal judge hearing Duffy v. Yardi refused to dismiss the case, noting that routing sensitive data through <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="1. The Vendors and How the Products Work">an intermediary, Yardi, to compile their commercially sensitive data... does not preclude the existence of an agreement</q>.

The legal interest in a shared algorithm is not the number it prints but the place the coordination happens. <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="7. The McLuhan / Forensic Framing">competitors never speak, yet one algorithm metabolizes their pooled private data and returns mutually reinforcing prices</q>, and the <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="7. The McLuhan / Forensic Framing">medium becomes the meeting that never happened</q>.

## The Canadian evidence is documentary, and much of it is the companies' own words

The earliest hard trace is a vendor's own marketing. <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="Key Findings">a June 2017 RealPage press release naming GWLRA subsidiary Vertica Resident Services as a YieldStar client reporting "2%–4% revenue outperformance"</q> is the documentary root of "used in Canada since at least 2017". After that the trail is a mixture of confirmations, denials and one unverified report. Woodbourne Capital <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="2. The Roster of Canadian Adopters (with evidence tiers)">publicly confirmed YieldStar use</q>. GWLRA <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="2. The Roster of Canadian Adopters (with evidence tiers)">confirmed to CBC it used YieldStar, then "terminated" it after an internal review (Oct 2024)</q>. Tricon Residential told CBC it stopped in summer 2024 and that the software <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="2. The Roster of Canadian Adopters (with evidence tiers)">never impacted rents</q>. QuadReal's adoption surfaces in <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="2. The Roster of Canadian Adopters (with evidence tiers)">a 2024 leasing-associate ad instructing staff to conduct monthly market surveys</q> that had to be updated in YieldStar. The Breach reported that Starlight Investments was <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="2. The Roster of Canadian Adopters (with evidence tiers)">one of at least 13 companies in Canada with more than $5 billion in revenue that have used the YieldStar software</q>, a claim resting on a database the publication did not name. CAPREIT's answer to CBC was flat: <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="2. The Roster of Canadian Adopters (with evidence tiers)">We have not, are not, and will never use</q> YieldStar.

The statement of claim named RealPage and 14 landlord or manager groups, and the caveat that comes with those names matters: <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="Caveats">The class-action allegations were never tested and are now discontinued; naming defendants reflects pleadings, not proven conduct.</q>

The size of Canadian use was never established independently. RealPage's spokesperson put its Canadian presence at a <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="1. The Vendors and How the Products Work">one per cent penetration rate</q> and described the software as <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="1. The Vendors and How the Products Work">purposely built to be legally compliant</q>. <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="Caveats">The 1% Canadian-penetration figure originates with RealPage and is self-serving</q>, and the Bureau did not publish a share of its own.

## The Competition Bureau closed on market share; the class action never reached a ruling on the merits

The Bureau opened a file in August 2024, ran an algorithmic-pricing consultation that drew 103 responses, and <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="3. The Competition Bureau Record">discontinued the RealPage/Yardi inquiry on November 10, 2025</q>. It tested abuse of dominance and anticompetitive collaboration and found neither, <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="3. The Competition Bureau Record">explicitly because adoption "did not reach the anticompetitive thresholds" and had fallen since late 2024</q>. That closure was <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="Caveats">not a ruling that the software is lawful</q>. The Bureau <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="3. The Competition Bureau Record">remains concerned</q>, can reopen the file on <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="Caveats">new and compelling evidence</q>, <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="3. The Competition Bureau Record">issued four diagnostic compliance questions</q>, and warned that even anonymized competitor data used behind the scenes can let software <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="3. The Competition Bureau Record">act as a means for competitors to coordinate</q>.

The class action was filed in November 2024 on behalf of <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="4. The Class Action in Detail">all persons in Canada who leased a unit owned, operated, or managed by any defendant between November 26, 2009 and the present</q>. It was <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="Key Findings">discontinued by court order effective April 1, 2026, before any certification motion</q>. Tenants who might have claimed on their own now face the clock: <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="4. The Class Action in Detail">class members' individual limitation periods (suspended under s.28(1) of the Class Proceedings Act) resumed running on April 1, 2026</q>. And the country has no ruling either way: <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="4. The Class Action in Detail">The Canadian discontinuance leaves no domestic precedent on whether a shared algorithm constitutes an "agreement."</q>

> **Objection: adoption was never big enough to move a market**
>
> That is close to what the Bureau concluded, and the conclusion is narrower than it sounds. The test it applies is share: <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="3. The Competition Bureau Record">A firm generally needs ~50% market share (65% for a group) to prompt a dominance finding — a bar neither vendor met given low Canadian uptake.</q> A finding that a vendor is too small to dominate is not a finding about rents. The share figure in circulation is the vendor's own, and the withdrawal is what removed the evidence: the software <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="TL;DR">grew gradually, then retreated sharply after late-2024 public scrutiny</q>, and falling adoption is one of the stated reasons the thresholds were not met.

## The law asks for a handshake the software never needs

<q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="Key Findings">Sections 45 (criminal conspiracy) and 90.1 (civil agreements) both require an "agreement/arrangement."</q> That is a meeting of minds, not a shared subscription. The June 2025 amendments to the Competition Act eased several of the surrounding tests, <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="Key Findings">but none reach genuinely autonomous tacit coordination absent an agreement</q>. The Bureau's own consultation recorded the worry in plain terms: <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="3. The Competition Bureau Record">tacit collusion through algorithms typically falls outside existing competition law because the law requires evidence of a 'meeting of the minds.'</q>

Other jurisdictions wrote rules for the case instead of waiting for the agreement. <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="Key Findings">nine US municipalities plus two states (California, New York) have banned or restricted algorithmic rent-setting</q>. In Canada, <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="5. The International Regulatory Wave">No province or municipality has enacted or formally tabled an algorithmic-rent ban or disclosure rule.</q>

## The software retreated; the concentration that made it worth selling did not

Rent-setting software matters in proportion to how few landlords there are to sell it to. Canadian rental stock is concentrated and getting more so: <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="TL;DR">the 25 biggest financial firms held ~340,000 suites in 2021, about 20% of purpose-built multi-family stock, with some estimates of 30% financialized</q>. Turnover is where the money is, and Ontario's rules reward it: <q doc="price-without-discovery-from-the-signal-to-the-instruction" section="Key Findings">Vacancy decontrol — especially in Ontario — creates the unit-turnover incentive that revenue-management software exists to optimize.</q> Concentration outlasts any product cycle: <q doc="price-without-discovery-from-the-signal-to-the-instruction" section="Key Findings">Algorithmic rent-setting is dangerous in proportion to concentration, and Canadian concentration is high and rising even as YieldStar specifically retreats.</q> The category is not shrinking with that retreat either — the Bureau counted <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="1. The Vendors and How the Products Work">over 60 companies offering algorithmic pricing services</q> in Canada across sectors.

## What is still unproven is whether any Canadian rent moved

Nothing in the Canadian proceedings measured rents. The allegation was that tenants overpaid from 2009 onward; it was never tested, and the discontinuance ended the case before the stage where the American litigation found its evidence — <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="4. The Class Action in Detail">the Canadian plaintiffs never reached discovery to develop</q> the link between competing landlords that would turn a shared tool into an alleged agreement.

The American numbers are large and belong to a different market. RealPage's clients there <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="1. The Vendors and How the Products Work">comprised nearly 90% of the market for multifamily rental housing units of 50 units or more, and court documents cited landlords accepting the software's pricing recommendations 80–90% of the time</q>. The Justice Department's antitrust chief said <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="Key Findings">RealPage was replacing competition with coordination, and renters paid the price</q>, and <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="Key Findings">private US settlements total nearly US$360 million</q>. None of it measures a Canadian rent.

The measurement problem is the reason the question stays open. Listing prices cannot answer it: <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="6. The Detection Instrument — Feasibility and Design">Parallel pricing is the expected output of competitive markets, rent-control caps, and shared public benchmarks (Rentals.ca, CMHC).</q> Anyone claiming to detect coordination from advertised rents is drawing <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="6. The Detection Instrument — Feasibility and Design">exactly the inference the Bureau itself declined to draw</q>.

> **Objection: the American case already established what this software does**
>
> It established what American landlords did with it, under a different statute, and the settlement <q doc="price-without-discovery-from-the-signal-to-the-instruction" section="Key Findings">imposes no fine and no admission of wrongdoing</q>. The Canadian courts reached no merits in either direction: the class action stopped before certification, the Bureau closed on share, and a California state court accepted Yardi's claim that its product never touches competitors' private data. A settlement without an admission is not a finding, and a finding about American rents is not a finding about Toronto.

## An inquiry that ends because the conduct stopped has settled nothing

Both Canadian tracks ended at the point where the law would have had to say what an agreement is. That is the substance of the story rather than its loose end: <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="7. The McLuhan / Forensic Framing">the statute still hunts for the human handshake while coordination has relocated into the tool</q>. What the software changes is not only the level of a rent but the way a rent is arrived at — <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="7. The McLuhan / Forensic Framing">prices set neither by the friction of rivalrous markets nor by an overt cartel, but administered through a vendor's optimization engine</q>. A legal system that can see only the handshake will keep finding nothing, however many buildings run the same tool.

The question has not disappeared. It has moved to a sector where the Bureau has more at stake: its inquiry into Kalibrate, a retail-gasoline data service, <q doc="realpage-north-algorithmic-rent-setting-in-canada-a-forensic-investiga" section="3. The Competition Bureau Record">remains open — confirming the Bureau's algorithmic-pricing enforcement interest persists in another sector</q>. A decision there on what counts as coordination between firms that share a computation would be a Canadian precedent of a kind that does not yet exist, and it would apply to rents as readily as to petrol.

That is what this episode leaves. The software arrived, was documented by the companies that used it and by the vendor that sold it, and went out of use under scrutiny before anyone measured what it did to a rent. The concentration that made a shared pricing engine worth buying is still in place, and the legal question the software raised is now general rather than specific to housing: what a competition authority can prove when firms coordinate by subscribing to the same computation.
