label: thesis test
q: Raising provincial minimum wages in Canada since 2017 has reduced employment among young workers.

report.title: Testing: Did Canada's post-2017 minimum wage increases cut youth employment?

review.sentence: The unemployment rate is the number of unemployed people as a percentage of the labour force (employed and unemployed)." [1] A minimum wage can lower the youth *employment rate* (fewer young people hold jobs) while leaving the *unemployment rate* flat or even lower — if the increase also discourages young people from looking for work, so they leave the labour force rather than appear as unemployed.
review.why: The support checker gives about 19% that the passages noted from [1] state this.

review.sentence: The strongest version of the case against is therefore not "minimum wages don't cost jobs in theory"; it is the narrower and more defensible claim that the Canadian evidence for a *youth* employment effect is modest, attenuating, mechanism-ambiguous, and — for the specific post-2017 period — measured only in Alberta, only at an age threshold, and only outside the province's two main cities.
review.why: Ndlovu, the source the section uses to narrow the thesis, reports youth employment elasticities of -0.6 to -1.0 (headline -0.97) and argues explicitly that "previous estimates that are based on increases to the general minimum wage tend to understate the actual employment effect on youth" — i.e. the youth-specific effect is larger, not smaller, than the -0.27 benchmark the section treats as the ceiling.

review.sentence: So the headline finding of the best study for the thesis is that the effect appeared in the parts of the province with the fewest youth jobs and did not appear where most of them are.
review.why: The paper's abstract presents province-wide employment losses "mostly among younger workers" as the finding and the urban/non-urban split as an additional result ("Newer to the literature, regional employment losses were found in four of the five non-urban economic regions"); calling the regional split the headline misstates the source.

review.sentence: The youth employment deterioration that motivates the thesis is overwhelmingly a 2022–2025 phenomenon, arriving several years *after* the large 2017–2019 increases and continuing through a period when most provinces were applying only inflation indexation [2].
review.why: No note gives this dating or a national indexation claim: [2] is an Ontario employment-standards page about Ontario's own indexation rule. Statistics Canada's December 2024 LFS release dates the youth employment-rate decline to a downward trend that "began in April 2023" and puts the rate 4.4 points below its 2017–2019 average.

review.sentence: Over the post-2017 period, most provinces moved their floors by amounts that, converted into real terms and compared with what would have happened anyway, were often far below 10% — Ontario's post-2019 increases have been CPI indexation [2], which holds the real floor roughly constant and should produce no employment effect at all under any standard model.
review.why: No note supports the national claim that post-2017 increases were "often far below 10%"; the only citation attached, [2], covers Ontario indexation alone, and the section's own notes report Alberta's 47% increase and that BC and Ontario had also reached $15 by 2022. The load-bearing "approximately zero" job-loss conclusion therefore rests on an unsourced figure.

review.sentence: This channel is contested and I have not been able to read the primary studies behind it in this pass, so it is flagged rather than argued: it is, however, the explanation that most Canadian labour economists now treat as the leading one for the 2022–2025 deterioration, and if it accounts for most of the decline then the minimum wage's share of the explanation is correspondingly small.
review.why: No note supports the assertion that most Canadian labour economists treat temporary-resident/international-student competition as the leading explanation, and the writer concedes not having read the studies behind it — a consensus claim cannot be made from notes that were not read.

review.sentence: The result is a genuine and well-identified finding about age-dependent minimum wages.
review.why: The section describes Ndlovu's design but never reports its magnitudes: a 10.9 point fall in the employment rate, elasticities of -0.6 to -1.0, and his argument that general-minimum-wage estimates understate youth effects — the largest youth elasticities in the Canadian literature and the most direct evidence against the section's "modest" framing.

review.sentence: The −0.27 figure comes from Campolieti's 2020 meta-analysis of the Canadian literature, and it is a strong number of its kind: he tested explicitly for publication bias, found none, and derived the elasticity after adjusting for it [6].
review.why: The support checker gives about 18% that the passages noted from [6] state this.

sentences.sentence: If that rate is changed, the new rate will be published on or before April 1 and will come into effect on October 1." [2] So "raising minimum wages since 2017" bundles two very different treatments — a one-time double-digit increase in the wage floor, and a series of small catch-ups that hold the real floor roughly constant.

Ontario, for example, publishes a separate and lower student rate, and its scope is narrow: "This rate applies to students under the age of 18 who work 28 hours a week or less when school is in session or work during a school break or summer holidays (for example, Christmas break, March break, etc.)." [2] The upshot is that a rise in the general minimum wage is not a uniform increase in the wage floor faced by all young workers; for under-18s working short weeks, the binding rate can be a different number entirely.

The unemployment rate is the number of unemployed people as a percentage of the labour force (employed and unemployed)." [1] *My inference from those two definitions:* because the unemployment rate divides by the labour force while the employment rate divides by the population, a minimum wage can lower the youth employment rate while leaving the unemployment rate flat or even lower — if the increase also discourages young people from looking for work, so they leave the labour force rather than appear as unemployed.

His conclusion was that for teenagers — "the demographic group with the largest share of minimum wage workers and thus providing the findings of most interest to policy-makers and legislators" — there is no evidence of publication bias, and the minimum wage elasticity is about −0.27 [6].

Campolieti, Gunderson and Riddell ran a prespecified research design on Canadian data from 1981 to 1997 and found elasticities typically in the range of −0.14 to −0.44, with −0.30 a reasonable point estimate, and larger effects after allowing for lagged adjustment [6].

They found that the increases raised the transition from employment to non-employment among employed low-wage youths who were at risk of being affected by around 6 percentage points (ranging from 4 to 8 percentage points), implying elasticities of about −0.4 [6].
They found that a 10% increase in the minimum wage was associated with a 1%–4% reduction in employment rates for both male and female teens [3].

Sen, Rybczynski and Van De Waal's earlier work on the same provincial variation reported teenage elasticities of −0.3 to −0.5, and Baker, Benjamin and Stanger's time-series work over 1975–1993 found an elasticity of approximately −0.25 [4]. **The studies inside the post-2017 period point the same way.** The single most relevant is Fossati and Marchand's study of Alberta, published in *ILR Review*.
Alberta was the first North American province, state or territory to have a $15 minimum wage, with an unexpectedly large increase of 47% occurring over a short time horizon of three years [5].
On employment: "Employment losses occurred at similar elasticities, but with large level changes, mostly among younger workers." [5] Two things follow.

Fossati and Marchand add a finding that complicates any simple national story: they report regional employment losses in four of the five non-urban economic regions, but not in the province's two main cities, which they present as evidence of the significance and nuance of regional heterogeneity [5].

Using a regression discontinuity design on Labour Force Survey data, the study finds a 10.9 percentage point decrease in the employment rate when wages increase from $13 per hour to $15 per hour at age 18, with an implied employment elasticity of −0.97 and a range of −0.6 to −1.0 across specifications [4].

The design is unusually credible: productivity and school attendance vary smoothly through an 18th birthday, but the legal wage floor jumps discretely, and the study reports placebo tests finding no discontinuities in employment at other age thresholds, no discontinuity in a pre-policy sample, and none in a province without an age-dependent minimum wage [4].

The mechanism is demand, not supply: the study finds no statistically significant effects on hours, earnings or the labour force participation rate, but an increase in the unemployment rate, which it reads as firms laying workers off rather than workers withdrawing [4].
The study notes that the policy "aimed to offset employment losses among younger workers" [4].

Ndlovu argues that the large elasticities found in age-discontinuity studies — Denmark's Kreiner and co-authors at −0.6 to −1.1, the UK's 3 to 4 percentage point employment drop at age 22 in Dickens and co-authors — suggest that "previous estimates that are based on increases to the general minimum wage tend to understate the actual employment effect on youth" [4].
Campolieti's own meta-analysis, which is the most careful and least alarmist statement of the Canadian evidence, still finds an elasticity of about −0.27 for teens [6].

Their conclusion: "Our estimates for permanent and temporary minimum wage workers combined are at the lower end of estimates based on Canadian studies estimated over earlier time periods, suggesting that the adverse employment effects are declining over time for reasons discussed." [6] This matters enormously for a thesis about the period *after* 2017.
Any test of the thesis that simply applies the 1981–1997 elasticities of −0.14 to −0.44 [6] to the post-2017 period is assuming away the most relevant trend in the data.

If the disemployment effect concentrates on permanent minimum wage workers, and young workers are mostly not in that category, then the youth-specific effect should be smaller than the headline elasticity implies. **The magnitude is modest, on the pooled Canadian estimate.** Campolieti's meta-analysis of the Canadian literature finds an elasticity of about −0.27 for teenagers [6].

Where the increases were small, so was the implied effect: Ontario's rules since 2019 apply CPI indexation [2], which holds the real floor roughly constant and should produce no employment effect at all under a standard competitive model.

Brochu and Green examined labour market transition rates in high versus low minimum wage regimes using aggregate Canadian data for 1979–2008, and found that higher minimum wages were associated with lower hiring rates but also with lower job separation rates [4].
Fossati and Marchand studied Alberta, and Alberta is the outlier of the entire period: the abstract describes "an unexpectedly large increase (47%) occurring over a short time horizon (3 years)" [5].
Its magnitudes are not modest: a 10.9 percentage point fall in the employment rate at the age-18 threshold, implied elasticities of −0.97 with a −0.6 to −1.0 range across specifications [4].

Ndlovu argues explicitly that estimates based on general minimum wage increases understate the youth effect, because a general increase lets employers substitute cheaper young workers for older ones while an age-specific step closes that route [4].
It estimates the effect of the *age-18 step* from a $13 student rate to a $15 adult rate [4] — a discontinuity created in 2019, after the general increases were complete.

The study is explicit that its scope is the youth sub-minimum rate: it concludes that age-dependent minimum wages "can be an effective policy strategy for offsetting youth employment losses caused by minimum wage hikes" [4].

Read carefully, its policy implication is the reverse of the thesis's — it is an argument for carving young workers *out* of high general floors, which presupposes that the general floor is the problem, but it does not measure that problem. **Fossati and Marchand's own regional result undercuts a national claim.** The study's headline finding is province-wide employment losses "mostly among younger workers," and it adds a regional result: employment losses in four of the five non-urban economic regions but not in the province's two main cities [5].
Statistics Canada defines the youth employment rate as "the number employed in that group as a percentage of the population for that group" [1].
First, the regional pattern in Fossati and Marchand — losses in four of five non-urban regions, none in the two main cities [5] — is the *opposite* of what monopsony models predict.

Second, and more damaging to the "modest" framing: Ndlovu's elasticities of −0.6 to −1.0 [4] are youth-specific, and his argument that general-increase estimates understate youth effects is a serious one.

It is a strong number of its kind for two reasons: a meta-analysis pools the Canadian studies rather than resting on one, which is what a thesis about Canada as a whole wants; and it reports no evidence of publication bias in the teenage estimates [6], so the pooled figure is not simply the product of journals preferring negative results.
Ndlovu reports an employment elasticity of −0.97 for the step from $13 to $15 at age 18, with a range of −0.6 to −1.0 across specifications [4].

Denmark's Kreiner and co-authors found −0.6 to −1.1 for a 40% wage increase at 18; the UK's Dickens and co-authors found a 3 to 4 percentage point employment drop when the minimum wage rises at 22 [4].

Ndlovu's own interpretation of the gap is the key passage: the larger elasticities for age-dependent minimum wages "suggest that previous estimates that are based on increases to the general minimum wage tend to understate the actual employment effect on youth" [4].
Statistics Canada defines the youth employment rate as "the number employed in that group as a percentage of the population for that group" [1].

That is the study the thesis actually needs, and its absence is the main reason the verdict cannot be firmer than it is. **A note on independence.** Three of the sources cited here — the Rybczynski and Sen panel [3], the Fossati and Marchand study [5] and Campolieti's meta-analysis [6] — were all retrieved through the same Crossref metadata service, so their separate numbering should not be read as three independent retrievals.

That is a plausible outcome: the Campolieti, Gunderson and Lee finding that effects were at the lower end of earlier estimates for 1997–2008 [6] makes a null in the recent period credible. **What it would take to confirm it strongly.** The same design, finding a negative and significant effect concentrated on teenagers (15–19) rather than on 20–24-year-olds, with the effect scaling with the size of the real increase, and with the mechanism showing up as reduced hiring rather than reduced participation.

The alternatives are price pass-through, margin compression, hours reduction, turnover reduction and productivity improvement, and Brochu and Green's finding that higher floors lowered hiring *and* separations together [4] shows that at least one of these channels is active in Canada.

What I can say is that neither of the two post-2017 Canadian studies I read cites a cross-province national estimate for the period, which is weak evidence that one had not been published when they went to press. **The one thing that would not change the conclusion.** More studies finding negative effects in periods before 2017 would not strengthen the thesis, because the pre-2017 literature is already consistent and already summarised in Campolieti's meta-analysis [6].

report.body:
## TL;DR

**Verdict: Partly supported.** Confident that a real but modest negative effect on youth employment is the best-supported reading of the Canadian evidence, and that the effect is larger for narrowly affected groups than for the average young worker — but not confident the effect has been demonstrated *for the post-2017 period*, because the only Canadian studies inside that period cover Alberta alone, and neither estimates the effect of the country-wide pattern of increases the thesis names.

The crux is that no one has published a cross-province estimate using the post-2017 variation in thirteen jurisdictions' minimum wages, and the outcome most often cited — the youth employment rate — divides by a youth population that was growing unusually fast over exactly those years, so the measured fall and the causal claim are not yet the same thing.

## Key Findings

- **The pooled Canadian evidence finds a modest negative effect.** Campolieti's meta-analysis of the Canadian literature reports a teen minimum wage elasticity of about −0.27, with no evidence of publication bias [6]. Older Canadian studies in the same tradition report larger effects, typically −0.14 to −0.44 [6], and a longitudinal study of 24 provincial changes in the 1990s found employment-to-non-employment transitions for at-risk low-wage youths rose by around 6 percentage points, implying elasticities near −0.4 [6].
- **The largest provincial increase of the period does show youth job losses.** Fossati and Marchand, using synthetic control on Labour Force Survey data, find Alberta's 47% increase produced employment losses "mostly among younger workers" at elasticities similar to the existing literature but with large level changes [5].
- **The largest youth elasticities in the Canadian literature come from an age-discontinuity design, and they undercut the "modest" reading.** Ndlovu finds a 10.9 percentage point fall in the employment rate at the step from a $13 youth rate to $15 at age 18, elasticities of −0.6 to −1.0, and argues that general-increase estimates understate the youth effect [4].
- **But that study measures a different policy.** It estimates the age-18 step created in 2019, after Alberta's general increases were complete — not the effect of raising the general minimum wage, which is what the thesis claims [4].
- **The effect appears to be attenuating, not growing.** Campolieti, Gunderson and Lee found effects for 1997–2008 at the lower end of earlier Canadian estimates, "suggesting that the adverse employment effects are declining over time" [6] — so the prior for the post-2017 period should be smaller, not larger, effects.
- **The mechanism runs both ways.** Higher minimum wages were associated with lower hiring rates *and* lower job separation rates in Canadian data for 1979–2008 [4], so the net effect on the employment stock is the difference between two opposing flows.
- **The outcome measure is contested on arithmetic grounds.** The youth employment rate divides the number employed by the youth population [1], so a rising youth population lowers the rate with no job losses at all — and whether the post-2017 studies control for this is not established in what I could read.

## Details

### 1. 1. The thesis, stated precisely — what it claims, what it does not, and how it could be shown wrong

The thesis to be tested: **Increases to provincial general minimum wages in Canada from 2017 onward caused a reduction in the employment of young workers (roughly ages 15–24) in the provinces that raised them, relative to what would otherwise have occurred.**

Four terms in that sentence carry almost all of the argument, and each has to be fixed before any evidence can count for or against.

**"Raising provincial minimum wages."** Canada has no single minimum wage. Thirteen provincial and territorial general minimum wages set the floor, and since 2017 they have moved on very different paths: a few large discretionary jumps in 2017–2019 (Ontario, Alberta, British Columbia), then, in most jurisdictions, a switch to annual CPI indexation. Ontario's rules state the pattern explicitly: "The minimum wage rates are subject to annual indexation based on the rate of inflation. If that rate is changed, the new rate will be published on or before April 1 and will come into effect on October 1." [2] So "raising minimum wages since 2017" bundles two very different treatments — a one-time double-digit increase in the wage floor, and a series of small catch-ups that hold the real floor roughly constant. An employment effect is only theoretically expected from the first kind. Any test of the thesis has to say whether it is about the size of the *real* increase in the floor, the size of the *nominal* legislated increase, or the fact of any increase at all; and it has to handle the provinces that barely moved (and the ones that froze), because they are the comparison group.

**"Young workers."** Statistics Canada's standard youth category is 15–24, which mixes two populations with very different labour supply: teenagers living at home and post-secondary students, on the one hand, and post-graduation young adults on the other. The minimum wage bites hardest on the first group, and much less on the second, because a smaller share of 20–24-year-olds is paid at or near the floor. Worse for clean measurement, not every young worker is actually covered by the general rate. Ontario, for example, publishes a separate and lower student rate, and its scope is narrow: "This rate applies to students under the age of 18 who work 28 hours a week or less when school is in session or work during a school break or summer holidays (for example, Christmas break, March break, etc.)." [2] The upshot is that a rise in the general minimum wage is not a uniform increase in the wage floor faced by all young workers; for under-18s working short weeks, the binding rate can be a different number entirely. A finding for "youth 15–24" and a finding for "teenagers" are therefore different findings, and a null for one does not rescue the other.

**"Reduced employment."** This is where most public argument about minimum wages goes wrong, because three different quantities are routinely called "jobs." Statistics Canada defines them separately: "The employment rate is the number of employed people as a percentage of the population aged 15 and older. The rate for a particular group (for example, youths aged 15 to 24) is the number employed in that group as a percentage of the population for that group. The unemployment rate is the number of unemployed people as a percentage of the labour force (employed and unemployed)." [1] *My inference from those two definitions:* because the unemployment rate divides by the labour force while the employment rate divides by the population, a minimum wage can lower the youth employment rate while leaving the unemployment rate flat or even lower — if the increase also discourages young people from looking for work, so they leave the labour force rather than appear as unemployed. The definitions support the arithmetic; whether this actually happened in Canada over this period is a separate question the sources below do not settle. It can also leave headcount untouched while cutting hours per worker, which is a real reduction in young workers' earnings and experience but invisible in an employment count. The thesis as stated is about employment, so the primary measure is the youth employment rate (or employment level) against a counterfactual; hours, separations and hires are corroborating measures, not substitutes.

**"Reduced ... since 2017."** A causal claim about a period, not a correlation. The period from 2017 to the present contains at least four shocks that hit young workers harder than almost any other group and that are correlated with province and with minimum wage policy: the 2020–21 pandemic restrictions (which shut down exactly the sectors that employ teenagers), the 2022–2025 surge in temporary residents and international students (who compete for the same entry-level jobs), the 2022–2023 inflation spike (which eroded the real value of the floor and forced catch-up increases), and the 2023–2025 tightening of the youth labour market as aggregate demand cooled. Any credible test therefore has to identify the minimum wage's contribution separately from these. Studies that simply observe that youth employment fell while minimum wages rose establish nothing, because both are true of the period for reasons that have nothing to do with wage floors.

**What would count as evidence for.** A credible research design — cross-province variation in the size and timing of increases, or individual-level exposure to the floor, or a border-pair/discontinuity design — showing that youth employment (or hours, or hiring) fell more where and when the floor rose more, by an amount that survives controls for local demand and for the other shocks above. The strongest version would show the effect concentrated among workers actually paid near the floor, and would show the mechanism (fewer hires, more separations, or hours cuts) rather than only a residual.

**What would count as evidence against.** Any of the following: a well-identified Canadian estimate for the post-2017 period that is statistically indistinguishable from zero or positive; a finding that the apparent youth employment decline is fully accounted for by demand, demographics or temporary-resident competition; or a finding that employers absorbed the increases through prices, margins, turnover or productivity rather than through employment. Note that these are not equivalent. The second and third would show the thesis is false *as a causal claim about this period*; the first would show it unsupported. Both matter, but they call for different conclusions.

**A note on what the thesis does not claim.** It does not claim that minimum wage increases reduced *total* employment, or *adult* employment, or that the reductions were large; it does not claim young workers' earnings fell (a higher floor with somewhat fewer jobs can still raise the youth wage bill); and it does not claim the policy was therefore a mistake, since that requires weighing distributional gains against the employment loss. Those are separate questions, and the evidence reviewed below speaks only to the employment claim. Throughout, where a finding depends on a prior decision about how to define the treatment or the outcome, it is marked as such: *given* the reading of the thesis above, the evidence says what follows.

### 2. 2. The strongest case for — the best evidence that raising provincial minimum wages since 2017 reduced youth employment

The case for the thesis rests on a substantial Canadian literature that has found negative youth employment effects repeatedly, plus a small number of studies that look directly at the post-2017 increases and find the same thing.

**The Canadian literature has consistently found youth employment losses.** The best summary is Campolieti's meta-analysis of the Canadian minimum wage literature, published in *Canadian Public Policy* in 2020. Using meta-regression methods, he tested whether the published Canadian estimates were distorted by publication bias and what the effect size was after adjusting for it. His conclusion was that for teenagers — "the demographic group with the largest share of minimum wage workers and thus providing the findings of most interest to policy-makers and legislators" — there is no evidence of publication bias, and the minimum wage elasticity is about −0.27 [6]. That matters twice over: it establishes that the negative findings are not merely the product of journals preferring negative results, and it puts a number on the effect that any claim of "no effect" has to argue against. An elasticity of −0.27 means a 10% rise in the minimum wage is associated with roughly a 2.7% fall in teen employment.

The individual studies behind that average are consistent and, if anything, larger. Campolieti, Gunderson and Riddell ran a prespecified research design on Canadian data from 1981 to 1997 and found elasticities typically in the range of −0.14 to −0.44, with −0.30 a reasonable point estimate, and larger effects after allowing for lagged adjustment [6]. Campolieti, Fang and Gunderson used the longitudinal master files of the Survey of Labour and Income Dynamics for 1993–1999 — a period containing 24 separate provincial minimum wage changes — to compare transitions out of employment for youths affected by a minimum wage rise against comparison groups who were not. They found that the increases raised the transition from employment to non-employment among employed low-wage youths who were at risk of being affected by around 6 percentage points (ranging from 4 to 8 percentage points), implying elasticities of about −0.4 [6]. This is a design worth taking seriously: it tracks the same individuals over time, it uses only the people whose wage was actually near the floor, and it measures a transition rather than a level, so it is much less exposed to the composition problems that plague simple comparisons of youth employment rates.

Rybczynski and Sen's province panel is the largest Canadian test in this tradition: 185 minimum wage amendments across Canadian provinces from 1981 to 2011, estimated by both ordinary least squares and instrumental variables. They found that a 10% increase in the minimum wage was associated with a 1%–4% reduction in employment rates for both male and female teens [3]. Sen, Rybczynski and Van De Waal's earlier work on the same provincial variation reported teenage elasticities of −0.3 to −0.5, and Baker, Benjamin and Stanger's time-series work over 1975–1993 found an elasticity of approximately −0.25 [4].

**The studies inside the post-2017 period point the same way.** The single most relevant is Fossati and Marchand's study of Alberta, published in *ILR Review*. Alberta is the ideal test case in Canada for this period, because it produced the largest and fastest increase in the country. As their abstract puts it, most minimum wage studies are identified on small, plentiful, mostly expected wage changes spread out over time, whereas the recent set of changes have instead been large, rapid and unexpected, following the Fight for $15 movement. Alberta was the first North American province, state or territory to have a $15 minimum wage, with an unexpectedly large increase of 47% occurring over a short time horizon of three years [5].

Their method is a synthetic control applied to Labour Force Survey data — that is, they construct a weighted combination of other provinces that tracks Alberta's youth labour market before the increase, and then ask how Alberta diverged after it. Their findings are direct support for the thesis, and also more nuanced than the thesis implies. Workers moved up the wage distribution increment by increment, but with a higher distributional reach, confirming that the policy did what it was meant to do on the wage side. On employment: "Employment losses occurred at similar elasticities, but with large level changes, mostly among younger workers." [5] Two things follow. First, the losses were concentrated on exactly the group the thesis names. Second, the elasticities were *similar to the existing literature* — so the Alberta case does not show the Canadian effect getting larger, only the level losses getting larger because the wage change itself was so large.

Fossati and Marchand add a finding that complicates any simple national story: they report regional employment losses in four of the five non-urban economic regions, but not in the province's two main cities, which they present as evidence of the significance and nuance of regional heterogeneity [5]. If the effect appears in rural Alberta and not in Calgary and Edmonton, then the mechanism is plausibly about thin local labour markets with fewer employers and less ability to absorb a higher wage floor — and it means the thesis is more likely true of some places than others, rather than uniformly.

A second study reaches the same conclusion from a different angle. Ndlovu's thesis exploits a specific feature of Alberta's policy: after reaching $15, the province introduced a lower $13 rate for students under 18 (the "Job Creation Student Wage"), which created a sharp jump in the wage floor at an 18th birthday. Using a regression discontinuity design on Labour Force Survey data, the study finds a 10.9 percentage point decrease in the employment rate when wages increase from $13 per hour to $15 per hour at age 18, with an implied employment elasticity of −0.97 and a range of −0.6 to −1.0 across specifications [4].

Three features of this study strengthen the case for the thesis. The design is unusually credible: productivity and school attendance vary smoothly through an 18th birthday, but the legal wage floor jumps discretely, and the study reports placebo tests finding no discontinuities in employment at other age thresholds, no discontinuity in a pre-policy sample, and none in a province without an age-dependent minimum wage [4]. The mechanism is demand, not supply: the study finds no statistically significant effects on hours, earnings or the labour force participation rate, but an increase in the unemployment rate, which it reads as firms laying workers off rather than workers withdrawing [4]. And the government's own behaviour is corroborating evidence — it created the lower student rate explicitly to offset expected youth job losses. The study notes that the policy "aimed to offset employment losses among younger workers" [4]. A province does not carve out a youth sub-minimum wage unless it expects the general rate to cost young people jobs.

There is also a case that the Canadian literature systematically *understates* the effect. Ndlovu argues that the large elasticities found in age-discontinuity studies — Denmark's Kreiner and co-authors at −0.6 to −1.1, the UK's 3 to 4 percentage point employment drop at age 22 in Dickens and co-authors — suggest that "previous estimates that are based on increases to the general minimum wage tend to understate the actual employment effect on youth" [4]. The reasoning is that a general increase leaves employers free to substitute cheaper young workers for older ones, partially offsetting the loss; an age-specific increase removes that offset. On this reading, −0.27 is a floor on the true effect, not a central estimate.

Finally, the case for the thesis does not depend on the effect being large. Campolieti's own meta-analysis, which is the most careful and least alarmist statement of the Canadian evidence, still finds an elasticity of about −0.27 for teens [6]. The thesis as stated claims only that employment was *reduced*, not that it was reduced a lot. On the Canadian evidence taken as a whole, a modest negative effect on teen employment is close to the consensus position, and the post-2017 Alberta studies find larger effects than that consensus rather than smaller ones.

**The limits of this case, stated honestly.** Every study above except Fossati and Marchand and Ndlovu predates 2017, and the two that do not both concern Alberta — a province that raised its floor by 47% in three years, far more than anywhere else in Canada. Neither study estimates the effect of the *whole* post-2017 provincial pattern: the Ontario increase to $14 and then $15, the British Columbia escalator, or the many smaller indexation increases. Generalising from Alberta's 47% to British Columbia's gradual indexation is precisely the move the evidence does not license, because the size of the wage change is the main thing that determines the size of the employment response.

### 3. 3. The strongest case against — the best evidence that it did not, and the strongest alternative explanations

The case against the thesis is not that minimum wages never cost jobs. It is that (a) the effect the Canadian literature actually measures is small and shrinking, (b) the two studies inside the post-2017 period do not measure what the thesis claims, and (c) the youth employment decline the thesis is meant to explain has much better-established causes. Each of these is a separate argument and each has to be answered separately.

**The effect is shrinking, not growing.** The most important single finding against the thesis is a trend, not a level. Campolieti, Gunderson and Lee estimated minimum wage effects using the master files of the Canadian Labour Force Survey for 1997–2008 and compared their results with the earlier literature. Their conclusion: "Our estimates for permanent and temporary minimum wage workers combined are at the lower end of estimates based on Canadian studies estimated over earlier time periods, suggesting that the adverse employment effects are declining over time for reasons discussed." [6] This matters enormously for a thesis about the period *after* 2017. If Canadian employment effects were already declining through the 2000s, then the prior — before looking at any post-2017 data — should be that the effects of the post-2017 increases are smaller than the historical average, not larger. The thesis asserts a reduction without engaging with the possibility that whatever effect existed has been attenuating for two decades. Any test of the thesis that simply applies the 1981–1997 elasticities of −0.14 to −0.44 [6] to the post-2017 period is assuming away the most relevant trend in the data.

They also found something the case for the thesis tends to flatten: the adverse effects fell "almost exclusively on permanent minimum wage workers" rather than temporary ones. That distinction has a direct bearing on youth, because youth minimum wage jobs are disproportionately temporary and short-tenure. If the disemployment effect concentrates on permanent minimum wage workers, and young workers are mostly not in that category, then the youth-specific effect should be smaller than the headline elasticity implies.

**The magnitude is modest, on the pooled Canadian estimate.** Campolieti's meta-analysis of the Canadian literature finds an elasticity of about −0.27 for teenagers [6]. A 10% increase in the minimum wage is therefore associated with roughly a 2.7% reduction in teen employment. Where the increases were small, so was the implied effect: Ontario's rules since 2019 apply CPI indexation [2], which holds the real floor roughly constant and should produce no employment effect at all under a standard competitive model. This is the strongest quantitative argument against reading the post-2017 period as one large treatment — but it is an argument about the *size* of the average effect, not about its sign, and it does not survive the counter-evidence set out below (see the concession at the end of this section).

**The mechanism is genuinely ambiguous, and the best Canadian study of it says so.** The strongest theoretical objection to the thesis is that a higher wage floor does two opposite things to employment flows at once. Brochu and Green examined labour market transition rates in high versus low minimum wage regimes using aggregate Canadian data for 1979–2008, and found that higher minimum wages were associated with lower hiring rates but also with lower job separation rates [4]. Fewer workers are hired, but fewer are also let go. The net effect on the stock of employment is then the difference between two opposing flows and can plausibly be close to zero — and, importantly, the *welfare* implication is different from the thesis's framing: a world with fewer hires and fewer separations is one where the workers who hold minimum wage jobs keep them longer. A thesis that reports only the hiring side of this is reporting half the mechanism.

**The two post-2017 studies do not measure the thesis.** This is the strongest argument against, and it is a problem of external validity rather than of method. Fossati and Marchand studied Alberta, and Alberta is the outlier of the entire period: the abstract describes "an unexpectedly large increase (47%) occurring over a short time horizon (3 years)" [5]. The thesis is about provincial minimum wage increases since 2017 generally — which includes British Columbia's gradual escalator, Ontario's indexation, Quebec's and Manitoba's smaller adjustments, and provinces that barely moved. Generalising a 47% shock to a 3% indexation increase is precisely the error the elasticity literature warns against, because the size of the wage change is the main determinant of the size of the response.

Ndlovu's study has an even sharper limitation, and also provides the largest youth elasticities in the Canadian literature. Its magnitudes are not modest: a 10.9 percentage point fall in the employment rate at the age-18 threshold, implied elasticities of −0.97 with a −0.6 to −1.0 range across specifications [4]. Ndlovu argues explicitly that estimates based on general minimum wage increases understate the youth effect, because a general increase lets employers substitute cheaper young workers for older ones while an age-specific step closes that route [4]. That is a direct challenge to the "modest" framing above, and I take it seriously rather than dismissing it. The limitation is scope: the study does not estimate the effect of Alberta's general increases at all. It estimates the effect of the *age-18 step* from a $13 student rate to a $15 adult rate [4] — a discontinuity created in 2019, after the general increases were complete. The result is a genuine and well-identified finding about age-dependent minimum wages. It is not a finding about whether raising the general minimum wage in Alberta between 2015 and 2018 reduced youth employment. The study is explicit that its scope is the youth sub-minimum rate: it concludes that age-dependent minimum wages "can be an effective policy strategy for offsetting youth employment losses caused by minimum wage hikes" [4]. Read carefully, its policy implication is the reverse of the thesis's — it is an argument for carving young workers *out* of high general floors, which presupposes that the general floor is the problem, but it does not measure that problem.

**Fossati and Marchand's own regional result undercuts a national claim.** The study's headline finding is province-wide employment losses "mostly among younger workers," and it adds a regional result: employment losses in four of the five non-urban economic regions but not in the province's two main cities [5]. I should not overstate that second result — it is presented as an additional finding, not as the main one. But it matters for a national claim, because Calgary and Edmonton are where most young Albertans live and work. The most the regional result supports is that the effect was uneven within the one province studied, and that a national thesis cannot assume the Alberta effect generalises uniformly across urban and rural labour markets.

**The decline the thesis explains may have other causes, and the timing is not established here.** Here the argument moves from the minimum wage literature to the labour market as a whole, and I have to be careful: I was not able to obtain the Statistics Canada Labour Force Survey series for youth employment over 2017–2025 in this pass, so I cannot date the deterioration or say how much of it falls inside the period of large increases. That gap is flagged in Open questions rather than papered over. What can be said is structural rather than dated.

Two candidate explanations compete with the minimum wage, and one of them is arithmetic. First, demand: a general cooling of the youth labour market reduces hiring of exactly the entry-level service jobs young people take. Second, population, and this one bears directly on the measure the thesis uses. Statistics Canada defines the youth employment rate as "the number employed in that group as a percentage of the population for that group" [1]. The youth population is the denominator. When the denominator of a rate rises faster than the numerator, the rate falls even if the absolute number of young people with jobs is unchanged. *My inference, not a sourced finding:* if Canada's youth population grew faster than youth employment over this period, a substantial part of any observed fall in the youth employment rate could reflect more young people entering the population rather than any young person losing a job — which is why the case against insists on employment levels or hours, conditional on demand, rather than the raw rate.

A third channel — competition from temporary residents and international students for the same entry-level jobs — is widely discussed but I did not read the primary studies behind it, so I do not assert it here, and I make no claim about how far Canadian labour economists agree on it. If it accounts for part of any youth deterioration, the minimum wage's share of the explanation is correspondingly smaller; that conditional is all the evidence I have supports.

**The good-faith concession.** Two pieces of the case for the thesis survive the case against intact, and they should be stated rather than buried.

First, the regional pattern in Fossati and Marchand — losses in four of five non-urban regions, none in the two main cities [5] — is the *opposite* of what monopsony models predict. If employers in small markets have wage-setting power, a higher floor should raise employment there and not in competitive cities. The study finds the reverse. That pattern is more consistent with competitive labour demand than with monopsony, so the case against cannot rest on monopsony as its rescue.

Second, and more damaging to the "modest" framing: Ndlovu's elasticities of −0.6 to −1.0 [4] are youth-specific, and his argument that general-increase estimates understate youth effects is a serious one. If he is right, then the −0.27 pooled estimate is not a ceiling on the youth effect but a downward-biased average, and the case against should not treat it as the number the thesis has to beat.

So the strongest version of the case against is narrower than a claim that minimum wages do not cost jobs in theory, and it is not that the effect is small. It is this: for the specific post-2017 period, the Canadian evidence is measured in one province, at one age threshold, and — for the province-wide result — without a published decomposition that separates the wage floor from the growth in the youth population that divides the outcome measure. That is a claim about what the post-2017 evidence can bear, not a claim that the effect is absent.

### 4. 4. The crux — the measure, design or study the disagreement turns on, and what it shows so far

The disagreement does not turn on whether competitive theory predicts job losses — everyone agrees it does — nor on whether Alberta's 47% increase was large. It turns on three things that can be separated: the *elasticity*, the *measure*, and the *counterfactual*.

**Crux one: is the elasticity −0.27 or nearer −1?** This is the single number the whole dispute reduces to, and the two candidate values come from designs with different scopes.

The −0.27 figure comes from Campolieti's 2020 meta-analysis of the Canadian literature. It is a strong number of its kind for two reasons: a meta-analysis pools the Canadian studies rather than resting on one, which is what a thesis about Canada as a whole wants; and it reports no evidence of publication bias in the teenage estimates [6], so the pooled figure is not simply the product of journals preferring negative results.

The higher estimates come from age-discontinuity designs. Ndlovu reports an employment elasticity of −0.97 for the step from $13 to $15 at age 18, with a range of −0.6 to −1.0 across specifications [4]. Denmark's Kreiner and co-authors found −0.6 to −1.1 for a 40% wage increase at 18; the UK's Dickens and co-authors found a 3 to 4 percentage point employment drop when the minimum wage rises at 22 [4].

These are not competing estimates of the same quantity, and that is the crux. Ndlovu's own interpretation of the gap is the key passage: the larger elasticities for age-dependent minimum wages "suggest that previous estimates that are based on increases to the general minimum wage tend to understate the actual employment effect on youth" [4]. The mechanism he offers is substitution. Under a *general* increase, an employer facing a higher floor for everyone can replace expensive older workers with cheaper young ones, offsetting some of the youth job loss. Under an *age-specific* step, that escape route is closed at the threshold, so the full effect shows up. If that reasoning is right, −0.27 is not a central estimate of the youth effect of a general increase; it is a downward-biased one, and the truth for the affected group is closer to the age-discontinuity range.

Which is more credible depends on what the thesis is about. For the thesis as stated — *provincial general* minimum wages — the meta-analytic −0.27 is the directly applicable number, and the −0.97 is measuring a different policy instrument. The age-discontinuity studies tell us that the wage floor bites hard on the workers it binds tightly; they do not tell us the size of the effect of the general floor, because the general floor by construction allows the substitution that the age-specific floor blocks. So the crux resolves, on current evidence, in favour of a modest negative effect for the thesis as written — while warning that the modest number is an average across workers, some of whom (those near the floor, in thin markets) face a much larger effect.

**Crux two: the employment rate or the employment level?** This is where I would put the largest single source of disagreement, and it is a measurement question that neither side in the public argument addresses squarely.

Statistics Canada defines the youth employment rate as "the number employed in that group as a percentage of the population for that group" [1]. The population is the denominator. Over precisely the period the thesis concerns, Canada's youth population grew unusually fast. *My inference, from the arithmetic of the definition:* if the number of employed young people is constant while the youth population rises, the employment rate falls by construction, and no one has lost a job. A study that regresses the youth employment rate on the minimum wage during a period of rapid youth population growth will attribute to the minimum wage whatever the denominator did — unless it controls for population or uses the employment *level*, hours, or employment conditional on participation.

This cuts both ways, which is why it is the crux rather than a point for one side. If the denominator effect is large, the measured fall in the youth employment rate overstates any real reduction in youth employment, and the case against is right. But the same point implies that Fossati and Marchand's finding — built on a synthetic control in which the comparison provinces are weighted to match Alberta's *pre-period* levels — could be biased either way depending on whether Alberta's youth population diverged from its synthetic counterpart after 2015. Alberta's population grew rapidly over exactly those years. The published abstract does not say how population was handled. Until that is checked in the full text, the strongest study for the thesis carries an unquantified measurement risk on its central outcome. I flag this as an open question rather than a defect, because I have not been able to read the full paper.

**Crux three: the counterfactual for the whole country.** Neither of the two post-2017 studies estimates the effect of the Canadian provincial pattern as a whole. Fossati and Marchand give the effect of one province's 47% shock; Ndlovu gives the effect of an age threshold created after that shock. There is no study I have found that uses cross-province variation in the post-2017 increases — the natural design, since thirteen jurisdictions moved by very different amounts at very different times — to estimate a national effect. That is the study the thesis actually needs, and its absence is the main reason the verdict cannot be firmer than it is.

**A note on independence.** Three of the sources cited here — the Rybczynski and Sen panel [3], the Fossati and Marchand study [5] and Campolieti's meta-analysis [6] — were all retrieved through the same Crossref metadata service, so their separate numbering should not be read as three independent retrievals. They are independent *studies* by different authors in different journals, which is what matters for weighing them, but the weight comes from the fact that they are separate research designs on separate data, not from the retrieval.

**What the crux shows so far.** Taking the three together: the elasticity evidence favours a real but modest negative effect on youth employment for general minimum wage increases (−0.27), with larger effects on narrowly affected groups; the measurement evidence shows that the outcome most often cited, the youth employment rate, is contaminated by a fast-growing denominator in exactly this period; and the counterfactual evidence covers one province out of thirteen. The disagreement therefore turns less on economic theory than on whether the post-2017 national increase can be treated as one experiment — and the honest answer is that it cannot, because the increases were too different in size, timing and persistence for a single elasticity to describe them.

### 5. 5. What would change the conclusion — the evidence that would overturn it, and whether anyone has looked

Three kinds of evidence would move the verdict, and they are not equally difficult to obtain.

**1. A cross-province study of the post-2017 increases.** This is the study the thesis needs and, on my reading, it does not exist. The design is straightforward and the data are public: thirteen jurisdictions raised their general minimum wages by very different amounts at very different times between 2017 and 2025, which provides exactly the variation a difference-in-differences or synthetic-control panel needs. Run youth employment (and hours, and hires, and separations) on the real minimum wage relative to the provincial median, with province and year fixed effects, controls for provincial demand, and — critically — the youth population as a separate regressor so the denominator cannot drive the result. This design would produce a national elasticity for the period, and it would settle whether Alberta's 47% is representative or an outlier.

**What it would take to overturn the current verdict.** A well-identified national estimate for 2017–2025 that is statistically indistinguishable from zero, or that turns positive once the youth population is controlled for, would move the verdict from partly supported to not supported. That is a plausible outcome: the Campolieti, Gunderson and Lee finding that effects were at the lower end of earlier estimates for 1997–2008 [6] makes a null in the recent period credible.

**What it would take to confirm it strongly.** The same design, finding a negative and significant effect concentrated on teenagers (15–19) rather than on 20–24-year-olds, with the effect scaling with the size of the real increase, and with the mechanism showing up as reduced hiring rather than reduced participation. The teenage-versus-young-adult split is the key test: because a much larger share of teenagers is paid at or near the floor, an effect that appears for young adults but not teenagers would be suspicious, and an effect that appears for teenagers but not young adults would be strong corroboration.

**2. The population-denominator audit.** Someone should take Fossati and Marchand's published estimates and check how Alberta's youth population evolved relative to its synthetic control over 2015–2019, and re-estimate using employment levels and hours instead of rates. If the finding survives, the thesis's strongest evidence gets considerably stronger. If it does not, the single best study for the thesis is partly a demographic artefact. This is a modest replication exercise and I could not find that anyone has done it.

**3. A firm-side study of what employers actually did.** The thesis presumes the adjustment ran through employment. The alternatives are price pass-through, margin compression, hours reduction, turnover reduction and productivity improvement, and Brochu and Green's finding that higher floors lowered hiring *and* separations together [4] shows that at least one of these channels is active in Canada. A study using administrative payroll or firm data to decompose the response of low-wage employers to the 2017–2019 increases — how much went to prices, how much to hours, how much to headcount — would identify which margin absorbed the cost. No such Canadian study appears to exist for this period. Its absence is why the thesis and its denial can both point at aggregate youth employment and disagree.

**4. A direct test of the competing explanations.** The 2022–2025 youth labour market deterioration has at least three candidate causes — demand, temporary-resident competition, and the minimum wage — and nobody has published a decomposition that assigns shares. A shift-share design exploiting variation across provinces and industries in exposure to temporary residents, alongside variation in minimum wage bite, could separate them. Until that is done, any claim that the minimum wage caused the post-2022 youth employment decline, in either direction, is inference rather than measurement.

**Has anyone looked?** I have to be plain about the limits of this pass: my search allowance was spent before I could run targeted searches for items 1 to 4 against the agencies' and provinces' own releases, Statistics Canada tables, or recent working papers. So I cannot report these as confirmed gaps in the literature, only as gaps in what I was able to reach. What I can say is that neither of the two post-2017 Canadian studies I read cites a cross-province national estimate for the period, which is weak evidence that one had not been published when they went to press.

**The one thing that would not change the conclusion.** More studies finding negative effects in periods before 2017 would not strengthen the thesis, because the pre-2017 literature is already consistent and already summarised in Campolieti's meta-analysis [6]. The thesis is a claim about a specific period, and only evidence from that period, with a design that separates it from the period's other shocks, can settle it. Stacking more historical studies on the case for the thesis is the main way this argument is usually made badly.


## Open questions

**The study the thesis actually needs has not been found, and I could not search for it properly.** A cross-province estimate using the post-2017 variation — thirteen jurisdictions raising their floors by very different amounts at very different times — would settle the question. My search allowance was spent before I could check Statistics Canada's research series, the provinces' own releases, or recent working papers for such a study. Neither of the two post-2017 Canadian studies I read cites one, which is weak evidence it had not been published when they went to press, but that is not the same as a confirmed gap.

**Nobody has published the population-denominator check.** Fossati and Marchand's estimates are built on employment rates, whose denominator is the youth population, and Alberta's youth population grew rapidly over exactly the years in question. Whether their synthetic control matches on population, and whether the result survives re-estimation on employment levels or hours, is not answered in the abstract I read. I could not obtain the full text. Until someone runs that replication, the strongest study for the thesis carries an unquantified measurement risk on its central outcome.

**The timing of the youth deterioration is not established in this report.** I was unable to pull the Statistics Canada Labour Force Survey series for youth employment across 2017–2025, so I cannot say how much of any decline falls inside the period of large increases and how much after it. This matters: a decline concentrated in the later years, after most provinces had switched to indexation, is not well explained by the increases. Anyone continuing this work should get that series first.

**No Canadian study decomposes what employers actually did.** The thesis presumes the adjustment ran through employment. The alternatives — prices, margins, hours, turnover, productivity — are all plausible, and Brochu and Green's finding that hiring and separations both fell [4] shows at least one non-headcount channel is active. A firm-side decomposition for the 2017–2019 increases does not appear to exist in what I read.

**The competing explanations for the youth labour market are not weighted against each other.** Demand, population growth, and competition from temporary residents and international students are all candidates, and no published decomposition assigns shares. I did not read the primary studies on the temporary-resident channel, so I make no claim about its magnitude or about how far economists agree on it.

**What the evidence does not settle at all.** Whether young workers' total earnings rose or fell (a higher floor with somewhat fewer jobs can raise the wage bill); whether hours per worker fell; and whether the policy was worth it. The thesis is about employment only, and nothing here speaks to the distributional case for a higher floor, which on the wage side is well supported — Fossati and Marchand found workers moved up the wage distribution with a higher distributional reach [5].

**A note on how this report was built.** Several quotations are drawn from publisher abstracts rather than full texts, because the full texts of Fossati and Marchand and of the Crossref-indexed papers were not reachable in this pass. The abstracts state the findings and methods, but a full-text check of the regional breakdown, the population controls and the specification count would strengthen or qualify several claims above.

## Beyond this question

The methodological point generalises past minimum wages. The thesis is a claim about a period containing at least three shocks that hit young workers harder than anyone else, and the evidence available is almost entirely from before the period or from a single province within it. That is the ordinary condition of Canadian labour-market policy argument: the natural experiment exists — thirteen provinces moving at different times — but the study using it has not been done, and in its absence both sides cite historical elasticities as though they settled a contemporary question.

The measurement point is the more portable one. Any claim about a *rate* over a period when that rate's denominator moved sharply needs the denominator handled explicitly, and Canada's post-2020 population growth makes this true of a wide range of youth and low-wage labour market claims, not just this one. A youth employment rate that falls while the youth population grows 10% is a different fact from a youth employment rate that falls while the population is flat, and the two get quoted interchangeably.
